Precision measurements of the lifetimes of B^0_s mesons are crucial in understanding how consistency we can expect from different decay processes, particularly those involving quantum fluctuations that may be indicative of new physics outside the Standard Model. By studying the decay sequence B^0_s to muon pairs and identifying pairs that are not complementary (same-sign muons), we have derived a measurement of the B^0_s lifetime, specifically the delta lifetime difference, by examining data from 18.5 femtobarns of LHCb data at a 7 and 8 TeV collision energy. This value for the delta lifetime difference has been determined to be 0.1 plus or minus 0.1, in a scenario where the penguin pollution has a minimal impact. Additionally, within the same dataset, we have measured the B^0_s lifetime as 1.408 times 10 to the power of -12 seconds, with an uncertainty of 0.018 times 10 to the power of -12 seconds. Both of these measurements represent the most precise standards set by data alone, and have been confirmed by independent means.

This study offers a novel approach to addressing rough data discontinuity issues in stochastic control problems by leveraging a specific type of rough path convergence. Specifically, we demonstrate that by utilizing a rough path expansion, we can analyze the performance of a control system with a variable but convergent initial condition, ultimately leading to a well-defined and consistent optimal control outcome. This finding enables us to establish a consistent dynamic optimal control policy. Notably, we can ensure the consistency of this policy without relying on excessive regularity assumptions in the data, which is a notable advantage of our approach. To achieve this, we incorporate a rough path perspective, combining elements from the studies of Bales, Rangouy, and Stricker as well as the research of Souganidis and Delarue.

The study presents an analysis of cosmic ray anisotropy at extremely high energies, using data from Telescope Array and HiRes detectors in the TeV neutron background model. The research finds a significant anisotropic effect in the form of a dipole, with the amplitude increasing from 3.5% at 4 EeV to 15% at 300 EeV, confirming a previous study's findings. The new results also reveal a quadrupole component in the anisotropy, with a amplitude of about 2%, with a preference for the alignment of the "elf ears" with the direction of the Galactic Center. However, this finding is subject to significant statistical fluctuations and requires further confirmation.

Our research investigates the link between heavy ion collision centrality and the $N_{\rm sub}$ dependence of the nuclear modification factor $\mathcal{N}(\eta, N_{\rm sub})$ using PYTHIA 6.4 and its variant PYTHIA 6.4$+$WEP, which takes into account the effects of wake-glass detectors on charged particles. Since WEP-based calculations mirror measured data more accurately than their unscaled counterparts, this study can provide experimental teams with valuable information for interpreting future results. Additionally, our analysis explores how $N_{\rm sub}$ affects the centrality distributions of $\mathcal{N}(\eta, N_{\rm sub})$ in both cases.

Noncommutative quantum mechanics is studied to reveal its dynamical properties. The position and momentum operators are expressed in a form related to differential operators, which facilitate the transformation into a commuting momentum space. This allows the identification of noncommutative coordinates with a nonabelian nature. A harmonic oscillator example is analyzed to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, and the results are compared with the theory of momentum-dependent coordinates. Both methods yield the same results, and this agreement is validated for all orders of perturbation theory.

A cutting-edge approach combines computational modeling and machine learning to analyze cancer cells within digitized tissue sections, offering valuable insights into cancer progression, metastasis, and treatment options. By leveraging large-scale virtual screening, this method helps identify the most effective cancer therapies and predicts their efficacy based on the specific genetic characteristics of a patient's cancer. Additionally, it can determine the effectiveness of cancer vaccines and predict when cancer tumors will become aggressive and start metastasizing. Furthermore, it can estimate the ability of the immune system to fight cancer based on the presence and location of immune cells within the tumor and guide strategies for enhancing the immune system's cancer-fighting capabilities.

This research combines the Joint Weighted Detector Field Estimator (JWDFE) and Maximum Likelihood Sequence Estimator (MLSE) methods to enhance the optical communication system's ability to handle burst errors. By incorporating the JWDFE pre-processing step, the MLSE algorithm's performance is significantly improved, and burst errors are mitigated. Our research develops the JWDFE-MLSE algorithm and evaluates its effectiveness using the digital back-to-back method and real-world data signals from a 28 GBAUD polarization-mode multiplexed optical transmission system. Test results indicate that the JWDFE-MLSE algorithm exceeds the error performance of both the JWDFE-MLSE and conventional MLSE methods by at least 1.5 dB in 7-Gb/s data reception.

Our proposed TCAN accelerator utilizes a novel automatic dilation optimizer to efficiently deploy EfficientTCAN on hardware. This optimizer reduces model size by up to 2.3 times and inference latency by up to 3.3 times without degrading the high accuracy of EfficientTCAN, which maintains an F1 score of 98.5% on the 8GB dataset. The optimized ECAN exhibits comparable performance to the original ECAN, which has a score of 98.4%. The design of TCAN utilizes 16,832 memory units and achieves an overall area of 0.4mm^2, showcasing the potential for deep neural network applications. The acceleration of ECAN accelerates it 25.8 times faster than the baseline and enables real-time video recording processing in under 30ms.
This study examines the finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras in 3-dimensions over any commutative ring with characteristic not two, classifying them by their nilpotency or solvability properties.

We developed a multi-dimensional hydrodynamic model that simulates the plasma's evolution and connects it to experimental observations in smaller systems. Our goal is to explore the connection between initial condition fluctuations and the hard component, specifically in p-Pb collisions. The existing algorithm for LE-inductive and DLE-inductive correspondents, which computes a specific correspondent given a formula, has been enhanced with a new technique called ALBA. This new method, ALBA, enables the efficient calculation of all corresponding formulas of a particular type, resulting in a significant improvement in computational speed and a more efficient use of memory in comparisons to the previous method. Specifically, ALBA accelerates the computation of LE-inductive and DLE-inductive correspondents by at least 10 times and 5 times, respectively, for infinite universes, whereas for finite universes it achieves an order of magnitude improvement of at least 100 and 20 for LE-inductive and DLE-inductive correspondents, respectively. Additionally, ALBA leads to a memory reduction of at least a factor of 2.5 when computing LE-inductive correspondents and 2 for DLE-inductive correspondents, in comparisons to the existing algorithm for infinite universes, whereas for finite universes it results in a memory reduction of at least a factor of 5 and 2, respectively.

We introduce a four-valued database evaluation method based on the DLV system, aimed at enhancing consistent query answering despite data inconsistencies. This approach builds on the original three-valued approach employed by DLV, extending it to accommodate two additional values representing conflicting and unknown data. Despite the theoretical benefits of four-valued logic, our proposal retains a key aspect of the existing two-valued approach, which has proven effective in practice. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposal, we conducted a comparative analysis of consistent query answering results using both three-valued and four-valued approaches. Our findings show that the four-valued approach can provide more accurate answers, especially in scenarios with few data, although it may fail to provide answers more frequently than the three-valued approach. Additionally, our results indicate that the four-valued approach yields more consistent queries than the three-valued approach, as measured by the Koehler consistency criterion. However, our analysis also reveals that the four-valued approach may lead to increased computational costs in consistent query answering.

The proposed Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model incorporates a flexible nonlinear time-varying parameter space to capture rapid changes in a non-count time series, potentially stemming from rapid changes in underlying count time series or through external factors. Due to its adaptive nature, TV-PARX emerges as an exceptionally robust alternative for analyzing data sequences with complex dynamics and structural shifts, without relying on robustization techniques for the parameters. We have derived theoretical bounds for the consistent estimation of TV-PARX parameters using maximum likelihood estimation, in addition to establishing the asymptotic distribution for the estimation. We have also evaluated the performance of TV-PARX through numerical simulations. Furthermore, a real-world application of the model has been demonstrated through its application to analyzing escape rates from refugee populations in Germany.

The ability to learn complex manipulation tasks quickly is a key aspect of adaptive behavior. Sadly, vast amounts of demonstration data are often required to achieve this, which is impractically high for our current research standards. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called Neural Descriptor Fields, which uses a distinctive object representation to decode a compact description of the task goal. By combining this representation with a manipulation-related field, guided by a simple pairwise distance metric, we can learn to predict the desired final state of the environment from just a few demonstrations. Our approach proves to be highly versatile, integrating easily with existing policy optimization methods, and significantly improves performance when compared to baseline methods using traditional representation learning techniques. With easy experimentation setup and clear performance metrics, we showcase the effectiveness of NDF by applying it to various challenging manipulation tasks on three different platform scenarios: simulation, physical robotics, and a combination of both.

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands in the Higgs boson and top quark research areas. The SiD's calorimeter system, consisting of highly fine-grained silicon-based forward detectors and central energy measurement modules, ensures accurate energy measurement for electrons and photons. With a total energy coverage of 80% of the total solid angle, the system provides a jet energy resolution of less than 3% at 10 TeV, which is essential for top quark analysis. Additionally, the detector's ability to identify incident energies through its calorimeter system, coupled with its ability to operate at a luminosity of 10^34 cm^-2 s^-1, results in a usable top quark sample of 10^6 events per year.

An in-depth analysis of chemical compositions for 19 members in the high-metallicity cluster Tononzintla 2 has provided insights into the cluster's metallicity and abundance patterns. By analyzing multiple spectral observations, we found the metallicity to be $-0.12^{+0.05}_{-0.04}$ or $-0.24^{+0.07}$ depending on the method used, placing Tononzintla 2 among the most metal-rich globular clusters in the Milky Way. Our findings in abundance of multiple elements including oxygen, carbon, nitrogen, and iron suggest a wide range of variations among members with some stars having abundance twice as much as typical metal-rich globular cluster stars. The abundance of abundance variations in Tononzintla 2 is unique among the most metal-rich globular clusters in the Milky Way, surpassing clusters like NGC 6254, with its multiple population characteristics, and NGC 6723, with its iron abundance variation, but lacking abundance variations in abundance of elements like oxygen and carbon, often seen in inner Galactic metal-rich globular clusters with multiple populations like omega Centauri, despite having a similar metallicity to some of its members, but with a more narrow abundance variation in elements like iron, suggesting Tononzintla 2 could be a smaller analog of omega Centauri, with our findings also indicating abundance variations in elements like carbon and oxygen often seen in outer Galactic metal-rich globular clusters like TOL 1

This study examines the dependency graphs underlying formal proof archives in Coq and Isabelle, focusing on the distribution of nodes' in-degrees within these graphs. The findings show that the in-degree distribution in each archive follows a scale-free pattern, similar to many complex networks. However, upon removing the highest degree nodes (vertices with in-degrees greater than 5), the resulting networks resemble Poisson distributions. A proposed new ranking model incorporates the tendency of researchers to build upon popular results. Despite being simple, this model accurately predicts the in-degree distribution in many situations.

QCD in three dimensions has a phase transition at a critical temperature related to Euler characters. Conducting a precise analysis for the Wilson action, we explore the effects of next-to-leading lattice corrections on z_c's magnitude for N=2, N=4, and N=6, and find that for N=4 it is twice as large as for N=2, while for N=6 it is around 1.4 times as large as for N=2.

The approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm is a popular approximate inference method that is widely used and effective, especially in the analysis of its performance on complex systems and random graphs. However, the reasons behind AMP's success and limitations remain poorly understood. This study reveals a crucial connection between the targeted average-field (TAP) free energy and AMP's convergence in the $	ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem. Specifically, it is shown that AMP converges if and only if it corresponds to a local minimum of the TAP free energy. Additionally, we establish that this convergence criterion is equivalent to the event that the matrix $\mathbf{Y}^T \mathbf{W}^T \mathbf{\eta} \backslash \mathbf{\sigma}$ follows the Gaussian free noise model with a specific covariance matrix, where $\mathbf{Y}$ is the generated data matrix, $\mathbf{W}$ represents the underlying weight matrix, $\mathbf{\eta}$ denotes the transmission matrix, and $\mathbf{\sigma}$ is the diagonal matrix containing the standard deviations of the noise components. As a result, we derive the phase transition thresholds for the $	ext{Z}_2$-synchronization problem, and find that these thresholds match those of prior studies. Moreover, we examine the relationship between the TAP free energy and AMP's convergence in the general Bayesian inference framework.

Effective design tools for metasurfaces rely on microscale electromagnetic theory, which involves making assumptions and simplifying complex surface characteristics into manageable parameters. Recent advancements in Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions have provided a solid foundation for this approach. By leveraging GSTCs, researchers can create detailed analyses of general metasurface properties, now utilizing these insights, a comprehensive framework is established to facilitate simulation, numerical modeling, and data interpretation in computational electromagnetics. A unified theoretical approach is developed to accurately characterize the electromagnetic behavior at metasurface boundaries and a systematic method is proposed for extracting essential parameters from simulation results, enabling seamless integration with design algorithms. This work lays the groundwork for a unified theory to extend the applications of GSTCs to an even broader range of complex surfaces.

The described approach in the proof of the blowing-up method for orbital linearization theorems is detailed. By analyzing the original proof by B. K. Kerman and M. Reeder from 2015, we break down the process of proving orbital linearization theorems via the blowing-up method. We then provide a simplified explanation of this process, offering a more straightforward understanding of the necessary steps.

Deep learning has successfully improved various physical descriptors, including the correlation between electrons, using potential functions, despite being difficult to derive from first principles. To address this challenge, a neural network called the extended compact neural network potential (eCPNN) was developed to learn potential functions that accurately capture the electronic correlations from first-principles energies. This type of neural network is unique in using a non-periodic data representation to analyze and express the potential functions that govern the spatial relationships among electrons within different supercells, which has been shown to yield highly precise energy values for various materials systems. By leveraging the flexibility of neural networks, the eCPNN can also generate a wide range of potential functions that are currently difficult to derive from first principles, making it possible to apply this method to more comprehensive and realistic material scenarios.

A extensive arc structure, comprising multiple galaxy clusters and grouping, has been identified in the desert sky and dubbed the Giant Arc. It shares superficial similarities with the Sloan Great Wall. The Giant Arc's size, spanning approximately 1.2 billion light-years, makes it one of the largest known structures in the universe. It is notable for being relatively thin, at about half the width of the Sloan Great Wall. The Giant Arc presents an opportunity to study the distribution of Lyman-alpha forest particles within a massive wall-like structure and may provide insights into the presence of supervoids. A analysis of the forest particles within the Giant Arc shows a concentration of particles on the wall's near side and a void on the far side, confirming previous findings. The void on the far side of the Giant Arc is estimated to be about 0.8 billion light-years wide and contains a massive galaxy cluster, and a potential void the size of a galaxy group is found within the Sloan Great Wall. The distribution of forest particles within the Giant Arc is consistent with predictions from computer simulations that model gravitational growth.

Wide-field photometry encompasses a broad range of techniques that allow for the measurement of atmospheric aerosols at multiple angles of view. This approach can provide vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) estimates without the need for absolute calibration, adding a new observational capability to complementary techniques like lidar and Raman scattering spectroscopy. To illustrate the method's effectiveness, VAOD was calculated from photometric data collected at the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and the Atacama B-mode Experiment (ABE) in the Atacama Desert and also from data taken in Barrow, Alaska. These VAOD estimates were derived from VAOD and scattering angle relationships, where the range of scattering angles determined the optical depth contribution. The validity of these measurements was verified through comparisons with independent estimates from two other techniques in the Atacama and Lidar in Barrow. VAOD measurements from the ACT and ABE sites showed good agreement with independent estimates and were significant at the 3.3 sigma level. The method also yielded VAOD values for certain weather conditions in Barrow that matched lidar measurements. The method's sensitivity to VAOD variations was validated through modeling and indicated that the method could detect VAOD changes greater than 0.1 in both locations. We tackle the challenge of identifying the position and orientation of multiple objects within a complex and partially obscured environment. Our contribution involves expanding the use of projection grouping techniques from two-dimensional representations to three-dimensional representations. We design two novel algorithms that integrate 3D object models with projection grouping principles to recognize and position all visible projections of an object, regardless of whether they appear complete or fragmented. Our methods are capable of estimating the orientation and location of an object even when its projections are non-contiguous. We further develop two variants of this approach for identifying multiple objects. To evaluate our proposals, we conduct numerous experiments using real-world data, incorporating the LINEN dataset and additional datasets containing synthetic data. Our results indicate that our methods successfully recover accurate representations of objects in scenarios with both simple and complex backgrounds. Notably, our approach proves particularly effective in addressing the challenges posed by fragmented projections, a scenario that is currently poorly addressed in the field.

The peridynamic model, a nonlocal framework, has been the subject of various kernel studies including the micromechanics kernel, gradient kernel, and damage kernel. Researchers have particularly been examining the role of nonlocality in relation to crack propagation and fracture. This paper introduces a new type of kernel called the potential energy kernel, which is based on the energy released by peridynamic fields during the formation of cracks. By analyzing the microstructure, it becomes apparent that the potential energy kernel corresponds to the extension of like-osmose and van der Waals forces to nonlocal dynamics. Using this new kernel, a peridynamic model with a variable horizon was developed and demonstrated through numerical simulations and benchmark tests for predicting cracks in materials. Compared to traditional nonlocal elasticity models, the potential energy kernel produces more accurate results, particularly in scenarios involving soft materials and fragile materials with multiple cracking.

We explore an advanced version of Graphical Lasso, a widely-used sparse inverse estimation technique, by incorporating latent variables. Our study includes theoretical convergence rates for optimal algorithms and empirical evidence illustrating the method's efficacy.

To evaluate the effects of diverse numerical approaches on simulations of biomolecular systems, we employed a combination of intense computing resources and various methods for solving the NVT molecular dynamics equation of state, focusing on the alanine dipeptide as our test subject. A leading method, named BEAGLE, was utilized to compare the performance of multiple techniques, incorporating techniques such as the minimum image rule, finite size scaling, and multiple finite difference methods, as well as an implementation of the BEAGLE algorithm using GPU acceleration. Our findings revealed that the most computationally efficient algorithm, based on our BEAGLE implementation using GPU acceleration, was approximately 7 times more efficient than the fastest CPU-based method, resulting in a significant reduction in the required computing power from $10^{12}$ instructions per second to 140 GHz. Despite this change, the accuracy of the results remained unchanged, indicating that using GPU acceleration for these simulations is an acceptable approximation with no need for further correction.

Using a technique to solve the Euler equations systematically, we developed a method to simulate complex binary systems under influence from surrounding matter. By incorporating this method into our simulation, we investigated the behavior of binary black holes surrounded by a dense, pressureless medium affecting their orbits. Our analysis revealed that, regardless of the system's initial conditions, its trajectory is consistently drawn to a specific orbit - one that is controlled by the mass of the binary system and the density of the surrounding matter. The hope is that, by extending this research, it will become possible to develop a more comprehensive model for predicting the behavior of binary systems in the future. This is particularly important because such systems often provide important opportunities to study gravitational waves first-hand. The simplicity of our current model makes it easily integrable with other more complex simulations of binary black hole mergers.

We investigate a specific mechanical system consisting of a star-shaped graph with two infinitely stiff edges that connects to a flexible plate. The other edges are elastic, with the exception of one stiffer edge that connects to the plate. We study the exponential stability of a static equilibrium by developing a linearized model and applying it to determine the exponential stability of the system. Our findings demonstrate that the stability is guaranteed when the gradient operator on the slope of the edge is complete, specifically when elasticity is absent on the edge's slope. Additionally, we validate our theoretical findings by conducting numerical simulations on a practical example.

This study seeks to characterize the acoustic properties of a novel bonding agent, Stycast 1090SI, in comparison to a well-characterized polymer, PMMA. A comprehensive analysis of sound wave propagation through these materials is conducted, involving measurements of acoustic impedance, absorption, and scattering, as well as spectroscopic analysis of PMMA. A comprehensive evaluation of sound wave propagation through these materials is presented, showcasing the implications for clinical applications, particularly ultrasound imaging, and revealing that Stycast 1090SI exhibits distinct acoustic characteristics which differ significantly from PMMA. Notably, Stycast 1090SI displays reduced acoustic impedance and scattering, along with increased sound absorption, which are crucial factors affecting ultrasound image formation. In order to inform researchers planning similar experiments, the advantages of using PMMA as a reference material are highlighted, along with the benefits of using highly homogeneous materials such as PMMA and Stycast 1090SI.

In complex multilayer networks, multiple interconnected layers represent the fundamental structure for exploring various systems, including electrical circuits, social relationships, and biological tissues. When analyzing these networks, assignment tasks or flow computations can lead to intriguing inquiries about node centralities or importance, which typically involve interpreting results within specific layers. However, these calculations usually overlook the inter-layer connections, which often contain critical information for understanding the networks' global dynamics. This limitation sparks the inquiry as to whether the definition of node importance is isolated to specific layers or if it holds broader implications across the network. To address this, we propose a novel framework for determining node importance that considers the intra- and inter-layer dynamics. This approach results in the derivation of a centrality measure that can be computed efficiently using a decentralized method. To further illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, a numerical example and an experimental simulation are provided to demonstrate its applicability and superiority over existing measures.

The color-dependent point-spread function (PSF) causes color distortion in digital cameras, impacting their ability to take clear images. This phenomenon arises from the difference in wavelength of various color channels and the camera's optical and sensor characteristics. A mathematical model developed previously describes the color-dependent PSF in optical imaging systems. This model's application is demonstrated with a hypothetical camera system, resulting in a $480\times 648$ image matrix with three color channels. A generated synthetic image incorporates the color-dependent PSF, leading to a restoration of the original image using the Wiener filter. This method's effectiveness depends on the accuracy of the PSF, which can be determined through measurement, calculation, or a combination of both. Alternatively, the model can be used to predict the PSF based on the camera's optical and sensor characteristics. Regardless of the approach chosen, the model can be utilized to estimate the PSF.

A recent study has shown that a complex spacetime corresponding to the $R$-Minkowski spacetime can be analytically continued to the de Sitter spacetime. This analytical continuation allows for the mass parameter $R$ to be expressed in terms of the de Sitter spacetime's radius $L$, as $R$ equals $L$ minus the mass parameter $m$. Conversely, setting $R$ equal to the mass parameter $m$ results in the de Sitter spacetime being able to be analytically continued to the $R$-Minkowski spacetime. As a result, the mass parameter $R$ can be interpreted as a mass in the Dirac equation in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, also applying to the conformally flat spacetime represented by the Einstein static universe.

The 'cdt' package offers a causal graph modeling framework that incorporates structural equation modeling, graphical models, and time series analysis through Causal Dynamic Systems. This implementation provides access to popular software tools like RStan, R2jags, and Rjags for Bayesian estimation via MCMC methods. The package facilitates estimation and prediction within this causal framework using various models such as CDS for discrete variables, continuous outcomes with correlation between variables, and an extension of CDS for seasonal time series. Additionally, 'cdt' offers functions for analyzing intervention effects through the CDS model.

This paper offers a detailed analysis of the surface seal interaction with a moving cavity using a novel moving mesh method. We develop a non-overlapping interaction boundary technique to efficiently handle the complex behavior of the seal-cavity interface. A specially designed mesh is created to accurately capture the moving cavity boundary and the developed method is applied to investigate the surface seal dynamics. We study the impact of increasing speed on the pressure within the cavity and its effect on the seal surface, and further examine how the behavior of the surface and the flow within the cavity change as the speed increases. Validation of the method is conducted through comparison with existing studies of moving cavity tests.

Following the premise of Witten's correlation function formula, we have derived an analytical expression for the entropy of charged black holes in Einstein gravity theories coupled with a scalar field, using a conformal field theory perspective. The entropy calculation is validated for both asymptotically AdS and asymptotically flat spacetimes. The Witten effect is then generalized to include the entropy of multiple charged states, and we demonstrate that it is aligned with the concept of non-abelian Chern-Simons theory. The entropy formula also reveals the spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity, which is expressed in terms of the conformal field theory's particle spectrum. Notably, the generalized Witten effect holds for both deformed and undistorted entropy formulas.

Once an operating system is developed, its underlying framework typically remains static throughout a device's lifespan. This concept is now applied to a typical operating system like Android and iOS, which are modified to remain consistent with their original design. A novel approach called OctopOS proposes a system where an operating system can shift between multiple modes to achieve optimal performance in various applications. This might involve changing the security features to protect sensitive information or optimizing energy efficiency. We envision OctopOS being useful for powering next-generation smartphones that run various applications requiring different levels of security and efficiency, such as a single device capable of either secure financial transactions or efficient gaming. Our research involves developing a module called OS-Mode Switcher, which allows us to easily transition between different operating system modes, each with its own performance characteristics, by switching between various device modes. This is done without compromising the security of sensitive information and without requiring modifications to the operating system itself. We also created a prototype of OctopOS for a real-life setting, based on a Raspberry Pi device, to demonstrate the effectiveness of his method. Finally, we discuss potential future improvements and innovations that could take advantage of OctopOS's mode-switching capability.

We investigate a critical challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) where an agent is subjected to misleading data resulting from external interference. A new algorithm is devised for responding to this threat, ensuring the agent remains resilient. Theoretical guarantees are provided for the algorithm's effectiveness, demonstrating that it can achieve a learning rate similar to that of the policy gradient method under ideal conditions. The algorithm learns at a rate of $\sqrt{K}/\sqrt{t}$ for the expected reward, and with episode complexity $O(\sqrt{K})$ for bandit RL. The result can be applied to offline learning by leveraging the diversity of trajectories. A simpler algorithm is also proposed for the case when the proportion of corrupted data is known. The methods are evaluated on multiple RL benchmarks, yielding comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/heng6xu/filtpg.

The classic Box Game Paradox has a straightforward solution that involves the element of choice. However, the issue becomes more complex when the number of boxes increases to an uncountable amount, as in the case presented in this paper. Our analysis involves modifying the element of choice to accommodate a certain type of larger set, specifically the set of all real numbers. This modified element of choice is used to arrive at a solution to the paradox in the context of uncountable boxes.

We employ ab initio density functional theory to examine the properties of cubanite, a key component of uraninite tailings that has a complex electronic structure. Our analysis indicates that its stable charge state and ferromagnetic behavior can be explained by the presence of partially filled bands that resist changes in charge and contribute to magnetic ordering through exchange interactions. Additionally, the unique electronic structure of cubanite may contribute to the retention of uranium in uraninite and other phases, and its potential to facilitate chemical reactions makes it worthy of further study.

We investigate a semiconductor quantum dot coupled to two acoustic cavities, where the interaction between the quantum dot and one cavity is strong enough to create Rabi oscillations. The driving laser for the quantum dot is tuned to a specific frequency that matches the energy difference between the Rabi states. However, due to a slight variation in the driving frequency caused by laser vibration, the expected coherent transition between Rabi states is impaired. Our findings show that by adjusting the driving frequency to match the cavity's coupling frequency with the quantum dot, we can restore coherent transition between Rabi states. Additionally, we observe that adjusting the driving frequency to match the energy difference between the Rabi states can significantly impact the absorption of a coherent light pulse. Depending on the initial state of the system, we may enhance or reduce the absorption by adjusting the driving frequency. Finally, we propose using the drive frequency as a new means of controlling the absorption of coherent light in quantum dot-coupled acoustic cavity systems.

We examine a one-dimensional Guglielmi-Hennebert Hamiltonian with competing nearest-neighbor interactions that alternate in direction, representing a herringbone lattice. Our analysis applies a continuous and continuous-discrete duality transformation to transform the model into a form suitable for finite-temperature phase diagram analysis. We investigate the effects of different perturbations on the lattice's properties by applying this transformation and examining the resulting Hamiltonian's behavior at finite temperatures.

Single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be produced via two approaches: beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. Our research compares the catalyzed states achieved through these methods, focusing on their probability of creation and associated quantum entanglement properties. We found that SPCCSs generated using a beam splitter model exhibit significantly higher success probabilities than their counterpart produced with a parametric amplifier, directly contributing to the quantum interferences that characterize the catalyzed states. Consequently, the quantum entanglement in the SPCCSs produced with the beam splitter model is both more persistent and stronger than that generated with the parametric amplifier. Furthermore, we proposed an optical experiment to create these states and demonstrated the superiority of the beam splitter model in such a scenario.

The Newman-Penrose formalism is a highly effective framework for analyzing Einstein's field equations in general relativity. However, this method's usefulness is significantly tempered by the complexity of the equations' solutions due to the large number of unknowns involved, which are described by numerous differential equations. Despite the simplicity and clarity of the formalism's principles, its execution is masked by a dense notation, making it difficult to visualize the relationship between the conformal gravity coefficients and the physical parameters of a spacetime. We demonstrate that by employing a specific redefinition of the Weyl coefficients from the Newman-Penrose formalism, which are typically expressed as complex quantities, we can transform them into real values that reflect the actual characteristics of the spacetime. We then establish the equivalent forms of various well-known spacetimes' Weyl coefficients using this new definition.

In our proposed approach, we deviate from the conventional strategy of describing polymers as a collection of monomers. Instead, we establish a probability distribution that directly defines the distribution of polymer properties. This approach allows us to represent a polymer as a random variable with a specific probability density, independent of its constitutional units. By inferring this probability density from available data, we can establish a non-parametric relationship between the polymer structure and its properties. This relationship can then be utilized to predict properties for novel, unobserved polymers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method using a simple simulation and an analysis of actual data on the melting points of semicrystalline polymers.

During mass casualty events, it is not uncommon for multiple patients to require ventilatory support, leading to a critical shortage of ventilators. To address this issue, we propose an optimization approach that recycles expired air from patients being ventilated, using a single ventilator for up to four patients. By applying this method, we demonstrate the potential to provide each patient with their desired tidal volume using only two ventilator cycles. Additionally, we examine the efficacy of this approach through computational simulations and find that it can significantly reduce ventilator usage, even in scenarios with breathing patterns differing greatly from each other's.

Recently, Attention Unet has been successfully applied to esophageal tumor segmentation, yet it still faces challenges such as model complexity and external data reliance. To address this, a modified model called Dilated Dense Attention Unet is proposed, combining attention mechanisms with spatially expanded convolution layers for improved performance and efficiency. The new model utilizes dense connections between blocks to facilitate efficient propagation of detailed information and relies solely on internal learning without external support. The evaluation of the proposed method on a real esophageal tumor segmentation scenario shows a balanced achievement of high accuracy, low complexity, and self-learning ability. The proposed model demonstrates a precise segmentation outcome, with a segmentation accuracy rate of 78.51%, a Dice coefficient of 0.7851, and a model complexity of 0.079.

The primary objective of evaluating a well bore involves estimating the resistivity of layers based on electrical conduction measurements. This estimation must be performed rapidly to guide drilling operations and typically requires a comprehensive neural network model that needs significant data and time to train. We propose an alternative approach, known as RML-EnRML (Model-Specific Neural Network), which incorporates an optimized neural network that can be trained quickly using a limited amount of data and efficiently evaluates well bore performances in real-time. Computational simulations demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current industry standards in terms of production and computation time. Additionally, the model excels in accuracy when compared to other rapid methods and even performs better than complex deep learning methods that require extensive training data.

This study is the first to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of corpus-level information on neural named entity recognition models. Our findings show that neural NER models benefit significantly from corpus-level information, with improvements of over 5% in F1 score in the best case. We also investigate the effectiveness of using corpus-level information for NER at different entity types and find that the benefit varies depending on the type, with the largest improvement being 11.6% F1 score for certain types. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that there are multiple effective approaches to incorporating corpus-level information, with the simplest technique of concatenating corpus-level features to entity mentions yielding a score of over 80% F1. We examine the implications of these findings for the design of neural NER models and suggest areas for future research. All of our models' results are available on the Neural N2Clf GitHub page.

We analyze how the position of twisting edges in the tropicalization of a geometric object affects the geometric object itself. We use this analysis to show that many classical results on rational curves, particularly those involving bitangents to plane curves, rely heavily on the assumption of avoiding edge twisting. As a primary example, we prove that for a smooth plane quartic defined over a non-hyperelliptic curve, having the property that its geometric object has no edge twisting is not a requirement for it to be rationally connected.

The ideal model assumes perfect sensor information and ideal message transmission, yet real-world implementations are influenced by factors such as sensor calibration and data transmission errors. To address this disparity, we design an efficient localization algorithm for a specific scenario and then develop a simulated environment to evaluate its performance. In this context, the algorithm's effectiveness is assessed under ideal conditions and compared to a more rigorous simulation that takes into account the mentioned limitations, resulting in a 1.5 times increase in average localization error.

Language technology has a vast potential to contribute greatly to society, especially in communities where multiple languages are spoken. To build more effective language models, it's essential to have a large, diverse dataset that includes material in several languages. Typically, NLP applications are developed for a single language, but we propose a framework that enables the generation of monolingual embeddings for multiple languages from the same mixed-language dataset. We evaluate this approach using a dataset of paraphrased sentences in three languages – English, French, and Spanish – and demonstrate that our method can create accurate embeddings for each language individually, even when the training data contains labeled language information. We show that our method surpasses alternative techniques in low-fi settings without the need for a parallel corpus, a crucial advantage for languages with limited available data.

The current state of image description guidelines is inadequate, mainly affecting visually impaired users who rely on these descriptions. To rectify this issue, we propose a set of new guidelines centered on visual experience, which are adaptable to various description purposes and styles. Our guidelines encompass three key components: what to include, how to present it, and the desired tone. To ensure these guidelines are effective, we provide a framework for evaluating description quality, which involves both automated methods using style and quality assessment tools and human-driven testing. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to multiple description applications, including alt text for images in articles, dialogue descriptions in TV shows, and audio descriptions in movies and video games.

To accurately model the energy loss functions of tantalum oxides, we incorporate local field corrections and spin-orbit coupling, using the $k$$\cdot$p method for this task. By including these factors, we obtain more precise results, especially in the upper band of the tantalum oxides. Next, we investigate how interactions with electrons from oxygen and vacuum modify the tantalum d bands, demonstrating that they form a narrow energy range close to the Fermi level. This analysis is relevant to understanding the taenioite phase in tantalum oxide, obtained through experiments using soft x-ray spectroscopy.

Our research examines the impact of a notable demographic shift, known as "The Big Sort," on the spread of online misinformation. Inspired by Paul Lindquist's theoretical concepts, we develop and test an empirical model, which focuses on the correlation between growing social distancing and online confirmation bias. Utilizing Google Trends data and geographic election data from the 2016 US presidential election, we found significant evidence to support our hypothesis. As areas that voted for Donald Trump or Hillary Clinton became more geographically isolated, online searches for conflicting information decreased. Moreover, Google Trends data revealed that searches for information confirming users' existing views intensified during the election campaign, especially in highly sorted areas. These findings highlight the potential for online platforms to exacerbate the spread of online misinformation in areas with significant social distancing.

Resource-constrained organizations can't afford to utilize sophisticated machine learning techniques due to their computational demands or the cost of annotating large datasets. Moreover, providing accurate real-time feedback to users through online learning is complicated because it requires simultaneous dataset annotation and model training. To address these challenges, we develop Feedback-Agnostic Online Machine Learning (FA-OLM), a framework that enables the efficient deployment of advanced online learning algorithms, even in real-time, without needing model parameters to differ significantly from optimal. FA-OLM achieves this by introducing a new algorithm, called Hyperband OLO, that incorporates a robust method for managing risks during online learning, adapting to changing difficulty levels, and maintaining the consistency of confidence intervals. Hyperband OLO is then combined with alternative methods that can handle streaming data, robust online loss minimization, and adaptive sampling. Our research demonstrates that FA-OLM can effectively support the development of new machine learning applications by providing a robust online learning framework that can handle complex, unpredictable data streams.

The way people speak during learning activities changes significantly based on the type of demonstration, instruction type, task complexity, and error type, which complicates the task of developing intelligent systems that can learn from verbal feedback. For instance, visual demonstrations and oral instructions may lead to descriptive language, while tasks with multiple steps might result in more abstract language, and making a mistake could cause negative emotions to be expressed. To explore and mitigate these variations and their effects on the underlying semantic structure of speech, a systematic variation of speech patterns is observed during learning processes where learners are correcting mistakes made by robotic arms. This research extends the capability of speech recognition systems to accurately identify a wider range of semantic concepts in speech, even in situations where the speech patterns vary significantly. Unlike traditional approaches that focus on recognizing specific words or sounds, this research uses a more advanced deep learning technique called semantic vector embedding to analyze the underlying semantic structures of speech. The results show that speech recognition systems can be highly robust and versatile when dealing with various demonstrations, instructions, task complexities, and error types, without requiring any prior knowledge of the demonstration, instruction, task, or error type.

This research introduces an innovative algorithm to generate ordered trees of predetermined shapes, alongside specified degree sequences. The novel aspect of the algorithm lies in its flexible management of outdegrees, enabling either random selection or fixed specification. The algorithm is composed of two key components: first, generating the structure of the tree and identifying its nodes; second, assigning labels to the nodes based on a given order. The algorithm can handle both uniform and non-uniform distributions of tree shapes, and can also accommodate specifications of outdegrees for specific nodes. The proposed method can be applied to the generation of ordered trees in various contexts, and has been particularly utilized in the construction of phylogenetic trees.

A novel geometric gradient flow is introduced to minimize a comprehensive energy functional across the space of smooth mappings from a manifold to a geometric structure. The gradient flow is rigorously defined through a system of Euler-Arnold equations and accurately represents the heat flow on geometric structures, particularly Hermitian metrics and Dirac operators. This research is significant in quantum field theory, where it helps to overcome an obstruction and provides a meaningful definition for the Chern-Simons action on geometric structures.

The rise of conversational systems demands efficient testing techniques, but their automated frameworks pose technical difficulties due to unpredictable user interactions and a vast number of possible pathway combinations. To address this challenge, we introduce Conquer, a approach that redefines testing as a planning task to overcome these obstacles. By modeling user inputs as actions that influence system state and goal definitions, we leverage planning algorithms to generate comprehensive test suites that maximize critical aspects of the system, such as user engagement. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to multiple types of applications, including dialog systems, with notable improvements in test coverage and efficiency, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods by up to 300\%.

Using existing gravitational wave data from the LIGO detectors at Hanford and Livingston, we've developed a new method to identify the influence of unknown massive objects on gravitational waves. This technique yields the effect of an unseen earth-mass object at approximately 90% of the sky's coverage, with a detection distance of about 200,000 light-years. Shifting the confidence level to 50%, the detection distance increases to about 300,000 light-years. This method may have implications for searching for massive objects in relation to gravitational waves produced by binary black hole mergers.

By utilizing a cross-lingual memory retriever, this method allows for the translation of monolingual sentences into target languages by leveraging sentence embeddings in multiple source languages. In comparison to traditional bilingual translation memory approaches, this method enables the inclusion of an infinite number of potential source languages, rather than being limited to just two. As a result, this method achieves better translation performance than baseline methods, even when only using monolingual data. Additionally, it was found that the cross-lingual memory retriever could translate difficult monolingual sentences better than sentences with clearer meaning. Furthermore, this approach outperformed a strategy that used language-specific encoders to translate text, while demonstrating linguistic resource independence and the ability to handle long monolingual sentences.

Recent research suggests that Hawking points and low-variance circles, defined by specific properties in the CMB, may be detectable with current technology. However, the associated statistical significance is heavily influenced by specific patterns found in the CMB and needs to be reevaluated in the presence of cosmological anomalies. By incorporating the effects of gravitational waves on the CMB and considering a more comprehensive set of configurations for Hawking points and low-variance circles, we find that their statistical significance is actually increased when certain CMB anomalies are taken into account. Specifically, we find that Hawking points become more noticeable (p-value < 0.01) when assuming a multivariate distribution and considering a wider range of configurations. On the other hand, the presence of gravitational waves and additional scenarios for Hawking points and low-variance circles do not significantly impact their detectability.

This work builds upon previous research by R. V. Chelsea and Y. Wang regarding the Yamabe flow's solvability in a higher-dimensional setting. The described approach and obtained results are similar to those found in the mentioned study. However, the presented analysis employs a more flexible argument to demonstrate the existence of solutions in higher dimensions, specifically beyond the 5-dimensional threshold.

To enhance robustness in few-shot learning, our proposed method, called the Variable Memory Vector (VMV), incorporates an effective outlier prevention framework. VMV divides the learning process into two phases: an initial phase where the model obtains an estimate of the mean and incorporates a memory vector, and a subsequent refinement phase where the model uses both vectors to achieve optimal results. By leveraging these two vectors, VMV ensures that outlier samples have a minimal impact on the learning process. We demonstrate the advantages of VME by evaluating the method across five datasets for the tasks of text classification and image classification. The experimental results show that our proposed method achieves superior performance compared to a range of baseline models, including both traditional few-shot learning methods and networks equipped with memory mechanisms.

Recently, the attention mechanism has been successfully applied in deep recommendation systems, successfully capturing user preferences. Nonetheless, the reliability of these methods heavily counts on accurate feature extraction from the embedding layer. They frequently fail to consider the diversity of user interests, leading to a limited capacity for handling novel aspects. To address this issue, we propose the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, a highly adaptable and transparent module for enhancing user preferences. This module is seamlessly integratable into existing networks through a dual-layer mechanism. It encompasses a self-enrichment component and a collaborative component. The self-enrichment component is designed to intensify preferences for established aspects, whereas the collaborative component is designed to identify and enrich preferences for novel aspects. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed GAPE module, we integrate it into Graph-based Deep Recommendation Network (GDN) and conduct extensive experiments on two real-world datasets. The results indicate that GAPE delivers superior performance over state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, an in-depth analysis of the empirical results provides strong evidence for the versatility and robustness of the proposed GAPE module.

Exotic cones, which include narcissus cones and M-cones, are unique geometric structures used to optimize certain problems. These cones can be viewed as a combination of a traditional cone and an outer cone, making them useful for modeling complex non-tightened conditions. For certain problems, an exotic cone formulation may be more natural and easier to derive than an extended formulation based on a traditional cone. Despite their complexity, exotic cones still retain the essential properties of a cone, which makes them applicable to a broad range of optimization problems. In particular, we explore whether the success of extended formulation can be extended to exotic formulation in the context of polynomial optimization with sparse constraints. Our research reveals that both types of formulation can yield similar efficiency in solving certain problems, but this efficiency may vary significantly depending on the sparsity of the underlying problem.

The primary goal of our research is to examine the impact of using tailored training datasets with varying content on medical image modulation techniques. We developed a set of neural network generators capable of producing high-quality MRI images from raw input data, such as coarse images and patient-specific modalities. Notably, these generators can also create novel MRI images based on semantical descriptions. We evaluated our approach using three complex datasets obtained from public sources. Notably, our results revealed that using tailored training datasets with specific patient characteristics significantly improves performance. Specifically, using a dataset composed of 25 different datasets without pathologies yielded better results than using a dataset with various pathologies. Additionally, our model performed better on unseen MRI data when the training dataset consisted of images with varying poses and expressions.

This paper introduces a framework for network-based multi-agent optimization issues that is broad in scope. It categorizes several significant problems within this framework, including submodular maximization, set covering, and k-set partitioning. To address these challenges, we develop a plain and efficient algorithm for single-commodity flow-based network problems. Our approach is versatile and applicable to various network-based multi-agent optimization applications. Additionally, we offer a detailed analysis of the optimality conditions and a concise representation of the framework in mathematical terms. To facilitate practical implementation, we provide an outline of key concepts, including problem-type classifications, problem instances, and solution methodologies. Lastly, we summarize the theoretical properties of the proposed algorithm and its computational advantages.

We introduced a file system optimized for NUMA architecture, called NOVA-relaxed NFS, in a previous study. It effectively minimized data migration and unnecessary memory copies. However, our initial investigation only assessed the benefits of optimizing memory access and did not analyze the impact of persistent memory (PM) optimizations. This research extends NOVA-relaxed NFS to support multiple Optane DC Persistent Memory Modules (PMMs) and examines the consequences of small, persistent writes on application performance. Our findings reveal that even though PMs are optimized for low overhead in persistent operations, the NOVA-relaxed NFS approach leads to substantial improvements. We observed a significant performance gain of up to 139% in our benchmark suite, which suggests that the benefits of optimizing memory access are not confined to applications with large persistent writes.

The Motivation Dynamics framework, a theoretical approach to studying social interactions, is expanded upon in this study to explore relationships between agents that converge to a common point other than their individual goals. A specific model is analyzed, with its stability properties investigated, and findings are applied to a broader context involving multiple agents that share a target point. A particular scenario, where agents exhibit a rendezvous behavior, can be better understood through this extension, and a related algorithm is proven effective in optimizing performance.

We investigated the interplay between electron localization and magnetic order in Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds using X-ray diffraction, electron localizability, and neutron scattering. Found to be approximately 1.2, the average number of electrons per atom is the same for all $x$ values, eliminating the need for a versus experiment. In these materials, increasing Cm composition leads to an enhancement of magnetic moment from 0.53$\mu_B$ to 0.76$\mu_B$, and eventually, for $x=0.8$, a transition to an antiferromagnetic long-range order occurs. Our findings suggest that the increase in magnetic moment results from a decrease in hybridization between Cm and Sn atoms, and that this transition may be understood in the context of the lattice degree of freedom and electron localization, where the interplay between two localized states gives rise to a long-range order state that is not captured by mean-field theories.

A comprehensive examination of heavy quark physics within QCD has been conducted,
exploring the interactions of heavy quarks and the particles they form, known as heavy
quark systems, which comprise mesons consisting of a heavy quark and a lighter antiquark
or four-heavy-quark systems. This study gathers relevant theoretical information from
heavy quark effective theory, combining it with the principles of heavy quark symmetry
and the heavy quark mass hierarchy to provide a comprehensive understanding. It also
includes a review of current experimental knowledge from the LHC and its various detectors
and anticipated future research at proposed future colliders. Finally, it discusses the
criteria and methods for determining the spectral parameters of heavy quark systems.

For the finite classical Coxeter group Bn, we establish detailed exchange laws for a generalized standard basis of its polynomial ring, building on earlier work which verified the validity of these laws for a specific standardized basis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the exchanges laws can be expressed in a manner that relies on the Coxeter length and descent set of a particular type, and that this formulation distinguishes between various standardized elements based on their position within this structure.

Theoretical predictions regarding cosmic events such as gravitational waves, high-energy gamma-ray signals, and missing mass may be confirmed through the study of galactic halo constituents. To better understand these cosmic events, their associated parameters including the cross-sectional area, radiation pattern, energy spectrum, and particle mass need to be constrained. The search for these parameters is carried out within the Earth's gravitational field by utilizing particle physics techniques such as time-of-flight measurement, velocity distribution analysis, and energy spectrum examination. The study is performed with both direct and indirect detection techniques at particle physics experiments operating under shallow depths, and the results show that only velocity distribution and energy spectrum can be constrained depending on the detection method. The most precise velocity distribution constraint is achieved with the time-of-flight measurement in deep laboratory experiments, whereas the most precise energy spectrum constraint is achieved with shallow laboratory experiments and moon and star based indirect detection experiments.

This study introduces a novel paradigm for stochastic analysis that is centered on a refined understanding of mathematical spaces. The established framework primarily draws upon basic notions from sublinear expectations and utilizes concepts like the Choquet integral to determine expectations in a polynomial form. The theory seeks to establish a simple, consistent approach to calculating expectations and stochastic integrals within the established context. The discussion is conducted entirely within the space of continuous functions, which serves as a fundamental structure for our theory. The associated stochastic calculus is an extension of the classical Itô calculus, and it encompasses sublinear versions of Itô's lemma and a formula for quadratic variation. The paper also explores the relationship between its own definitions and other existing approaches to stochastic analysis.

We investigate the optical properties of T centre ensembles in diamond to better understand their potential applications in quantum technology. Our analysis focuses on the unique spectral characteristics of T centres, specifically their distribution of optical transitions, and how they transform under a Vickers diamond window. We also explore how these optical properties are affected by the presence of a metal coating, and what implications this has for using diamond T centres in quantum communication. Additionally, we examine the influence of photoionization on the optical properties of T centres within a laser beam.

This research presents a novel, advanced method for identifying tumors in X-ray images, incorporating a combination of morphological analysis and region growth. The proposed approach combines multiple techniques to enhance tumor detection accuracy and minimize false positives. Initially, morphological tools are used to eliminate pulmonary lung regions, followed by the application of Region Growing Technique to identify tumor areas. To further validate the method's effectiveness, several variants are tested using different imaging modalals and region growing methods, including Simple Region Growing, Border Growing, and Hybrid Growing. The developed algorithm is implemented using MATLAB and its accuracy is measured by executing it on various lung X-ray images, along with real tumor marker data. The results indicate that the proposed method can achieve a high degree of accuracy in tumor detection.

This study explores the relationship between degenerate Bernoulli numbers, circulant matrices that contain Bernoulli polynomials, and Galois fields that share the same characteristic as the Bernoulli numbers. We establish a specific formula for calculating k-degenerate Bernoulli numbers by integrating circulant matrices, and we demonstrate that these numbers are extensive when the characteristic of the Galois field is two. Additionally, we prove that (k,p)-Euler numbers can be derived from the determinant of a p-circulant matrix with components (p-1)/2, and we express these numbers as mod p-gamma vectors. Furthermore, we identify a relationship between (k,p)-Euler numbers and mod p-gamma polynomials, and we find that the latter corresponds to the image of x^k under the Frobenius endomorphism.

We employ a randomized approach to select lines from spectroscopic line lists,
specifically from the DELS line list, to identify optimal combinations for minimizing
radial velocity jitter. Typically, existing strategies employ parametric techniques to
compile a optimal line list; however, our grid-based evaluation indicates that a
randomly chosen subset of lines exhibits substantially lower jitter levels than the
most precise parametric models. Whereas previous studies select the best-performing
lines using analytical models and incorporate jitter models with limited scope, we
conduct a comprehensive examination of various spectral features and employ a sophisticated
model of random fluctuations to determine the optimal line list. Our final suggestion
includes the most effective lines to employ and provides a criterion for assessing the
adequacy of line lists, thereby facilitating the selection of the most suitable line
list for specific stellar types.

This research proposal is centered on addressing the hidden terminal problem in wireless sensor networks by introducing a novel protocol called Hierarchical Range Sectoring. We first present a mathematical model to analyze HRS's performance, specifically focusing on how it optimizes range sector sizes to minimize hidden terminals and their resulting retransmissions. We then develop an efficient algorithm to achieve optimal sector sizes and conduct simulations to validate our model and test the HRS protocol. Results show that HRS effectively reduces hidden terminals and retransmissions, leading to an overall increase in network throughput.

Context-dependent object detection is a versatile object detection approach that
varies based on target objects and application contexts. This method combines the
strengths of category-agnostic and fully-faithful object detection. While it has
been effectively implemented through context-dependent object detection networks, 
the selection of the object detector remains an unsolved issue. In this study, we
propose a normative object detector selection framework based on object and
context characteristics. Additionally, we introduce an adaptive context-dependent
object detection framework that is both scalable and efficient. This approach uses
multiple object detectors with distinct targets and optimizes the activation of 
each detector based on the identified characteristics. Our method was evaluated using
the MS-COCO dataset and achieved superior performance compared to existing methods. The
code for this project has been made available on GitHub at the specified URL.

This paper explores the existence issue for a given elliptic system of equations involving the critical Sobolev exponent, under a specific, new-type function behavior definition. The existing approach, which relies on the Morrell's theorem, is expanded to address this new-type function behavior. Additionally, an investigation into the properties of a particular function reveals that the associated integral inequality does not hold when the function in question exhibits an odd-type behavior. To address this limitation, a new approach is proposed, based on an alternative definition of the Poincare inequality, to provide the necessary conditions for the existence of solutions to the given elliptic system of equations.

We establish new concentration inequalities for the sum of independent Bernoulli variables, given their total sum. These results are key in our analysis of the distribution of independent Bernoulli variables with a specific success probability, particularly in scenarios where this probability is near 1 or 0. Some notable derivations include: given $\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = m$, where $X_i$ are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability $p$, we can bound the probability $|\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(X_i) - \mathbb{E}[\sum_{i=1}^n p_i(X_i)]| \ge \lambda m^{\frac{1-\alpha}{2}} \sqrt{n}$ for any convex function $f$ with $|f(x)-f(y)| \le K|x-y|$ for all $x,y$ and any $\alpha \in (0,1)$; and the probability $|\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^k(X_i) - \mathbb{E}[\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^k(X_i)]| \ge \lambda \sqrt{n}$ for any even integer $k \ge 2$, where $\lambda$ is a function of $n$, $k$, and $p$. These results can be applied to model counter-examples and yield better bounds for the probability of the difference between the sum of

Let's consider a Noetherian, finite-dimensional scheme $X$ over the integers, along with its perfect closure $\widetilde{X}$, obtained by extending the field of integers to its Witt vector counterpart. We establish an intriguing connection between the torsion crystalline cohomology of $X$ and its torsion étale cohomology $\widetilde{X}$, mapping the latter to the former. This relationship holds for higher cohomology groups and can be viewed as a version of the Beilinson's conjecture on higher vertical versus horizontal cohomology.

To gain insight into the behavior of the dihadron fragmentation function, especially its dependence on the relative azimuthal angle $\Delta \phi$, it is essential to quantify the $\cos \theta_R$ asymmetry in single-hadron production accompanying dihadron production. This asymmetry is sensitive to $\Delta \phi$ and is not correlated with other observable quantities. We have measured this asymmetry in $e^+ e^-$ collisions at a center of mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 30.28$ GeV, using the FAIR storage ring and its future experiments, specifically the PANDA experiment, which will provide significantly improved precision. These measurements will significantly aid in testing the consistency of various theoretical models that describe the dihadron fragmentation process.

In this work, we've developed a novel perspective on the Fock spacetime transformation using the concept of invariant length, which results in a simplified expression and highlights the relationship between the spacetime and the symplectic structure. This understanding leads to an interesting observation: the invariant length represents the surface volume in the phase space, which remains constant over time in a stable harmonic oscillator. Additionally, this framework enables the visualization of spacetime as a hyperboloid in a four-dimensional vector space, which provides a geometric representation of the spacetime metric and the symplectic structure.

The number of conjugacy classes in a group can be determined by analyzing the irreducible components of conjugacy classes, along with their associated weights. Spitzer established a systematic approach to achieve this counting method. This study extends his findings to the symplectic group Sp2n(q) by identifying all conjugacy classes and their weights. The system of invariants employed encompasses two types of forms: quadratic forms with a specific dimension and symmetric matrices that can be expressed as the product of two non-singular matrices. By utilizing this framework, we can derive the total number of conjugacy classes, as well as the number of Ramanujan duals within the irreducible representations of the finite symplectic group Sp2n(q).

Personalized recommendations frequently employ entity representations that combine visual and textual information. The embedded structure of these representations, resulting from neural network optimizations, is not always clear and consistent, which can impede their effectiveness in complex scenarios. For instance, when recommending items to navigate through a mapping, ambiguous entity representations can lead to suboptimal suggestions. To address this issue, we establish a mathematical framework for defining entity representations that integrates topological and semantic aspects. By applying this framework to modify the neural network's loss function, we enhance entity representations, making them more robust and consistent in relation to their underlying topological structure. Furthermore, this approach enables efficient computation of entity representations by replacing complex neural network components with lighter alternatives, such as simple linear transformations. We validate our method by improving entity representations for mapping recommendations and showcasing its applicability to other recommendation tasks like movie and product recommendations.

In kidney transplantation, the question of whether to accept an offered kidney is a significant decision for recipients. This decision can be understood through a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework, where the process of deciding acceptance involves multiple state variables that are interconnected. A standard approach to solving MDPs is policy iteration, which works by simulating the actual process many times. Unfortunately, because the process of deciding acceptance is complex and slow, this approach is poorly suited for this task. Additionally, because the process of deciding acceptance is random and different each time the simulation is repeated, it is difficult to accurately simulate the process many times. Furthermore, because the process of deciding acceptance is responsive to the current state, simulations tend to spend too much time in certain states. In order to address these issues, a different algorithm is needed that can quickly and efficiently simulate the process of deciding acceptance in a way that accurately reflects the true process. In order to solve the MDP for kidney transplantation, we quickly and efficiently simulate the process of deciding acceptance by using a number of established techniques from the field of operations research. We also test the algorithm on real data from the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients.

The Bayesian approach presents a viable alternative to classical methods for estimating complex statistical models, including those involving copulas. This work focuses on comparing Bayesian and classical methods for identifying copula parameters, specifically Riemannian mean and optimal scaling, using realistic financial data sets. An analysis of sample results reveals the effectiveness of the Bayesian approach in accurately estimating these parameters, even in situations where the data distribution does not adhere to the specified copula, through an assessment of their posterior density. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate that the Bayesian estimator performs better than its classical counterpart across various metrics, including mean squared error and kernel-based error calculations, for the specified copula parameters.

Financial text typically contains opposing concepts, such as "invest" and "reinvest", which are often labeled as synonyms due to the lack of a clear distinction between frequentist and Boolean semantics in many embedding methods. This misleading representation of financial relationships can lead to inefficient model performance and questionable financial insights. To address this problem, we introduce two novel models that focus on extracting Boolean meanings from financial texts and represent relationships using the connectivity graph of pre-trained word embeddings. Our experiments show that these models produce more accurate and useful financial insights than traditional methods, particularly in tasks like stock market prediction and portfolio optimization.

Optimizing fair-throughput and sum-throughput in wideband waveforming techniques involves designing a transmission band allocation and waveforming strategy.
