Additionally, a novel interpretation of the electromagnetic field's wave-particle duality is proposed, relating it to the concept of the infinite hydrogen atom, which provides a theoretical foundation for previous findings on the quantization of energy in the electromagnetic field.

Deep neural network classifiers have vast potential, yet their ability to provide reliable confidence estimates is severely constrained. Unfortunately, research reveals that many of these models can be manipulated into producing unbounded prediction confidence, even when the input data is relatively limited. This phenomenon not only poses significant risks in the actual deployment of these models but also hinders the development of robust real-world applications. To address this issue, a crucial step involves incorporating a confidence model that effectively bounds the prediction confidence for any input, including untrusted input. To achieve this, our work introduces a novel approach that leverages a binary classification model to distinguish between trusted and untrusted input data. By doing so, we can ensure that the main classifier is only utilized for processing trusted input, thus ensuring the stability and overall effectiveness of the system. Moreover, our approach also enables the generation of more accurate predictions for untrusted input data. To facilitate the implementation of this method, we have developed a demonstration that incorporates a demonstration dataset. This demonstration showcases the capability to produce accurate predictions, even when confronted with untrusted input data, forming the basis for our proposed solution.

To effectively evaluate reinforcement learning algorithms, a careful and controlled modification to the curriculum is as important as understanding their fundamental properties. We introduce a new evaluation framework that incorporates a simple model for dynamic curriculum design, allowing us to examine in-depth the algorithm's underlying structure and its performance in complex scenarios. Specifically, we investigate whether current algorithms can explore and optimize a scenario with changing goals and varying reward scales, and whether they can adapt to a curriculum that gradually introduces more complex tasks. Our studies using discrete and continuous state and action spaces reveal that existing algorithms struggle with flexibility and scalability, and often fail to adapt to diverse and dynamic curricula. We find that the problem lies not with the curriculum design, but with the algorithms themselves. To address this issue, we propose a new challenge that evaluates the ability of reinforcement learning algorithms to discover and optimize a dynamic curriculum with multiple goals. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a new algorithm that excels in evaluating the underlying structure of reinforcement learning environments. Our results demonstrate the value of controlled curriculum changes in evaluating reinforcement learning algorithms and facilitating collaborative benchmark comparison.

Temporal Discrete-Flow Confirmation Graphs (TDFCGs) combine the capabilities of analyzing process behavior changes over time with those of detecting causal relationships within dynamic scenarios. Existing TDFCG generation methods are largely non-parametric and prone to model issues due to the use of nearest-neighbor based techniques. To address this, we develop a novel approach to automatically create TDFCGs (AFTCG) by applying dynamic optimal matching to match instances from different time periods, thus ensuring the consistency of causal inferences. Our method produces more accurate results in comparison to existing techniques and can be employed in a scalable manner for large-scale datasets.

In quasiperiodic lattices, certain photonic structures exhibit a complex behavior where light localizes and then releases itself by moving freely when a particular condition is met. Researchers have proposed that this reentrant transition could be influenced by the lattices' disorder. This study, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger quasiperiodic lattice with a dimerized diagonal coupling, reveals that the reentrant transition in this case arises primarily from the interplay between the lattices' Peierls instability and the localization properties of its eigenstates. The study also finds that the reentrant transition can be accelerated by increasing the intensity of the near-infrared pulse, while varying the lattices' disorder has a more substantial impact on the transition when the on-site potential exhibits a specific characteristic.

An X-ray High-Energy Storage Power Source is being developed in China called Liger, which will provide X-rays through a DRS-powered beamline. This paper outlines the concept of this beamline and highlights the advantages of using a DRS. Specifically, Liger's DRS can compensate for its limited storage capacity and pulse energy by separating a high-energy, long-duration X-ray pulse into multiple lower-energy pulses suitable for scientific research. This feature makes Liger's beamline capable of producing a wide range of X-ray energies while still utilizing its stored energy effectively.

Entanglement within multi-partite states is extensively examined however the spatial relationship between particles is constrained due to limited access. This issue is particularly apparent when attempting to measure the spatial entanglement of photons through symmetric splitting, as their separation affects measurement outcomes. A novel optical imaging technique has been developed, addressing this constraint and enabling the measurement of large-scale entanglement within multipartite states, including both symmetric and asymmetric splitting scenarios. This method involves splitting a multi-photon state into two parts: one observed through interference in a double-slit pattern and the other through its entire spatial entanglement in an imaging system with multiple slits. By combining these measurements, it's possible to accurately determine the Schmidt number of a multi-photon state. Additionally, this method may also be applied to entangled states generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion using a $\lambda/2$ plate, as well as other entangled photon sources.

This article examines the geometric and Hodge-theoretic compactifications of moduli
spaces of algebraic varieties, specifically looking at Deligne-Mumford spaces and
their analogues in higher dimensions. By exploring the relationships between these
compactifications, we provide insights into their connections and distinct characteristics.

Ecosystems exhibit complex and intricate patterns due to the interconnection between populations within them, influencing the behavior of a single population over time. To simplify understanding of these complex interactions, this research focuses on neighboring populations where relationships can be categorized as competition, predation, or mutualism. A theoretical analysis reveals that a specific set of conditions is necessary to identify moments when the population's behavior may suddenly change dramatically. In the case of local interactions where populations grow at similar rates, these conditions are enough to predict when the population will experience a sudden shift in behavior. However, when populations grow at different rates, additional factors come into play, and the current model is not sufficient to predict when the population will experience a sudden shift in behavior. Several examples, including a model based on the Lotka-Volterra equations, are provided to illustrate how to apply the required conditions in practical scenarios.

We analyzed near-infrared, optical, and UV data for over 140,000 galaxies within the Sloan Digital Sky Survey to investigate their color variations based on galaxy mass. By dividing galaxies into 10 equal groups based on mass, we observed a notable trend in near-infrared-less optical color that increases with mass, specifically above a mass threshold of approximately $10^{10.1}$M$_{\rm \odot}$. This trend couldn't be accounted for by changes in optical-less near-infrared color, stellar population, specific star formation rate, or density within a galaxy's local group. It is suggested that more massive galaxies above this threshold exhibit decreased star formation and lower aerosols in their near-infrared-less optical bands, potentially resulting from the absence of high-energy star formation and a lack of dust in these galaxies.

Using knowledge distilled from high-quality datasets in one language, a model can be trained to recognize sentiments in another language. This is because models are not strictly tied to a specific language and can capture the underlying relationships between words and their meanings. Despite this, a significant obstacle to cross-lingual sentiment classification remains: obtaining labeled datasets in the target language. A novel technique has been developed to overcome this challenge by utilizing unsupervised translation and sentiment classification to assign labels to a large dataset of labeled data in a different language. This allows a model to effectively learn the significance of certain words in expressing positive, negative, or neutral emotions. What's more, this technique has been designed to work even when there is no directly available data in the target language. Several experiments have been conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique in two scenarios: when there is no directly available data in the target language and when there is limited data available in the target language. These experiments involve testing the method with two pairs of languages: Spanish and English, and German and English. The results have shown that this technique can accurately classify sentiments in the target language even in scenarios with limited available data.

We introduce a novel verification approach for ensuring the correctness of programs that incorporates a new strategy to manage fence insertions in cache coherence protocols. By leveraging a set of safety and liveness properties, our method makes precise fence placements without over-reliance on program analysis, thereby maintaining program performance. We demonstrate that our technique is effective by applying it to practical scenarios and showcasing its efficiency on various programs. However, we also uncover a limitation in our method's ability to handle undirected links. To address this constraint, we propose a modified approach that facilitates verification in the absence of directed links. We validate our proposed method against existing, unoptimized programs and find it yields comparable performance results.

We examine a modified version of the Hyers-Leventhal theorem that considers finite sequences of integers within a bounded sum and explores their properties regarding arithmetic progressions. Specifically, we investigate the following questions: What are the characteristics of sequences with a limited number of terms that lack significant diagonals? How do their relationships with arithmetic progressions change when allowing a smaller number of summands? Our in-depth analysis provides lower bounds for the size of required diagonals, as well as specific examples for finite sequences with no diagonals or minimal diagonals.

Let $\alpha$ be a fraction with $0 < \alpha < 1$ and $B^\alpha$ be the associated fractional Brownian motion with Hausdorff dimension $d_\alpha= \alpha+1$. For a Borel set $A$ within $B^\alpha$, we establish that the density function $f$ for the density of $B^\alpha$ across $A$ has a continuous version if and only if the Hausdorff dimension of $A$ exceeds a certain threshold $d_\alpha - 1$. Notably, this condition is more permissive than requirements for the density function's continuity or the density itself having a version in the context of $B^\alpha$.

Using the Herman-Mirrahimi theory and a semiclassical approach based on an analysis of prequasi-classical instanton trajectories, we examine the occurrence of persistent orbits in the Hénon-Heiles model, a paradigmatic system exhibiting chaotic behavior. By relating the stable manifolds of unbound hyperbolic orbits and semi-classical persistent orbits through the action of the monodromy operator, we demonstrate the size of their intersection in the complex plane. This intersection forms a vertical line segment whose length decreases as the level of quantization increases. It is also shown that the real part of a persistent orbit may be expressed in terms of the action of a specific quantum state, thereby establishing a connection between quantum states and classical behavior in chaotic systems.

As the COVID-19 pandemic continues to evolve, monitoring its impact on critical care systems is increasingly important. With many COVID-19 cases being treated in ICUs, it is essential to allocate resources effectively to maximize chances of survival for the most vulnerable patients. While initial studies focused on overall system performance and identified key factors, they did not explore the specific features related to ICU admission that influence outcomes. To address this gap, this study examined existing literature and conducted additional analyses to determine the characteristics of patients with COVID-19 that are most significant in determining intensive care unit (ICU) admission outcomes. By identifying and prioritizing key features, such as ICU discharge, mechanical ventilation, and do-not-resuscitate orders, this research provides actionable insights for optimizing clinical resource allocation. Moreover, this study demonstrated how to prioritize these features to minimize outcomes such as mortality and length of stay in the ICU. To facilitate the adoption of this approach in a flexible and scalable manner, this research introduced a lightweight, open-source framework that incorporates feature prioritization based on outcome minimization. To validate this framework, the researchers conducted additional analyses on previously published datasets. Consequently, this study's methodologies and findings are valuable references for clinicians, researchers, and healthcare executives seeking to allocate resources effectively to maximize outcomes for COVID-19 patients requiring intensive care.

The universal bundle functor for a monad on simplicial groups corresponds to a geometric simplex structure, which induces a cochain complex. This paper establishes the connection between that structure and the Bergmann-Moerdijk simplicial group structure. The resulting cochain complex then inherits a differential component, which forms a cochain complex for each simplicial group. This paper also examines the associated cohomology rings and determines the cohomology rings for specific universal bundles using the Bergmann-Moerdijk structure.

Recently, by leveraging object detection networks, Visual Relationship Detection has achieved significant progress. However, due to the problem of sparse data, the issue of efficient model optimization remains unresolved. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel loss function-based sampling method called Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS). By sampling balanced categories and locations, BNPS simplifies the detection task by reducing the number of proposals needed for each class. This way, BNPS allocates model capacity more efficiently, and our experiments on the Visual Relationship Detection benchmark show improved performance when combined with recent state-of-the-art models using a weak dataset. When tested with a stronger model and larger dataset, VCNPS achieved a relation detection score of 5.53, surpassing the current best score of 5.31.

This paper explores the development of an intelligent system that can learn to recognize human actions through observation, and tests its ability to achieve this efficiently. We started with a standard machine learning approach, training a classifier using data from a vast pool of examples. This resulted in an error rate of 24.5% which we managed to reduce to 14.4% by narrowing down the dataset to a more relevant set of examples. Taking this further, we found that using a smaller dataset of just 3000 images from 50 actions, trained using a more advanced classifier, yielded a significantly lower error rate of 11.4%. This led us to investigate a more streamlined approach to action recognition, one that doesn't rely on comparing images to a vast library of known actions. Instead, we proposed using a system where the recognition process generates the classification itself, without needing extensive training. This led to some interesting results, including the discovery that certain action recognition tasks are inherently difficult, and that certain tasks can be solved easily by incorporating just a small amount of new data.

This report outlines the development of a Content Addressable Parallel Processor connected to a host computer. The communication link between the CAPP and the host was established using a serial interface, with data exchange facilitated through a simple program. The CAPP's core functionality was tested by executing programs that utilized find operations, data exchange with the host, and memory management within the CAPP.

The formation of galaxies is characterized by the accumulation of cold gas within a galactic potential well, followed by the dissipation of gas into a disk, and ultimately the formation of stars. Due to the immense mass of galaxies, their construction occurs over billions of years, during which their structure undergoes a constant evolution. Theoretical models suggest that the merger of galaxies takes place primarily during their early stages of development, leading to the creation of new stars and the addition of stellar disks. The most recent research indicates that galaxy construction involves the formation of stars through an active process of gas accumulation, where the formation of stars occurs nearly simultaneously with the process of gas accumulation. The most recent research on galaxy construction also indicates that the merger of galaxies contributes very little to their construction, with the majority occurring during their early stages of development. The most recent research on galaxy construction predicts that the merger of galaxies should result in distinct features, such as accretion streams that influence the structure of galaxies during their formation. We examine the Universal Texture Zero model, a recent proposal explaining neutrino findings, in order to calculate the masses of the neutrinos and the associated parameters that affect other processes. Utilizing a consistent numerical approach, we determine the complex matrix relationships in the context of two neutrino flavors. Additionally, we find the diskarded eigenvalues, crucial for predicting neutrino mass patterns, and derive formulas for predicting oscillation probabilities and beta decay rates. Using this, we explore the connection between the neutrino mass generation and its effects in oscillation and beta decay. Furthermore, we investigate the stability of the solutions under the influence of a third neutrino flavor using a perturbative approach.

This research investigates the unique characteristics of a specific solution type in a geometric equation proposed by M. Struwe and C. Taoui. The study establishes the local uniqueness of solutions that exhibit isolated behavior at a specific point, under certain conditions, and demonstrates that these solutions possess symmetry if a particular potential function has a specific form. Additionally, the study proves that solutions that exhibit isolated behavior at a particular point are steady states, and provides a criterion for their stability.

Despite significant advancements in neural-based program generation, they still struggle to overcome fundamental limitations. Essentially, neural networks don't truly "understand" the programs they are capable of producing. In this research, we argue that incorporating weak insights from a static program analyzer into a neural program generator can yield significant improvements. We devise a novel technique called neuroprogram repair, which leverages the analyzer to ensure the generated programs meet specified specifications. We demonstrate neuroprogram repair to be an effective approach, outperforming standard neural-based program generation in both accuracy and performance.

On November 7th, 2004, a massive geomagnetic disturbance occurred, categorizing it as a G4 severe storm. This event was triggered by a sudden solar flare and coronal mass ejection launched towards Earth. Researchers analyzed in situ magnetic field data from the Mars Global Surveyor, as the planet passed through the solar wind on November 18th, 2004. By identifying the entrance point of the wind and the shape of its density profile, they were able to estimate the time it took for the wind to reach Mars. Additionally, they observed the effects of the wind on the planet's magnetic field, including the delay of the shock front and the discovery of a magnetic field structure previously reported as anomalous.

We have derived the relativistic fluid dynamics equations for a single component of a multi-component fluid, assuming that the mesoscopic viscosity scale has a specific relationship with the thermalization time and the temperature, based on the theoretical approach of Hobbs and Minnaert. We then analyzed the dispersion relations for both spherical and planar entropy modes in relativistic fluids with non-zero viscosity, visiting previous work by Hobbs and Minnaert, and also considering an alternative approach by Kobayashi and Nishida. Our study shows that both the Hobbs-Minnaert and Kobayashi-Nishida equations yield identical entropy mode dispersion relations, with the viscosity parameter affecting the real and imaginary parts of the frequency in different ways. We found that the Hobbs-Minnaert equation corresponds to the linearized Israel-Stewart theory, but with an assumed constant mesoscopic viscosity, whereas the Kobayashi-Nishida equation represents the full nonlinear theory for a specific time scale. We also explored the relationship between the Hobbs-Minnaert and Kobayashi-Nishida equations in their respective domains, demonstrating that the latter can be viewed as the former with an additional non-linear contribution.

Deep learning-based methods have been highly effective in identifying anomalies in image datasets. Nonetheless, existing approaches are primarily suited for single-frame anomaly detection, and they frequently rely on supplementary information for improving performance. We develop an innovative, fully incremental learning algorithm for anomaly detection on sequential image data, such as video. This method allows for the incorporation of new data into an existing model without requiring any further adjustments. Through experimental evaluations using two types of data (faces and medical images), we demonstrate that the proposed incremental strategy surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in model maintenance. Additionally, we showcase successful anomaly detection on the LSP body part dataset with kinematic information and illustrate the algorithm's capability to handle diverse data streams. Our work is the first to explore incremental learning for anomaly detection. The code is available at https://github.com/zhengdaqi/IncCan.

A cryptographic scheme is considered non-recoverable if an authority can force a user to recover encrypted data without knowing the user's identity, provided certain conditions are met. A corresponding concept is denialability, where an authority can convince a third-party judge that the user with a specific identity used the scheme, without actually knowing the user's true identity. In our study, we examine the interplay between these two properties and their connections to privacy and anonymity. Our primary objectives are to thoroughly analyze existing protocols that incorporate non-recoverable encryption, deniable encryption, or anonymous authentication, and to explore novel directions for research in this area. Specifically, we explore the relationships between these properties in various scenarios, identify potential limitations in existing protocols, and highlight potential vulnerabilities. Our exploration focuses on conventional models and unlikely attacks, without considering more advanced threats or environments.

This research compares various MDI-QKD protocols through realistic assumptions of application scenarios, including analyses of different gain values, error rates, and final key rates. We examine the fundamental limitations of each protocol using the gain-error diagram, and further explore the effectiveness of some protocols in overcoming channel loss by utilizing the gain of the phase-sensitive Pauli error correction technique.

This study provides a focus on algorithmic research for a broad category of general-valued CSPs known as minimisation CSPs, specifically those with rigid, crisp constraints. Our investigations reveal the existence of a PTAS for solving these CSPs, building on previous work that established the applicability of FPT algorithms to this category of CSPs. Additionally, our research identifies both upper and lower bounds for the complexity of solving minimisation CSPs with arbitrary functions, demonstrating the complexity of determining the parity of the minimum weight to be minimized is NP-hard.

This research focuses on the development of high-order numerical techniques for evaluating time-dependent mean field games systems, particularly systems that incorporate delay terms. The existence and uniqueness of an equilibrium solution in such systems are established, along with a theoretical assessment of the convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(k^2)$ for the corresponding semi-discrete scheme and $\mathcal{O}(k^2 h^{1-k}, \, k\in [1,2])$ for the fully discrete scheme. A novel approach utilizing Gelfand-Tsaoui iteration is introduced to solve the fixed point equation associated with the equilibrium condition. Moreover, the proposed method can be applied to a broader class of mean field games systems. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the new method across various type of systems, including those with periodic and random fluctuations, systems with asynchronous behavior, and systems with delayed terms.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have reached a near-human level of performance, yet it's unclear how they manage to achieve this by incorporating millions of parameters. The lack of transparency in these models is a significant concern, particularly in sensitive industries like finance and healthcare. The field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) aims to provide insight into the decision-making processes of these models. The problem is further compounded by the fact that XAI techniques are often time-consuming and require significant computational resources. The proposed paper explores the use of regularization techniques to enhance the interpretability of self-attention mechanisms in deep learning models, specifically in the context of sequence-to-sequence tasks. The study utilizes the Hannes algorithm to optimize a self-attention regularization technique that prioritizes simple solutions, resulting in more interpretable models that rival the performance of state-of-the-art models. The method is applied to the task of machine translation, and the accessible models demonstrate a 1% improvement in accuracy. The study demonstrates that by incorporating self-attention regularization, models with reduced complexity can match the performance of more complex models, resulting in more accurate summaries of the models' behavior and a 30% reduction in unnecessary parameters.

KIC 9267654 is a star with a distinctive, enigmatic rotation pattern, and we propose an alternative explanation for this phenomenon. Initially, researchers believed it might be accounted for by the star's multi-part composition; however, our modeling suggests it can also be explained by the presence of a planet with an extremely close orbit. By combining the SPLCO code for spectral line profiling and the JPL ephemeris data, we found that a planet with a mass of approximately 6.1 times the mass of Earth and an orbital period of 0.44 days could be the cause of the star's unusual rotation pattern. Verify our findings will require spectrometric measurements of the star's spectrum, but we can also use planetary ephemeris data to predict when the star should exhibit the most pronounced variations in its spectrum.

The rapid spread of news through social platforms and the internet makes the dissemination of fake news a significant concern. Despite the importance of detecting fake news, existing methods are limited by targeting specific languages and being difficult to adapt to new data. Moreover, these methods often fail to utilize the contextual relationships within text and rely heavily on conventional neural network components, hindering their ability to accurately classify fake news. To address these challenges, we introduce a multi-lingual, contextual fake news detection model called MetaFEND, incorporating a novel memory-augmented attention mechanism that efficiently exploits contextual relationships within text. By incorporating a dual-layer structure and a specially designed modular component, MetaFEND effectively handles both local and global contextual cues, achieving exceptional performance and adaptability. Our experiments show that MetaFEND achieves exceptional performance, surpassing the state-of-the-art on six diverse fake news datasets in terms of fake news detection, achieving a minimum of 5% improvement on the F1 score. Additionally, MetaFEND demonstrates unparalleled adaptability, successfully converting to new languages and datasets with minimal additional data.

We examine a one-dimensional transport equation that is periodic, features nonlocal flux with no dissipation, and is applied to smooth odd initial data. The research reveals that the corresponding solution develops unbounded moments over time, exhibits a two-phase structure, and displays oscillatory behavior. Additionally, we derive an asymptotic model that characterizes the growth rate of the second moment's increase.

This paper explores the average age of information (AoI) in discrete time systems with stationary AoI distributions and contrasted with similar continuous time systems. We establish a general formula for the AoI distribution in discrete time and determine its stationary moments in systems where updates are generated by deterministic and stochastic processes. We discover that the AoI distribution in discrete time has a unique structure that can be characterized by a single parameter - the time between updates - and includes several well-known cases. We compare the AoI performance in discrete and continuous time systems, revealing that the latter's AoI tends to be older on average. Additionally, we derive optimal mean update times for discrete time systems that minimize AoI and determine the optimal update rate for continuous time systems.

This paper explores the concept of admissible Drinfeld twists, examining both set-theoretic and q-deformed scenarios. We establish the conditions under which such twists remain admissible in both cases, and also clarify the relationship between Drinfeld twists and factorizing automorphisms. Additionally, we outline the constraints for constructing both set-theoretic and q-deformed Drinfeld twists.

This paper explores the concept of quaternary Golay complementary array pairs in vector spaces over the field with elements. We provide a complete characterization of the parameters these arrays must adhere to, as well as a condition for their existence in any dimension. Our analysis reveals that only a limited set of dimensions satisfy these requirements. In particular, we find that Golay complementary array pairs are only feasible in dimensions 2, 4, 8, or 24. This research builds upon a previous study by Chen, Ding, and Yang, which introduced the concept of Golay complementary array pairs and established their necessity for pulse position modulation systems.

We have calculated the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction in a silicon crystal lattice, considering various locations for the dopants, and found that the interaction can be modified significantly. When the spin sources are placed at the lattice sites, we found the exchange interaction to be too small to be effective. Conversely, spin sources located at midpoints of bonds or further out in the interstitial sites can produce a much larger exchange interaction, greater than 100 $\mu eV$ for both perpendicular and parallel components. The magnitude of the interaction also shows sensitivity to the dopant type, with a greater effect for the perpendicular component. The possibility of using neutral boron or phosphorus, incorporated using standard semiconductor technology, is explored as a means of exchanging spin information, and the importance of spin orbit coupling and the possibility of optical spin transfer are also examined.

We address the challenge of using time series data to identify the underlying structure of a complex system that is not fully understood. This is accomplished by developing an iterative procedure to switch between two types of models: a probabilistic graph that underlies the system and a hidden Markov chain that generates the time series data. This Markov chain is used to derive insights into the system's behavior and is utilized in a practical application to forecast future time series predictions. Specifically, we apply this approach in medical research to analyze biological time series data and predict new time series observations in the same vein. However, our approach is versatile and can be adapted to tackle complex systems in other domains.

The paper explores the stable homotopy theory of graded polynomial rings, using these to interpret partitions, and connects this to the slice filtration and Drinfeld's theorem. It demonstrates that for a finite field $k$, the graded polynomial ring $k[\theta_1, \delta \theta_1, \theta_2, \delta \theta_2, \ldots]$ represents a limit that captures the structure of stable homotopy groups via the slice filtration. It further shows that this representation holds locally, and by analyzing this locally, the paper finds a connection between the stable homotopy groups of spheres and Drinfeld's theorem about the length of ideals in polynomial rings. It also identifies the graded part of the stable homotopy groups of spheres with the field $k$ as $\mathbb{Z}[\theta_1, \delta \theta_1, \theta_2, \delta \theta_2, \ldots]/(\theta_i^2, \theta_i \delta \theta_{i-1})$, and offers a generalization for fields of positive characteristic.

Recent advancements in convolutionsal neural networks (CNNs) have made significant contributions to automating the segmentation of structures within medical imaging. Combining these regions of interest (ROIs) is critical in nuclear medicine, where the accumulation of imaging agents at specific bodily areas is studied. To facilitate accurate ROI segmentation, an optimization technique called maximum a posteriori estimation is commonly employed. Nevertheless, the optimal pairing of CNN and MAP estimation for ROI segmentation in nuclear imaging remains unexplored. To address this, we undertake the qualitative and quantitative analysis of diverse network architectures and optimization strategies, incorporating the incorporation of spatial regularization and likelihood functions, aimed at enhancing ROI segmentation performance. Experimental results indicate that the integration of an iterative optimization method with a robust regression-based loss function and the inclusion of spatial prior information within the network's architecture significantly improves segmentation output. The proposed approach, leveraging a fully convolutional iterative network combined with MAP estimation utilizing a likelihood function and spatial regularization, serves as a reliable foundation for the automated segmentation of ROI in nuclear imaging.

In this context, we propose a strategy to illustrate strong quantum nonlocality in complex systems through the use of unextendible product bases. Our approach has already successfully demonstrated strong quantum nonlocality in triplets and four-party settings. Here, we extend this concept to multipartite settings of any composition, showing that strong quantum nonlocality can be displayed within any larger multipartite setup by constructing a suitable set of unextendible product bases that have a specific structure. This structure involves applying the idea of "simulating" single-qubit operations across different parties, which is foundational to our approach.

To facilitate massive spectroscopic surveys, identifying energy sources and mapping spatial distributions efficiently, a viable strategy involves sending a swarm of astrobots to analyze the sky. Developing effective and efficient astrobot trajectories that minimize downtime and avoid collisions among the fleet is crucial. This paper presents a approach utilizing a hybrid optimization method that combines coarse-grained global optimization with refined local search to create feasible and high-quality solutions. This method, capable of handling astrobot trajectory planning as a complex scheduling problem, prioritizes the execution of the most critical tasks while avoiding overlap and minimizing waiting times. Through computational testing on realistic astrobot scenarios, this paper demonstrates the performance of this approach, showcasing robust solution generation with optimal or near-optimal qualities. This method exhibits scalability and reliability, with successful applications in mapping the sky for the CAULTREX experiment.

The latest version of GP2 introduces a cutting-edge data structure called BigArray, which has been optimized for high-speed operations and has been successfully integrated into the graph processing system. In GP2, the BigArray data structure has been shown to significantly boost the performance of graph programs by reducing memory usage and increasing operation speeds. Furthermore, the implementation of In-Place Graph Partitioning, a time-complexity O(V) algorithm, has been achieved through the use of BigArray, resulting in a dramatic decrease of up to 5 times in partitioning time. Additionally, the improved data structure has facilitated the development of several new graph algorithms and has been effectively applied in multiple large-scale graph applications.

This research introduces a novel, multi-task deep learning framework that simultaneously solves both supervised and unsupervised feature extraction problems. The proposed network includes two separate component networks: one receives labeled input and produces a supervised feature, while another, unsupervised component produces an unsupervised feature without input data. Both features are combined and common representations are extracted from their joint manifold. Our method learns the unsupervised feature to correlate with the supervised feature, thereby indirectly meeting the supervision goal. This is achieved by minimizing a joint reconstruction error that weighs the influence of each feature. The proposed framework flexibly integrates both supervised and unsupervised learning samples, thereby contributing to a comprehensive understanding of how unsupervised and supervised learning can be simultaneously performed using deep networks. Experimental results on various datasets illustrate that this method produces more effective unservised features and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods even without incorporating the unsupervised data into the supervised learning process.
Two infinite families of graphs are constructed, whose automorphism groups contain primitive, solvable subsets, thereby extending the scope of recent research into graph domains.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method called Group Lasso, an innovative algorithm that selects crucial variables for analysis in both continuous and categorical data contexts. By leveraging the group structure, this method identifies key groups whose variables hold significant importance and should be retained, while also pinpointing individual variables with lesser value that could be dropped. We explore two types of Lasso estimators - the Lasso and Fused Lasso - that represent continuous and categorical data scenarios, respectively. A backward feature elimination technique, inspired by Group Lasso, is employed to prune variables from a comprehensive set, focusing on both individual and collective significance. We utilize RStudio to implement and evaluate this algorithm on synthetic and real-world datasets, and make the code publicly available for replication and extension.

Deep neural network models pre-trained on knowledge-based triples, often through contrastive learning, have shown significant potential in processing knowledge-based question-answering tasks. Yet, it's unclear whether pre-training on knowledge-based triples offers a similar boost in model performance when compared to traditional text-based data. Our research involves comparing multiple models pre-trained on both types of data and assessing their performance on diverse question-answering tasks. Our results reveal that, surprisingly, models pre-trained on knowledge-based triples exhibit no noticeable advantage over those trained on traditional text-based data. This finding holds true across several models, including RoBERTa and BERT, and is consistent across both knowledge-based and open-domain question-answering datasets. Further analysis of model performance through diagnostic tools suggests that the benefits of pre-training on knowledge-based triples may be outweighed by the tendency for models to rely on noise within the triples.

This study examines how classical partial differential equation models and their nonlocal counterparts are related, particularly focusing on measures of distance in data recovery applications and optimal transport. We first establish a general framework for nonlocal diffusion equations that incorporates well-posedness and stability criteria. Then, we investigate a specific case where the nonlocal interaction kernel mimics local behavior under fine-scale discretization, proving that the nonlocal model is equivalent to a classical PDE in this limit. We validate our theoretical findings with a numerical experiment demonstrating the similarity between the nonlocal and classical models as the kernel's size diminishes.

This research offers a novel approach for mobile device-based panoramic image construction, incorporating Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs). By leveraging IMUs, our approach enables accurate real-world mapping and subsequent image stitching, devoid of external hardware. We leverage a Monte Carlo localization method to efficiently integrate IMU data and map readings from the device's sensors, facilitating localized pose estimation and subsequent image alignment. This, in turn, allows for high-quality panoramic image stitching. Our system can generate panoramic images from isolated shots or consecutive video frames, incorporating data from both the device's cameras and IMUs. We evaluated our approach through various tests, including actual world captures using smartphones equipped with IMUs, demonstrating its practical applicability.

This paper investigates the decomposition of degenerate Eisenstein series on $GL(2)$ over a number field, focusing on cases where the field is not real. We establish a functional equation for these Eisenstein series by analyzing their Weyl group cosets and develop a link between them and integral transforms of Eisenstein series. By exploiting this connection and making use of character relations, we gain insight into the decomposition into irreducible representations and obtain specific results for certain cases.

The unique movement disorders characteristic of Parkinson's Disease (PD) make its assessment challenging, primarily during the early stages. Advanced computational models are being developed to improve disease understanding and develop effective treatments, which can be verified through realistic simulations mimicking the movement patterns of individuals with PD. Unfortunately, a lack of reference data impedes the normalization of these models, forcing them to be developed specifically for each new application. This research aims to adapt a complex computational model of the upper limb to detect virtual movement disorders, using a non-invasive sensing technique, without needing to rewrite the model's underlying dynamics. Although the model originally relied on internal state variables to identify movement patterns, this adaptation used a machine learning technique called dimensionality reduction to successfully recognize virtual Parkinsonian features on the arm. Resulting simulations demonstrated that this method could accurately identify normally functioning movement patterns, as well as those affected by PD. Furthermore, the study demonstrated the ability to distinguish between movements performed naturally with PD and those simulated on the arm. This breakthrough indicates that computational models of the upper limb can be normalized more easily than previously thought, which may facilitate their use in developing and assessing treatment strategies for movement disorders.

This research presents a novel algorithm for creating high-quality renditions of
font features, specifically focused on accurately rendering the connections between
letters. The existing approach used to produce these connections relies on curved lines
but can result in visible gaps when joining wide letters. These gaps can be mitigated
with our proposed method by treating the join area as a combination of two quadratics
but only if the letters have a circular shape. For broader letters, we suggest a technique
using cubic lines for better precision. We evaluated our algorithm against multiple
font types and found it produced more precise results than the original method.

A comprehensive analysis of high-redshift quasars suggests that the merger of galaxies plays a key role in the co-evolution of galaxies and supermassive black holes, with mergers triggering the growth of both. According to current understanding, AGN outflows play a crucial part in stopping gas from reaching the center of galaxies. These outflows, which can reach velocities of up to 300,000 kilometers per second, are powered by the energy released from the accumulation of gas onto supermassive black holes. Their impact on nearby host galaxies and surrounding intergalactic gas can be significant, and they may also play a major role in shaping the characteristics of nearby quasars, influencing the formation of galaxies, and potentially even contributing to the evolution of the universe's massive structures. This study utilizes massive quasars at high redshifts to investigate the properties of AGN outflows. According to their spectral analysis, these outflows are highly energetic, massive, and long-lasting streams of gas that are likely sustained by the energy released from supermassive black hole mergers. This research also provides evidence that these outflows are aligned with the movement of gas towards the center of galaxies, and that their formation is linked to the presence of stellar mergers that trigger the growth of supermassive black holes. This analysis implies that these outflows represent a critical stage in the development of galaxies and supermassive black hole mergers, and that they may also mark the starting point for the formation

This study introduces a novel class of rotated complex Hermite interpolants
for univariate functions within the space of harmonic functions, meeting the
requirements for both convexity and monotonicity. Building on the work of Huang
and Wang (2019), we develop these rotated complex Hermite interpolants through
a quasi-interpolation formula, where a new rotationally symmetric multivariate
radial function serves as the basis, and provide a model for calculating its
convexity and monotonicity constants. A set of rotated complex Hermite points
is also introduced and shown to be centered within the unit disk, achieving the
maximum distance of $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

Data augmentation within deep neural network training segments images into non-overlapping areas, labels just one area, and repeats this process to increase training data. This method is commonly used before classification images are finalized. Despite well-documented benefits, there are instances where data augmentation impairs performance. To address this, a technique called selective data augmentation involves identifying specific image regions that can be reliably classified and labeling the rest as uncertain. In this paper, a simple yet effective method for selective data augmentation is proposed, where specific image regions are delimiting masks and labeled as reliable or uncertain. This method is applied to multiple image classification tasks and demonstrates significant improvements over standard data augmentation.

A recent deep learning method known as the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) has gained attention for its effectiveness in speech enhancement, particularly due to the simplicity of its model and the robustness it provides across various conditions. Despite the promising results reported, the majority of DPCRN models have been trained with large amounts of clean data, which is not a realistic assumption for many applications. The current study focuses on enhancing the capability of DPCRN to handle noisy real-world data through the introduction of a new module called the Dual-Path Layer (DPL). This innovative DPL module is designed to reduce the model's reliance on abundant clean data and allow it to better exploit training data that includes noise. The proposed DPL module is characterized by its ability to minimize the spectral distance between two parallel pathways, which provides a means to balance the capabilities of speech spectrum reconstruction and spectral estimation. To validate the effectiveness of the modified DPCRN model, the results of numerous experiments are presented, which demonstrate significant improvements in performance over the baseline model and achieve state-of-the-art levels in terms of mean opinion score (MOS).

A recent study suggests that for certain cosmic scenarios characterized by a five-parameter structure, including two dark components, the ratio of turn-around radii can distinguish between models. This ratio is the focus of the research, and by analyzing it with perturbation theory, the distribution of objects within a Hubble volume is modeled. The analysis shows that the ratio varies significantly between structures composed of dark matter and those made of baryons, and that it breaks down when considering only the spatial distribution of objects. However, when the focus is on the overall structure within a Hubble volume, the ratio is found to be more consistent across different cosmic scenarios. It is further found that when observing only up to three-dimensional correlations, the structure of turn-around objects does not sufficiently break the degeneracy in parameters. But with the analysis of five-dimensional correlations, the required degeneracy is broken.

We develop a basic two-fluid model that incorporates both conductive and admissible fluid components within the same space, even though this isn't the only possible way to construct such a model. This two-fluid model is comparable to the quintessence model proposed by Kovalovska and Roudenko, but with the additional feature of being able to determine the heat flux at the top accurately. When the admissible fluid's viscosity is low and the Rayleigh number is high, we find that the model produces the $R^{1/3}$ heat flux scaling predicted by fast mode dominance theories. Conversely, when the admissible fluid's viscosity is high and the Rayleigh number is high, we observe the $R^{1/2}$ heat flux scaling characteristic of lattice models.

When placed in a cavity, a single atom with no initial correlation with the cavity phasing may induce significant multipartite entanglement in a series of connected atoms if it is part of a system that performs a critical function like Poincar\'e mirroring. A theoretical model showing that merely achieving this atom-cavity entanglement is enough to create notable multipartite entanglement in the atoms when the cavity field is initially set to a vacuum state can be proven true by an analytical approach and numerical simulation. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the same result can also be achieved with a cavity field that is not initially in a vacuum state.

Between 2016 and 2021, the CMS detector's power and cooling systems were revamped, enabling the silicon pixel detector to operate at a significantly reduced anisotropic heating rate. This improvement led to a substantial reduction in charge injection levels and heating-related instabilities within the detector, resulting in enhanced operating stability and reliability during LHC runs following the initial pause.

Our understanding of quantum chromodynamics is enhanced by studying glueball spectra, which provide valuable insights into the nature of the strong interaction and give quantum chromodynamics its unique character. Unfortunately, glueballs are difficult to study experimentally, so we must rely on theoretical calculations for their mass spectrum. By utilizing latticed QCD, we can determine the glueball mass spectrum through the calculation of two-point correlation functions of the chromodynamic field, which represent the probability of re-oberving a glueball as a function of time. Alternatively, we can also consider the probability of observing a glueball when watching the chromodynamic field at two different times, which allows us to calculate the kernel of the two-point function correlation and ultimately the glueball mass spectrum. In our study, we derive the expression for the two-point function correlation based on the lattice theory and determine the glueball mass spectrum for both pure gauge QCD and QCD with Nf=2 dynamical quarks by lattice Monte Carlo simulations at four different lattice spacings.

Twitter, a social media platform with vast user data, has emerged as an effective tool for public opinion tracking. Given the massive amount of user-generated content on the platform, establishing efficient and reliable social monitoring methods is crucial. This paper presents a comprehensive approach to sentiment analysis on Twitter, focusing on leveraging LSTM-based neural networks to enhance classification accuracy. Initially, a dataset was assembled through lightweight and efficient web scraping techniques, involving the collection of over 20,000 product review tweets. A optimized preprocessing strategy for text data was developed to minimize dimensions and weightage allocation for features, which was coupled with two different LSTM architectures to explore their classification performance. The experimental results showed that both models achieved superior classification benchmarks, with an average accuracy of 87.6%, outperforming conventional machine learning algorithms. The code and dataset associated with this project are available on GitHub.

A recent, non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter has been found to influence the shadow radius and thermal profile of black holes, resulting in the creation of new, warped profiles dubbed "quasi-kerr". This parameter is inherent to an approximation of an Einstein-Yang-Mills system, obtained through holographic mapping. By extending the holographic principle, we investigate the impact of this parameter on charged AdS black holes in an attempt to understand shadow radius variation. Due to the non-linear nature of Yang-Mills theory, direct analysis is complicated, and we must therefore utilize the 'holographic Dirac conjecture' to examine the bulk behavior. Formulating the Yang-Mills field in the bulk in terms of the boundary field, we find that this variation arises from the interaction between this representation of the Yang-Mills field and the gravitational field, and that it could also be achieved through alternative, non-dynamical boundary field profiles.

The study examines the connection between nonclassical behavior and optical tomography data, analyzing how entanglement or other unusual effects are reflected in the structure of optical fields. The research focuses on two-type and three-type atom cavity systems, using the Jaynes-Cummings model to describe interactions between light and matter. The collected data on the optical state are transformed into a format known as Wigner functions, which serve as maps of the optical field's phase space. The analysis compares classical and nonclassical behavior in these maps, revealing patterns that identify entanglement and other unusual effects. The study also explores how these patterns are affected by different parameters in the system.

Understanding role-based specifications is crucial in interactive agent design, particularly in interactive systems like web chatbots. These specifications, often provided through user input, define the context and objectives of the interaction and can significantly impact the system's performance, even degrading it if incorrectly interpreted. To address this challenge, we propose a role-specification understanding model that utilizes a role specification context and a context word to predict the next word in dialogue. This model is unique in that it incorporates a role specification representation that can be both sparse and labeled. To facilitate seamless integration with existing dialogue models, we design a simple yet effective architecture that builds upon existing dialogue models. Our experiments yield compelling results, and our approach notably outperforms baseline models across multiple evaluation metrics. The model's superiority is further underscored by low fusion costs when combining it with dialogue models without role specification understanding capabilities.

This research used a computational approach to model decision-making processes in agricultural practices, specifically focusing on the management of strawberries in Florida. We incorporated recent advances in reinforcement learning within a multi-agent framework, given that multiple factors influence decisions in this context. The model took into account key considerations like crop yield, profit, and the economic impact of controlling disease, and was trained with real-world data. The results showed that the model effectively learned to optimize outcomes and adapt to changing conditions, also demonstrating the benefit of integrating an agent that simulates the behavior of a disease with a regular agent, as this led to more efficient learning.

Immersive video viewing is gaining popularity due to the advancement in head-mounted devices and virtual reality technology. These developments have led to a surge in online immersive video content, which poses a challenge to traditional viewport prediction models. Current models fail to account for additional contextual information provided by video subtitles, which is crucial for enhancing prediction accuracy. In this research, we introduce a novel multi-modal viewport prediction model called the SubTitle-Attention Viewport Predictor (SAVP), which utilizes both visual and textual information from subtitles for enhanced performance. In evaluating SAVP, we conducted comprehensive experiments using real-world data and found that it surpasses the accuracy of existing baseline models by achieving a mean absolute error of 17.48%, outperforming the best baseline by 11.53%. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that SAVP's attention mechanism plays a crucial role in improving prediction accuracy, with an error rate of less than 20% when viewing the most relevant section of the video.

A key challenge in quantum many-body theory is finding efficient ways to create approximate quantum many-body states and time-evolution operators (TEOs) with low entanglement, allowing for realistic simulations while preserving the essence of quantum physics. These approximations can be achieved using matrix product operators (MPOs) with a bond dimension that increases polynomially in the system size, making them feasible for large-scale systems. Our work develops a universal and efficient framework for deriving MPO representations of thermal states and TEOs from their parent Hamiltonians using string product operators (SPOs), thereby providing a significant improvement over the strict polynomial scaling. Notably, this improvement enables the simulation of system sizes that are commonly studied in experimental research. Additionally, our method incorporates an adaptable truncation technique for MPOs, which ensures precise representation of physical properties within desired tolerance levels. Several examples, including the Ising model, Heisenberg model, and Lindblad dynamics, demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for obtaining accurate MPO approximations of thermal states and TEOs.

This paper builds upon our existing research in Taylor-based analysis and its applications to decoupling, strongly citing our paper titled "Taylor-based Analysis and Its Applications to Decoupling." A key concept in our work is the characterization of canonical surfaces that determine decoupling rates. We have previously demonstrated that any surface that doesn't align with these canonical surfaces can result in an improved decoupling rate. To expand our understanding of such surfaces, we introduce a new strategy combining Taylor-based analysis and surface classification. This approach enables us to identify specific conditions that ensure optimal decoupling in a broader range of settings. Furthermore, we apply our method to analyze the decoupling rates of variational methods, revealing that these methods yield optimal results when our criteria are met. Additionally, we provide a new perspective on the application of our approach to Taylor integrals.

This paper introduces the anisotropic capacity, a parameter that can be used in contexts where the Jacobian determinant is zero. We demonstrate that both the classical isoperimetric and Chernoff-Von Neumann inequalities hold for anisotropic capacity. Additionally, we establish relationships between anisotropic capacity and other geometric measures, including the regularized anisotropic surface area and the Orlicz-Anisotropic capacity. Our results provide a framework for understanding the properties of anisotropic capacity and its relationships to other geometric concepts.

During the investigation of an experiment called SPECS-1/2, which was conducted in the ISS, an unusual phenomenon known as a glitch was discovered. These glitches, which occur regularly, take the form of sudden, brief changes in data and can also be observed in other acceleration sensors. They pose a significant challenge in measuring acceleration, as they affect the results by introducing an unwanted noise. To better understand this glitch, researchers analyzed the data collected by the experiment and discovered that the phenomenon is linked to a specific type of wave called a Schumann resonance, which occurs when glitches interact with radio frequency signals transmitted by the experiment. Additionally, the analysis revealed that the glitch can be represented by a consistent pattern and amplitude, which may be influenced by other factors such as temperature and vibration. To minimize its effect, researchers suggest using specialized signal processing techniques to filter out noise.

Our research focuses on active dimers that move in a plane, for which we developed a general theory, resulting in exact solutions to their dynamics. We found that these dimers exhibit similar behavior to rotating wheels and could be used as precision drivers for transporting other objects. There are two primary states: the point-state and the ring-state. In the first state, the dimer moves in a straight line, whereas in the second state, it creates a circular force field. These states are interchangeable and can be converted using external fields. We measured the dimensionless torque required to switch between these states and found it to be on the order of 10^4 for dimers composed of Janus particles. We also discovered that dimers with this ability can be used to transport other objects and proposed a method to assess the dimer's torque through its interaction with a laser beam.

The k-strong shortest path union cover problem is a variant of the minimum strong shortest path cover problem, where we seek the fewest strong shortest path covers that can cover all nodes, using k-strong shortest paths per cover. In this study, we determine the computational complexity of this problem, revealing it to be NP-complete. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a solution can be classified in polynomial time across all possible k values, and we propose a parameterized algorithm based on the number of desired strong shortest path covers.

The infrared renormalons in the moment representation of a function such as moment G are evaluated, and their corresponding renormalon resonances in the moment variable N are identified. Additionally, the length scale $\Lambda$ and the moment N have a complex relationship that is examined using a generic function $G(N,\Lambda)$. The complex structure in $\Lambda$ is shown to be a consequence of this relationship and results from the interaction between $\Lambda$ and the moment variable N. It leads to uncertainty in the function's value even when its moment representation is determined exactly. This uncertainty can be expressed in terms of the size of the renormalon contribution to the function, and it persists unless the moment variable N is sufficiently large so that the renormalon effect becomes negligible. The complex structure in $\Lambda$ is also the source of the uncertainty in the parametric representation of a function such as $xG(x)$. It implies that the Borel sum (or the Penrose on-shell approximation) cannot provide the accurate value for the function's value at a given point, and it has to be supplemented by the additional information in order to achieve this accuracy. The proposed method for determining the function $xG(x)$ from its moment representation involves the following steps. First, determine the moment variable N that leads to the minimal uncertainty in the function's value; second, calculate the corresponding moment value $N_\psi$; and third, use this value to construct the corresponding Jost function

For trees of a specific high degree, we demonstrate that the transition from transient to recurrent behavior for the frog model occurs exactly at the critical point where the standard random walk becomes recurrent or transient. This finding simplifies the proof of this statement, which was previously proven with more complex techniques. Additionally, we show that for trees of higher degrees, there is a sharp transition at this point, while for lower degree trees, the transition is more gradual.

The unique interference between surface plasmons and a Rayleigh anomaly at the edge of a photonic crystal contributes significantly to the complex spectral properties of magnetophotonic crystals, particularly in regards to magneto-optical effects. This concept is demonstrated through in-depth analysis of the optical and magneto-optical transmission variations in a photonic crystal, with particular focus on the unusual features observed at the edge. The proposed model incorporates coupled wave theory to examine surface plasmon and Rayleigh anomaly interaction, revealing how this interference produces the distinct magneto-optical effects in the form of polarization rotation and dark current variation. Furthermore, the influence of plasmon and Rayleigh anomaly coherence on these magneto-optical features is explored in relation to wavelength and incidence angle. The proposed theory provides a foundational understanding of the surface plasmon-Rayleigh anomaly interaction and its magneto-optical implications, with potential to guide the design of surface plasmon-based magneto-optical devices.

In the process of training artificial neural networks, Knowledge Distillation (KD) plays a significant role. Our study introduces a novel, highly effective, and efficient model called DB3 - Decision-based Black-box Knowledge Distillation. Unlike traditional KD methods, DB3 selects specific difficult data samples from a teacher model and uses them to train a student model. This selection process is made by solving a minimum risk optimization problem, where the objective is to minimize the expected loss of the student model. Our proposed DB3 method is a general framework that can be applied to various knowledge distillation scenarios. Experimental results show that DB3 significantly improves the accuracy of student networks across multiple settings, including knowledge distillation from a single teacher, multiple teachers, and unsupervised knowledge distillation.

Determining the ratios of branching fractions for specific decay paths, such as $\Lambda_b \to p J/\psi$ or $\Lambda_b \to \Lambda_c \pi$, is crucial for understanding the behavior of $B$ particles. Our study utilizes approximately 3 separate days of data, gathered at an energy of 10.08 GeV with the LHCb detector, to calculate these ratios and determine the branching fractions by eliminating background and measuring the detected particle momenta. For the $\Lambda_b \to p J/\psi$ decay, the measured branching fraction is found to be greater than 0.006 $p^2$ and falls within a 1.3$\times 10^{-5}$ range for the $\Lambda_b \to \Lambda_c \pi$ decay. Additionally, the calculated ratio of branching fractions for $\Lambda_b \to p J/\psi$ to $\Lambda_b \to \Lambda_c \pi$ is determined to be more than 20 times greater than the latter.

Let $\mathbf{P}$ be a finite-dimensional, multiplicity-free $G$-module under the action of a connected solvable group $G$. This report outlines a systematic approach to reconstructing the lattice of submodules of $\mathbf{P}$ using information about the Weyl group of $G$ and the irreducible modules of the Lie algebra of the semisimple part of $G$. Additionally, if $\mathbf{P}$ is irreducible, this approach also efficiently determines the composition factors of $\mathbf{P}$. If $\mathbf{P}$ is not irreducible, this report provides a way to obtain its composition factors from those of its simple submodules. This construction process is then applied to modules $\mathbf{P}$ that are relative simple modules, i.e., modules whose lattice of submodules is connected and has no minimal elements except for simple modules.

This research paper investigates the Geodetic Recognition problem, a graph theory question. Given a potential geodetic vertex subset, the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem asks to confirm or deny its geodetic property. The task is to do this by using a restricted set of vertex distances, specifically distances between adjacent vertices. The study examines the computational complexity of solving this problem for various types of graph structures, including general graphs, undirected graphs, and directed graphs with weighted edges. The research also considers the case when the target geodetic subset is specified, as well as the impact of this specification on computational complexity. The results show that determining the minimum number of vertices required to geodetically cover a given target subset is NP-complete, even in undirected trees. However, the problem can be solved efficiently for certain types of graph structures, such as series-parallel graphs, by using trapezoid area minimization. The research also presents an efficient algorithm for strong geodetic recognition in undirected trees. The algorithm extends naturally to series-parallel graphs and weighted directed graphs with a specific property called the Dijkstra's property.

The main limitation of many imitation learning methods lies in their failure to account for correlations between action dependencies, resulting in poor performance. To address this, we introduce an efficient new framework for imitation learning, utilizing self-supervised learning to uncover the underlying action dynamics. Our framework triggers a significant boost in sample efficiency, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods by over an order of magnitude. Notably, our algorithm achieves precise action imitation on complex tasks, such as imitating an human operator's robotic arm movements.

Co-imitation learning encourages collaboration among multiple agents with distinct areas of expertise. Our research takes this concept in a novel direction by exploring an approach called Relative Error Guided Co-imitation Learning (REGC). Existing co-imitation learning methods primarily involve training multiple agents to achieve common goals and then having these agents provide feedback to each other. In contrast, our proposed REGC method identifies two agents, trains one as a model, and uses the model to generate relative error signals to guide the other agent towards improving performance. Unlike traditional methods that require expert demonstrations, REGC can work with unsupervised learning data. Additionally, REGC generates error signals relative to the model's performance, allowing the guided agent to surpass the model's level of performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of REGC through a study applying it to the challenging Game AI domain. Specifically, we used the Large Scale Cognitive Architecture (LSA) to create a complex game environment called the "intelligence room," and developed a co-imitation learning setup using REGC that successfully enhanced the performance of agents in this environment.

We investigated the properties of a sequential decoder that decodes polar codes under a polarized cutoff rate, q. Our findings show that, regardless of the density of the original source, the sequential decoder errors in thetas range from nearly zero when q is highly positive to nearly one when q is heavily negative. Additionally, we observed that the optimal q value often lies outside the estimated range and often differs from the actual source density. This variability of q is attributed to rounding errors inherent in the construction of polar code. Simulations validate our q density measurements and illustrate how it is often difficult for the sequential decoder to avoid errors due to these rounding errors, even when the code rate is as low as 0.4. Furthermore, when the code rate is 0.6 or higher, the sequential decoder often recovers the original message without error, indicating a potential benefit in using larger density codes for low-density sources.

We introduce a novel action space optimization approach called GSA-SML, 
which utilizes a generative adversarial procedure to fine-tune the action space 
for supervised machine translation tasks. Our method leverages a learned density 
estimator to craft a latent space that maximizes the likelihood of acceptable 
actions. In experiments, GSA-SML yields superior performance when compared to baseline 
methods and traditional reinforcement learning models. Our findings indicate that 
improving the action space results in significant gains in model efficacy, exceeding 
20% in BLEU score in the WMT'14 EN>DE translation task. The code is available at 
https://github.com/ghiplert/GSA-SML.

Lately, robot operators have relied heavily on human intuition and visual assessment for error-prone end-effector pose estimation during calibration. Yet, this approach falls short in ensuring the accuracy required for safe and productive robot operation. To address this issue, our research introduces a novel, autonomous system that leverages 3D rendering technology to generate realistic virtual environments, allowing for automated end-effector pose estimation and validation using machine learning-based computer vision techniques. By incorporating a depth camera to detect and respond to physical obstacles, our approach enhances the accuracy and robustness of the estimation process. Furthermore, this system is designed to minimize disruptions to regular production operations by validating the end-effector pose only when absolutely necessary.

This study explores the relationship between continuous retracts and quasi-finitely generated spaces in the context of metric spaces. We establish that the subset of continuous retracts from a metric space is closed under the Quasi-Finitely Generated Space (QFS) topology, and this closure property characterizes metric spaces with closed retracts that have the QFS topology. Additionally, we find that locally compact, metric spaces with closed retracts that have the QFS topology are equivalent to spaces with continuous retracts that have the QFS topology.

The rise of far-right nationalism in recent European elections has sparked concern about rising political polarization. Research into the digital footprints of political opinions typically focuses on direct expressions of opinion through comments, voting, or social media posts. In contrast, research into online opinion dynamics often overlooks the influence of browsing habits on political polarization. In this study, we investigate online browsing habits and their effect on political polarization, drawing on a large dataset of hyperlinks from 140,000 random Web pages. Our analysis reveals that users' browsing habits exert a more substantial influence on political polarization than hyperlink structures, with users consistently splitting into factions along ideological lines regardless of Web pages visited. Moreover, mapping the Web as a network of user connections reveals a higher degree of polarization than anticipated, with certain areas ("bubbles") exhibiting particularly strong ideological divides. Our findings suggest that online browsing habits merit closer scrutiny to understand online opinion dynamics and promote targeted initiatives to reduce polarization.

The Thompson group V is one of the earliest discovered finitely generated non-solvable group. Despite significant research, many basic properties of V remain unknown. This study focuses on the word problem of V, revealing a connection to deterministic context-free languages that contain no parallels. This relationship establishes a connection between the word problem of V and undecidability proofs relying on a closure property involving deterministic context-free languages. The associated Turing machine's existence or non-existence can be used to prove specific undecidability results, such as the impossibility of determining whether a context-free language contains a member of a defined set.

An open system that exchanges information with its environment can sustain a bi-directional flow of information, which we demonstrate using a quantum circuit can also be achieved without causal links between the system and environment. Using a photonic setup, we experimentally show that two-way information exchange occurs when a quantum process with information flow is applied to a state of light traveling through an optical circuit. This is proven through both theoretical description and experimental observation.
