Our findings uncover a novel aspect of quantum dynamics and offer a practical method for creating anti-zero-knowledge proofs within a quantum context.

This study explores how certain operators affect the conditions under which biharmonic hypersurfaces in the Euclidean space become minimal. Specifically, we establish the relationship between two types of operators, recurrent operators and conformal Ricci operator, and investigate their impacts on the conditions for biharmonic surfaces to be minimal in the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. Our analysis demonstrates that the application of either recurrent operators or the conformal Ricci operator to the second structure vector of a biharmonic surface results in the surface having a certain symmetry. Furthermore, we identify the condition necessary for a biharmonic surface to be minimal in the Euclidean space when subjected to the conformal Ricci operator. This research builds upon a previous study by the second author, addressing a question posed by it.

We provide a characterization for p/q-reducible subsets of the set (N_p/q)^d, showing it consists of elements that can be covered by a union of flat layers, each defined by a rational number q/p. Additionally, we offer a finite sequence of elements in (N_p/q)^d that can generate any p/q-reducible subset through application of the shift map. Utilizing this characterization, we offer methods for calculating the p/q-reachability and q/p-reachability matrices for any subset of (N_p/q)^d.

A comprehensive, predictive framework is presented where the electroweak vacuum is stabilized and the strong CP problem is solved through a complex transformation in a $a_u$MSM model. This transformation makes the complex field contribution to the Thompson parity breaking term negligible, thus naturally providing a solution to the strong CP problem. Furthermore, the model incorporates six dimensional threshold corrections that further minimizes the axion-like particle mass. As a result, the model predicts the mass of the axion-like particle to be 23.5 MicroeV, which can be verified or rejected with upcoming experiments using light dark matter detectors. Additionally, the model forecasts the mass of the next largest threshold correction to be above 700 MeV, which can be confirmed or contradicted with data from charm, bottom, or top meson decay studies.

This study presents a catalog of binary candidates based on data from the Large Sky Area Multiobject Fiber Spectrograph (LAMOST) time-domain survey. The catalog contains 133,331 candidates across 1.8 square degrees in the sky, comprising 12,046 new periodic variable star candidates, 121,285 new binary candidates, and 1,000 new small-amplitude double-line spectrum binary candidates. The LAMOST time-domain survey lasted two years, during which 38,044 new variable star candidates were detected. The catalog is the largest of its kind, formed through a automated workflow that used observational data from the LAMOST. The catalog is first filtered for variables and spectrum line binaries, and is visually inspected to be accurate. Many interesting objects have been discovered from this catalog, and further research is needed to verify the status of these candidates.

In the context of image segmentation, the conventional approach of using Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) has been widely adopted and refined. To overcome the limitations of this method, the Edge-Gated CNN (EG-CNN) recently emerged as an alternative and superior solution. By incorporating an external edge map obtained through Simple Linear Transform (SLT), EG-CNNs utilize this map to guide the network through an edge-gating mechanism, ignoring irrelevant features and focusing on essential ones. As a result, EG-CNNs have displayed superior performance in multiple datasets, surpassing the performance of standard DCNNs in image segmentation tasks. Despite the success of EG-CNNs, the underlying theory and reason behind their effectiveness remain unclear. In an effort to provide a theoretical basis for the edge-gating mechanism, we proposed the Conceptual Brain-Inspired Edge-gating (C-BIE) model, a mathematical framework that illustrates the network's ability to leverage edge maps through the EG-method. Through this model, we derived the Condition for Maximum Accuracy (CMA), a key finding that offers insights into the optimal design of EG-CNNs, thereby facilitating the development of more efficient and effective networks. Our experimental validations revealed that the proposed C-BIE model can be applied across diverse networks, leading to significant improvements in multiple datasets. Moreover, the derivatives of the model can be utilized as performance indicators to monitor and optimize network efficiency. Ultimately, our theoretical framework has the potential to empower the

We analyze the concurrency properties of three high-level concurrency theories: weak isolation, strong isolation, and rigid isolation. Two-case studies of real database systems are examined: WIREDTIER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER deployments in MongoDB, and Oracle RAC with Oracle Database, with a discussion on how they relate to these theories. This work also formulates testable implications for these database systems and applies them to evaluate the accuracy of previously published statements about the concurrency properties of these systems. Furthermore, it introduces and evaluates more complex concurrency models that these database systems aim to satisfy.

Given a Dyck path $\pi$, the $e$-positivity of the corresponding chromatic symmetric function $X_\pi$ holds if all coefficients in its expansion via Schensted correspondence are non-negative. Previous research established the $e$-positivity of certain combinatorial objects, including their underlying Downset posets, by demonstrating strong similarities between these posets and Boolean algebras corresponding to posets of standard Young tableaux, which in turn are linked to Schensted correspondence and $e$-positivity. This paper introduces a novel approach to ensuring the $e$-positivity of $\pi$ by focusing directly on the Downset posets $A_\pi$. It is shown that if the interval module $A_{\sigma\circ\pi}$ exhibits $e$-positivity for all Dyck paths $\pi$, then $\sigma$ is an avatar of a Dyck path, and further, $A_\pi$ has $e$-positive intervals if and only if $\pi$ is derived from another Dyck path $\sigma$ such that $A_{\sigma\circ\pi}$ has $e$-positive intervals. Additionally, this research introduces the Downset poset $A_{\pi^c}$ corresponding to the complement of a Dyck path $\pi$, and demonstrates that $A_{\pi^c}$ has $e$-positive intervals if and only if $\pi$ has an optimal weakly

We're exploring a novel idea called hindsight summarization to reduce the negative impact of inaccurate predictions in learning sequences. This technique involves using past events to gain a more accurate understanding of a previous event whose meaning was initially misunderstood. We introduce a condition called the Summarization Property, which ensures that hindsight summarization can decrease the amount of error accumulated over time. We also examine two types of summarization - one that involves learning a new summary based on a previous understanding and another that is already known. For the first type, we show that a correct prediction can be achieved with a linear learning rule. For the second type, we provide examples of both linear and logarithmic learning rules that can result in correct predictions. Our results demonstrate that hindsight summarization can prevent the accumulation of prediction error, which is a crucial concept in the theory of learning from example.

The success of machine learning in medical image analysis relies on the quality and relevance of the training data. However, certain implicit biases built into image datasets can cause models to perform poorly when applied to different populations. This phenomenon can be observed in the AT&T Western Face Dataset, which contains images of Caucasian individuals with facial injuries. Despite its limited size, the dataset is effective in predicting X-ray images of facial fractures. Yet, the model exhibits a significant lack of generalizability when applied to images of African individuals. This phenomenon can be attributed to the implicit bias present in the dataset. To overcome this limitation, a new dataset of face images has been created, consisting of 1000 X-ray images of facial fractures in both sexes, along with corresponding machine learning models that demonstrate improved generalizability.

We study an Ising model where a network of connected triangles interacts with each other through different coupling strengths, considering a magnetic field that influences the spins at different strengths. By examining the model's hysteresis loop as it's heated and cooled under varying conditions, we find that the shape of the loop changes in a way that's influenced by the spin-spin interactions within the triangles, and that certain patterns emerge that are distinct from those found in similar studies of random networks. Additionally, we develop an exact analytical method to analyze the model's behavior as it's subjected to increasing temperature, and our calculations are verified through numerical simulations and comparisons with traditional mean-field theories.

New measurements of the energy distribution of solar particles taken at very close ranges to the sun have been analyzed. Despite the challenges of collecting data under these conditions, observations within 0.36 AU by the ENERGY and GOES spacecraft allowed for a comparison with typical solar particle energy patterns at 1 AU. The data show that the energy structure depends on the speed of the particles and their starting point, with the distribution becoming more uniform at very small distances due to the influence of solar gravity.

Our proposed Multi-Lingual Multi-Data Emotional Expression Recognition (MLMDER) model aims to enhance adaptability in identifying emotions beyond single languages and small datasets. This is because current facial expression recognition techniques often rely on data from speaking populations and are typically designed to function across multiple languages without consideration of the significant differences in facial anatomy between languages. To achieve adaptability in FER, we believe it's essential to develop a model that can effectively utilize data from multiple languages. To this end, we introduce an attention-based multi-lingual multi-data attention network (AMANDA) that incorporates a novel technique to learn context-specific attention for each emotional expression across multiple datasets in different languages, allowing the model to efficiently process multiple datasets with different facial anatomy. The AMANDA model demonstrates its superiority over the current state-of-the-art approach in cross-language FER in our experimental results, showcasing enhanced adaptability when handling datasets with different facial anatomy.

Applying high hydrostatic pressure causes a significant transformation in the crystal structure of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$, a complex oxide with spirally connected Aurivillius layers.  At 4.5 GPa, the material undergoes a first-order phase transition from its tunable $a$-axis polar structure to a nonpolar tetragonal structure.  Throughout this transition, the lattice parameters show distinct variations, with the $a$-axis length decreasing by over 8 percent and the $c$-axis length increasing by over 14 percent.  Once the material reaches 7.8 GPa, the structure reverts back to its initial form as pressure drops to 0.1 GPa.  Notably, this structural transformation is marked by a sudden shift in dielectric behavior, with the polarization becoming fixed in the same direction initially present below the phase transition's onset.  This phenomenon indicates that seed polar domains play a crucial role in determining the material's electrical properties.  Consequently, the material exhibits hysteresis in dielectric behavior upon decreasing pressure, mirroring its electrical response when pressure is increased.  This unique behavior could have potential applications in data storage technology.

We analyze the impact of an alternative error bound metric, localized error bound comparison, on the accuracy of discrete paths compared to optimal continuous trajectories in time-expanded graphs. We demonstrate that localized error bound comparison leads to tighter bounds on the approximation error, resulting in an O(1/h^2) error bound, which is similar to that achieved by dynamic programming under the standard error bound metric in certain cases. However, our method incorporates localized error bounds into the policy iteration framework. We further establish that the benefit of localized error bound comparison is most significant in scenarios with limited discretization, particularly those with slow variable change. Additionally, our method is applicable to a broader category of problem structures, including those with non-separable cost functions. We illustrate the performance of localized error bound comparison through numerical experiments on multiple example problems.

The perfect shock wave theory was expanded to account for the effects of viscous forces in a recent study. The results from this research indicate that another unique phenomenon emerges near the center of highly powerful shocks, characterized by sudden, almost instant formation. This phenomenon is observed in a specific range of adiabatic powers greater than three. The relationship between the shock's rotation period and the time it takes to form the shock wave was found to be proportional to the square of the shock's rotation period. This rotation-induced formation of shocks explains the observed delays in certain rotating star explosions. Estimates suggest that such shocks could result in the production of gravitational waves of a specific frequency, related to the shock's own rotation frequency. Furthermore, this could lead to detectable signals in future experiments such as LIGO, particularly in shocks formed through the implosions of sub-mass black hole mergers. These explosions might also provide a potential opportunity to study particle acceleration in this context.

Decay rate parametrizations introduced by Caprini, Lellouch, Neubert, Boyd, Grinstein, and Lebed have been widely adopted, though it's only recently become clear how these models relate to each other. We've investigated decay rate parametrizations in a comprehensive manner, exploring their underlying connections and distinct characteristics. Our findings suggest that the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed frameworks represent parallel frameworks, each offering valuable insights into decay rate behaviour. We've also determined the relevant parameters required for each framework, as well as the relationships between them, and have explored the potential for further decay rate parametrizations. Moreover, we've investigated the role of heavy-quark symmetry in decay rate behaviour and identified potential areas for future research within this field.

We establish a polynomial Heisenberg algebra that maintains one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics non-singular potentials equivalent to the harmonic oscillator. Our framework encompasses both regular and reversed potentials, alongside their intricate combinations. The polynomial Heisenberg algebra is comprised of three generators: one charge and two operators, with two distinct 'echo' properties. We demonstrate that our algebraic framework yields precise spectra for all non-singular potentials derived from the SUSY QM, including those involving periodic functions, and that our harmonic oscillator representation can be applied to both Schr\"{o}dinger and Dirac equations.

This study develops an approach for approximately determining a key characteristic of continuous time systems - Lyapunov exponent values - using periodic orbit trajectories from the corresponding discrete time systems. The proposed method is applicable to a broad range of systems and can be employed to identify both short and long-term Lyapunov exponents. The technique is primarily focused on non-singular, distinct eigenvalues and may need additional analysis to be applied to systems with repeated or imaginary eigenvalues. The method does not involve differentiating the system's parameters in relation to the observing variables. Instead, it directly utilizes the parameters of the discrete time system that corresponds to the original continuous time system. The proposed method has the advantage of being computationally efficient as compared to other available methods. Furthermore, it has been found that in the context of harmonic periodic orbits, the Lyapunov exponent approach provides an accurate measurement of the system's dynamics. This is because such orbits are localized in the phase space and represent a stable or unstable manifold of the system. The results of this study can also be applied to switching dynamic systems that consist of continuous time systems with distinct parameters. The proposed method has been successfully demonstrated through its application to well-known systems, such as the Van der Pol oscillator and the Chua circuit with a nonlinear resistor.

This research investigates the switching current in an asymmetric Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) consisting of two Josephson junctions that are not isolated from each other. An important factor influencing the switching current, particularly in macroscopic quantum phenomena, is the presence of a fixed voltage state caused by phase locking between the junctions. An asymmetric SQUID can exhibit two fixed-voltage states, one with a high voltage state dominant in the $0$ phase-locking region and another with a low voltage state prevailing in the $\pi$ phase-locking region. An asymmetric SQUID with two highly coupled junctions is modeled by combining the resistive model and the flux-quantum model. Our study shows that the presence of phase locking between the junctions significantly affects the switching current, particularly in the $\pi$ phase-locking region where it is reduced due to the junctions' coupling. Moreover, the minimum resistance required to stabilize the $\pi$ phase-locking state is proportional to the junctions' resistance. This proportionality holds for both the flux-quantum and arc-voltage approximations. The model is experimentally verified using an asymmetric SQUID device incorporating vanadium nitride junctions, where the theoretical $\pi$ phase-locking current is calculated and compared to actual measurement data.

We've developed a unified approach to investigate the non-abelian aether term's impact on thermal radiation and the Casimir energy for both simple and complex systems. Our analysis indicates that the non-abelian aether term influences the Stefan-Boltzmann law in a manner dependent on the interaction type, whereas its effect on the complex systems' Casimir energy is found to be $- \pi^2 k_B^4$ for the scalar field and $- \pi^2 (k_B^2 + (2\mu c)^2)(N+1)k_B^4$ for the vector and Dirac fields, when interacting with a perfect mirror.

This research develops a novel numerical approach for estimating the expected liquidity cost of a derivative instrument before hedging. The method employs a Black-Karasinski interest rate model and a closed-form formula for the expected liquidity cost, which the study modifies to accommodate numerical approximation. The proposed method calculates the expected liquidity cost through a first-order integration formula, allowing for faster convergence than Monte Carlo simulation. The research compares the results from the new method, the Monte Carlo simulation, and the original closed-form formula to demonstrate its effectiveness.

This paper expands on a previous study by Duvaut and Raouau about analyzing integral functionals in a deterministic setting, where the dependencies of energy models are limited by linear differential equations with non-constant coefficients. We develop a computational method for determining the optimal strategies that minimize these constrained dependencies, using a control-theory approach. By extending the method to account for stochastic factors and considering the problem of controlling singular stochastic partial differential equations with linear constraints, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach.

We've completed a comprehensive analysis of tidal features in early-type galaxies using the Survey of Planetary Systems (SPS) and the Survey of Science with a Spatially Unbiased Telescope (S$^2$Ute). Our observations revealed a significant correlation between tidal features and planetary systems in the data set, with a correlated pattern occurring at a 99.9% confidence level. The features are likely the result of collisions between galaxies and their planetary systems that occur as the galaxies move at their own cosmic speed over a period of billions of years. The frequency of tidal features increases with the mass of the galaxies and their surrounding planetary systems. However, the probability of observing tidal features does not correlate with the mass of the galaxies' central black holes. The shape of the galaxies also influences the probability of observing tidal features, with more irregular shapes indicating a greater likelihood of visible tidal features. The probability of observing tidal features is estimated to be between 10% and 30%, indicating that many early-type galaxies with no visible tidal features may still be affected by galaxy systems.

A society's distribution of opportunities affects the future socioeconomic status of its offspring, which can have far-reaching consequences on social mobility, equality, and overall social structure. This study explores the interconnectedness of opportunity allocation across generations through a comprehensive framework that incorporates various forms of intergenerational exchange. Our analysis reveals that certain equilibria may yield unequal opportunities with limited social mobility, while others can facilitate equal opportunities and social mobility. Interestingly, some pathways that lead to unequal opportunities can actually promote equality in the long run. Furthermore, we find that certain forms of intergenerational exchange can exacerbate inequality, whereas others can help attain equal opportunities. Our most striking discovery is that certain types of exchange can give rise to nonlinear effects on social mobility, influencing it in an opposite direction than anticipated.

This paper delves into the intricate task of precisely modeling advanced CPA and NLO-based laser systems that incorporate a high-power pre-amplifier, a CPA system with a high number of pulses, and a combination of NLO crystals with varying probabilities of conversion. By examining these systems, we identify three key factors that significantly complicate their simulation: the intense, potentially damaging nature of CPA systems that require special safety precautions; the unpredictable fragmentation of pulses occurring during NLO conversion; and the difficulty of measuring quantum fields quantatively. Utilizing field theory, we develop a novel approach to simulate these systems and apply it to a specific example, a CPA-based laser system. The experimental observation of quantum effects in these systems is shown to be accessible by our method. Furthermore, our approach allows for the simulation of THz NLO effects, and we demonstrate its usefulness with a hypothetical example.

For $p = 1$ or $p > 2$, the unit ball of $\ell_p$ doesn't have an isometric linear reduction to a finite-dimensional space with an relative error of $\varepsilon$. Alternatively, this equivalence is also shown for $1 \le p \le 2$ with $\varepsilon$ smaller than $2 - \sqrt{2}$.

Precise measurements of beam-beam interactions in colliding beam experiments are crucial for understanding possible limitations on luminosity due to beam separation constraints in future colliders. This study involves analyzing the beam-beam effects at the HL-LH, specifically in the interaction point, using a 3.9 TeV center-of-mass energy and a 45 kHz beam collision rate. Through detailed simulation, we have derived closed orbit differences between incoming and outgoing beams for various transverse motion settings. These measurements are accurate to within 0.1 $\mu$m. The results also show that beam-beam interactions cause the formation of persistent long-range forces, resulting in shifts in beam energy of up to 20 MeV, and distinct time-dependent oscillation frequencies in both horizontal and vertical planes. These phenomena directly correlate with the beam's native oscillation frequencies. Additionally, we have determined the optimal 4-D fill structure and closed orbit settings that minimize beam-beam effects at the cost of increased native oscillation time or reduced native oscillation frequency, respectively. These findings can inform future optimization studies in similar colliders.

We've developed a innovative method for solving distributed optimization problems, where some nodes have access to sensitive data and want to keep it private. These nodes, who are essentially agents on a network, want to run a optimization algorithm while protecting their information. The challenge is that some agents may deliberately attempt to disrupt the process, whereas others strive to maintain smooth communication. To tackle this issue, we're proposing a decentralized approach where the focus is on designing a robust optimization algorithm that can perform well even in the presence of malicious nodes. The system is represented by a undirected connected graph, where each node has a private function value and data vector. The goal is to minimize the cumulative function value while estimating the cumulative data vector. The main contribution here is a decentralized double public auditing algorithm for a specific scenario where the graph has an odd number of nodes and exactly one trustworthy node. The algorithm is then adapted for a broader scenario where any number of nodes can be trustworthy. The study shows that the proposed algorithm achieves the optimal robust no-regret rate of O(sqrt(T)), where T represents the number of iterations.

The forthcoming generation of cosmological instruments will necessitate a more precise understanding of instrumental systematic effects, potentially affecting future experiments such as CMB-S4. To facilitate this, we introduce a public software suite that generates realistic instrumental effects and related systematic impacts on CMB maps and experiment data. This software comprises: a data generation module based on real-time Monte Carlo simulations, which models instrumental effects and related systematic effects on temperature and polarization maps and experiment data; a legacy data analysis module, utilizing existing data and analyses to inform Monte Carlo simulations; and a visualization and reporting module, providing users with easy access to systematic effect maps, model parameter adjustment, and simulation status. This software is designed to be adaptable to future applications and is already utilized in ongoing research related to CMB-S4.

BART is a robust word-ordering model that has seen significant use in recent years. Nonetheless, a crucial aspect of its effectiveness remains poorly understood: how does it generate orders? A thorough analysis of BART's order-generating capabilities is a crucial step in unlocking the potential of its hidden representations for tasks like text generation and language processing. To this end, we examine the model's performance in word ordering and a related task called partial tree linearization. Our findings reveal that BART excels in both tasks, surpassing LSTM-based models and achieving accurate results. Interestingly, we observe that the order outputs of BART and another strong model, T5, correlate highly with the original order, but also exhibit the ability to be manipulated through input manipulation. These properties of BART provide a strong foundation for further research into the analysis of its hidden representations and the integration of order generation with other language models.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic multimedia across social platforms is fueled by automated deepfake technology, which poses significant risks to the reliability of online information. To address this issue, deepfake detection methods have rapidly evolved, with particular focus on creating systems that can effectively identify fake content across various media types. While previous research has primarily concentrated on developing single-domain deepfake detection tools, the latest work lies in creating networks that can simultaneously identify deepfakes in multiple domains. This paper delves into existing cross-domain deepfake detection approaches and proposes a novel architecture that integrates two complementary systems: a feature extraction module and a capacity-enhanced module incorporating cross-stitch connections. The proposed architecture is then applied to a deepfake detection network that can operate across multiple domains and is demonstrated using the FaceForeniscs++ dataset, achieving exceptional performance that surpasses current standards.

The performance of iterative decoding methods, such as log-domain semi-analytical threshold analysis, can be efficiently assessed for complex, variable-density erasure channels. However, these methods can only provide limited insights into the underlying structural properties of sparse, variable-density code ensembles. In contrast, degree-degree correlations, crucial for understanding code ensemble dynamics during iterative decoding, are completely captured by the standardized version of the degree distribution matrix. Specifically, this work investigates how negative degree-degree correlations affect the maximum erasure probabilities that can be handled by density-evolution-based LDPC codes. Numerical techniques, such as exact-to-PCA distance calculation and iterative application of the PCA equation, are used to analyze the effects of variable-density correlations on parity-check matrix structures and decoding dynamics. In the limit of infinite code size, the impact of correlation on first-spacer probability is analyzed in detail. Additionally, this research demonstrates that LDPC ensembles with specific, negative degree-degree correlation patterns can exhibit superior performance superiority over those with zero correlation and no inherent density distribution structure.

We have developed an efficient attack on a weak decoy state QKD system, employing a single-photon source as a vacuum reference, without causing a spike in detection data. This attack occurs before the side information exchange phase. The attacker uses the vacuum reference to identify entangled states sent by the user, and extracts information from these states. The attacker then sends a weak decoy state and observes the decoy state's phase, allowing them to distinguish sent codewords from entangled states. The success of this attack is demonstrated with weak decoy states, using a source with high encoding efficiency, specifically the COJEN source, which poses a significant threat to the security of QKD systems that utilize a vacuum reference.

In the context of edge computing, minimizing data transmission and processing costs amounts to controlling energy consumption at these facilities. The ECO-APX algorithm is introduced to optimize energy efficiency, with a larger problem formulation also being solved by the ECO-UB algorithm. Both algorithms process data at the edge, with the option to utilize the main server for certain queries. The choice of algorithms is shown to have a significant impact on energy consumption, with the option to use the main server costing twice as much. The problem is confirmed to be NP-hard, with a data transmission cost metric defined to categorize the problem as APX-hard. The evaluation utilizes a simulated environment based on real machine data, with the results showing the algorithms to have effective energy efficiency. The evaluation also examines the impact of different algorithms on energy consumption, with the option to use the main server proving costly.

This paper expands on previous work by Kazda, Stepan, and Sotirov, who defined an 'angle function' which enables conformal embeddability in certain types of spaces (parabolic, elliptic, and some hyperbolic spaces). We extend this concept to include metric spaces with a loop space structure, specifically those with riemannian metric loops where the loop measure has a non-negative norm. We demonstrate that this generalized 'angle function' is bounded, and can be used to establish a necessary and sufficient condition for conformal embeddability in such spaces.

We derive a broad inequality that applies to a vast majority of isomorphism classes of orders in number fields F, specifically involving the product of certain norms from subfields L within the isomorphic class. This inequality links the product of m-torsion points under various Frobenius operations in L, to a similar product in F. By narrowing our focus to cases where the isomorphism class contains an order with distinct real embeddings, we can establish a more direct connection - namely, the product of m-torsion points under various Frobenius operations in L equals the product of similar elements in F, both products being greater than 1. This finding builds upon earlier work by David, Gramel, and Karras, and has implications for estimates involving isomorphism classes of orders in number fields F, particularly when considering subfields L of minimal degree [L:F]=2.

The breakdown of granular temperature gradients in a nitrogen jet lifting off from a horizontal surface has been examined using particle imaging velocimetry and laser doppler velocimetry. The investigation focused on jets with low pressure and high velocity, where flow separation occurs. Results show that increasing pressure reduces the extent of granular turbulence, as observed in suspended particles. However, when measuring velocity, an increase in pressure actually reduces the accuracy of measuring velocity gradients, despite needing a higher resolution to capture flow separation. This distinction highlights different scaling for measuring granular temperature and velocity, with the former relying on higher resolution due to more gradual changes and the latter requiring higher resolution only in areas with large velocity shifts, such as flow separation.

The early stages of planet formation are not well understood, but it's thought that particles must first coalesce into smaller solid bodies, called planetesimals, before eventually becoming full-fledged planets. While researchers have varying opinions on the exact mechanisms driving their formation, it's generally accepted that vortices in protoplanetary disks could play a significant role. A recent study by Rottmann et al. analyzed the behavior of vortices using high-resolution simulations. They focused specifically on a portion of the disk where material is being swept up by a forming planet, and observed how vortices formed, grew, and broke apart under these conditions. According to their findings, vortices initially maintained their stability, and ultimately gave rise to four distinct streams of particles traveling in different directions, including one that ultimately contributed to the formation of a new planetesimal. High-resolution snapshots of the vortex can be found on YouTube at https://youtube/VvC7H6A79lo.

Building on the edge-channels formulation, we developed an efficient method to identify neutral modes in a broad range of systems driven out of equilibrium, extending beyond quantum Hall systems to superconductors, topological insulators, and photonic systems. This approach simplifies the calculation of neutral mode currents by leveraging a slow variation hypothesis, and can be applied in scenarios where a drive operator and its hermitian conjugate have distinct edge-channel projections. By utilizing this method, we created a simulation tool that quickly detects neutral modes in both continuous and discrete time models, and demonstrated its effectiveness in several examples, including quantum Hall systems, topological superconductors, 1-dimensional topological insulators, and photonic systems with spatially extended drives.

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra over the complex numbers, and set $\mathfrak{h}_0$ to be its Cartan subalgebra. For a given parameter $q$, in the set of non-zero complex numbers, we denote the quantum group associated with $\mathfrak{g}$ as $\mathbf{U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$. A given set of elements $\bar{\Theta}$, which consists of $\Theta_1,\ldots,\Theta_m$, serves as a basis for $\mathbf{U}_q(\mathfrak{g})$. By leveraging Turaev's work, we establish that the set $\bar{\Theta}$ upholds certain characteristics. Firstly, the braid group action outlined by Lusztig is correctly defined on $\bar{\Theta}$. Secondly, the Dynkin automorphisms $\sigma\mapsto s_w(\sigma)^{-1}$, where $w$ represents a permutation within the Weyl group, exert the same action on the elements of $\bar{\Theta}$ as they do on the corresponding elements of the original basis $\Theta$. Thirdly, the scalar product defined by Lusztig, often denoted as $(\cdot,\cdot)_q$, is reflexive upon the set $\bar{\Theta}$. Lastly, the T-systems of Lusztig derive their origin from the action of the Kostant section

We develop a new decentralized stochastic gradient descent method called DR-DSGD, which achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{KT} + K^{2/3}\log^{1/3}(T))$ in the decentralized learning setting. This convergence rate is refined to $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{KT})$ under the scenario of minimization. Our approach is characterized by devices communicating with each other and a central server, with data replication allowing for direct information exchange. We model data replication as a random graph and establish a connection between it and the DR-DSGD algorithm, enabling an analysis based on the graph's properties. Our results demonstrate that DR-DSGD outperforms existing decentralized learning algorithms in terms of convergence rate and simplicity.

The iconic hard-disk model has been the subject of numerous studies despite the celebrated phase-transition scenario that arises from it being intensely debated, with many considering it the most intricate to grasp in statistical mechanics. This dissertation focuses on the Shapiro-Love anomaly, a peculiar feature that occurs during the transition and has an especially great difficulty in being understood. We've established a reliable method for detecting first derivatives, and specifically tailored it to address the anomaly's measurements. We've used this approach to analyze various ensembles, and our results reveal that the Shapiro-Love anomaly is an intrinsic component of the hard-disk model's transition, with the proposed method also providing the most accurate measurements to date. Additionally, our research has the benefit of simplifying the analysis by eliminating the need to differentiate raw profiles, and has the theoretical implication of contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of the anomaly through the examination of its derivatives in isolation.

Our study investigates how nuclear parton distribution functions affect jet shape in LHC experiments, specifically considering the effects of parton cascades and parton-hadron interaction. Calculations are performed using the PYTHIA program, modified to incorporate EPOS and JEWEL simulations, and compare jet shapes in proton-proton and heavy ion collisions to find the distinct nuclear impact. Additionally, we analyze how using different nuclear parton distribution functions affects jet structure, and provide guidelines for reducing the influence of PDF choices in future experiments.

Our research examines the underlying dynamics of pyramid schemes, specifically focusing on Forsage, a well-known multi-level marketing platform. Forsage operated from 2019 to 2020 and attracted over 760,000 participants worldwide, largely in developing countries. Through a comprehensive analysis of over 18 million transactions and over 780,000 user accounts, as well as a detailed study of over 1.5 million referral relationships, we have obtained significant insights into Forsage's behavior. Unfortunately, our findings reveal that nearly all users, at a rate of about 99.5%, ultimately suffer financial losses as a result of being involved in Forsage. We have identified various mechanisms employed by the scheme to extract value from users, including recurring donations, exaggerated earnings, and forced purchases. Additionally, we have observed that Forsage's top earners continue to profit significantly, taking home over $150 million in 2020, largely by exploiting members who lose money. Our study offers an in-depth view of Forsage's internal workings and the methods it uses to defraud its users, providing valuable insights into the fundamental nature of pyramid schemes and their ability to succeed despite being unsustainable and universally losing for users in the long term.

Three new globular cluster candidates within the Milky Way have been investigated using advanced imaging and spectroscopic analysis from the VLT and the 10.4m Gran Telescopes. Initially discovered as anomalous globular clusters by the Pan-STARRS survey, we employed a novel approach that incorporated data from the APOGEE spectroscopic survey to explore the structural and chemical characteristics of these objects. Initially, we based our investigations on assumptions that they were 10 billion years old and had masses similar to those of established globular clusters. However, our analysis revealed that these objects exhibit features more common in younger clusters and are likely 7-10 billion years old. Furthermore, we observed that one of these candidates, MGC-1, is distinguished by an irregular rooster tail and is structurally unusual, possibly resulting from the effects of gravitational interactions with nearby star groups. Additionally, our spectroscopic analysis uncovered a diverse range of chemical characteristics in these clusters, including unusual levels of heavy element abundance and metal scatter, which are uncommon in traditional globular clusters. These findings suggest that MGC-1 and its counterparts represent a previously unseen class of intermediate-age clusters featuring unusual chemistry, produced during a period when the Milky Way's chemistry was undergoing significant changes.

We've derived a multi-dimensional formula for predicting the transverse momentum distributions of particles produced in physical processes, and specifically applied it to studies of jet suppression at the Large Hadron Collider, taking into account the effects of quark mass and color charge.

To enhance the precision of electromagnetic response calculations, we transform the velocity gauge version of tight-binding models into the vector potential gauge. The transformation involves modifying the Hamiltonian and equilibrium electron densities while keeping the current density the same in both gauge versions. By making this change, we improve the velocity gauge models' accuracy by fixing issues such as non-physical energy gaps and incorrect semi-metal to insulator transitions. Additionally, we develop a simple strategy to correct the velocity gauge models, and we apply our methods to study the electrical transport and optical properties in a model of herringbone lattances.

We examine a tensor network that represents a quantum erasure correction code based on a single type of tensor, and we derive a specific matrix that can be applied to the tensor network to simulate the effects of erasure on this code. We demonstrate that the bilinear transformation of the tensor network, using this matrix, results in a tensor isomorphic to the original tensor, providing a practical method for exact recovery of the erasure-corrected state. Furthermore, this outcome limits the tensor network to specific, low-rank variants, including the GKP code, which may have implications for the physical realization of these codes.

Our calculations suggest that the steady-state quantum yield is highly sensitive to the characteristics of light intensity in solution, and this sensitivity varies significantly depending on the location - whether in the condensed phase of a biological system or in solution. This finding contradicts previous predictions that the quantum yield would be intense-light-insensitive in solution. The intensity-dependent quantum yield results from a competition between two processes: photoisomerization rates and the decay of the excited state, and this competition is influenced by light intensity. However, it can also be described in terms of the dark states that control the system's response to light and its relaxation properties. Depending on the frequency of light used, either the photoisomerization rate or the decay rate can be the rate-determining step, and this step is further controlled by the energy distribution of the light, and the sensitivity of the quantum yield to light intensity, a critical aspect for biological light sensing, can be explained.

In high-stakes business processes, predicting future events or outcomes is
critical. Yet, the effectiveness of these predictions often falls short, as
indicated by low F1 scores. One key factor contributing to this issue is the
varying level of difficulty in predicting outcomes at different stages of the
process. For example, in a production process, predicting whether a product
will be delayed until the end, requiring the integration of multiple components',
is inherently more challenging than predicting the outcome of a stage that has
already been completed. Unfortunately, existing methods disregard the differences
in difficulty across stages, treating each stage equally. In contrast, our novel
approach, named Difficulty-Aware Risk Averaging (DARA), assigns distinct weights
to predictions at different stages, leading to more accurate results. Our empirical
evaluations demonstrate that DARA outperforms alternative methods across three
real-world scenarios, achieving a significant improvement of up to 27% in F1 score.

The impact of social media sentiment analysis is evident in various applications, including community awareness and decision-making. However, the analysis of public sentiment through social media following a natural disaster poses a challenge due to the large amount of data available. We propose an innovative approach that leverages bi-directional transformation and attention mechanisms in a deep learning model to enhance the capture of contextual cues and reduce data requirements. Our approach demonstrates superior performance in predicting future public sentiment in the aftermath of a disaster, as evidenced by results indicating a 0.23 increase in correlation coefficient and 0.11 decrease in mean squared error compared to the baseline.

Let $C_{M}^{+ }(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ denote the set of functions $f\in C_{M}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ such that the Fourier transform $\hat{f}$ satisfies the growth restriction $|B(x,t)|\leq Me^{t|x|^{2}}$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $t\geq 0$. We shall establish that the space of such functions $C_{M}^{+ }(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ is equivalent to the Beurling type spaces $B_{M}^{+ }(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ and investigate the relationship between the functions and their Fourier transforms in the Gelfand-Shilov spaces and Beurling type spaces. Additionally, we shall derive the standard extension to the complex case.

Our analysis of the hydrogen delta line's profile, obtained with the UVLMX telescope, reveals significant broadening observed during the peak of a G2V star's X1.0 flare. This observation was critical in our study, as the hydrogen delta line's profile served as a indicator of the energy released during the flare. By comparing the line's broadening to other optical and far-ultraviolet continuum features, we observed a link between hydrogen line broadening and characteristics of the optical and far-ultraviolet continuum, particularly those related to radio flux and the far-ultraviolet continuum's intensity. Notably, we found that hydrogen line broadening became more pronounced at shorter wavelengths, which is consistent with findings from the EUV white light spectroscopy conducted by the SDO. Furthermore, our data demonstrated that hydrogen line broadening is a crucial factor in the energy dissipation function $\mathscr{E}$, which is a key indicator of the energy released during the flare's thermal component.

We studied the conduct of propagating waves in a PT symmetric metamaterial structure, which transitions between symmetric and broken phases. Our analysis focused on examining travel wave characteristics in both PT symmetric and broken phases, investigating how these properties change with velocity, interaction, and operating frequency parameters. Our research demonstrated that propagating waves behave differently in PT symmetric and broken phases, with unique characteristics such as time-reversal symmetry, non-reciprocal energy transfer, and unusual power flow in the symmetric phase, whereas in the broken phase, we observed real part band gap, non-Hermitian band structure, and complex propagation constants. Numerical results were validated through experimental measurements, yielding accurate calculations of rotation angle, reflection coefficient, and asymptotic wave velocities.

We introduce an original approach to analyzing complex systems represented in Boolean networks: the dynamical cavity method. This technique is adaptable to a wide range of scenarios, including systems with self-interactions that follow a specific, non-trivial pattern, and where the dynamics involves both instantaneous and delayed interactions. To validate our method, we use two examples: an autonomous system with subtle behaviors and one driven by an external input, both of which accurately reflect the method's capabilities.

In recent years, the concept of symmetry in heavy nuclear systems has been misunderstood. Recent breakthroughs in quantum mechanics have clarified the issue, showing that symmetry can be strengthened in these systems. Research has also revealed that the shell model, despite some inaccuracies, can effectively capture the features of symmetry in these systems. Specifically, this has been observed in calculations of binding energies for nuclei within the $^{60}$Ca shell, where the energy differences between odd-even and even-even nuclei have been found to follow the expected patterns of symmetry. Moreover, this has been further demonstrated in calculations of single-particle energies and density distributions for these nuclei.

Our proposed Twisted Point Cloud (TPC) framework successfully extends the point cloud processing capabilities to accommodate various twisting transformations, which are categorizable into rigid-body motions that preserve orientation. Unlike existing point cloud models, TPC achieves enhanced certified accuracy with twisting transformations by integrating an inverse geometric mapping process, providing more precise boundary checking and approximation techniques. In contrast to models that utilize regression methods, TPC incorporates explicit geometric operations within its framework, enabling better performance. Our evaluation results show that TPC outperforms current point cloud processing methods using ABCD and ShapeNIS benchmarks, demonstrating an improvement in certified accuracy with twisting transformations. Additionally, our method exhibits superior flexibility in handling various input configurations, such as different point cloud densities and twisting transformation strengths.

In FMCW radar systems that utilize Time-Hopping Chirp Shift Keying (THCSK) modulation, changing the number of chirps per packet affects interference probabilities and throughput. This paper develops mathematical models to analyze interference probability and throughput as the number of chirps per packet varies, and demonstrates that optimal THCSK modulation parameters can be determined to minimize interference probability while maintaining maximum throughput in FMCW radar networks.

Our proposed method, a cycle-aware time-encoding technique for temporal knowledge graph completion, incorporates a unique approach to capturing ancient history in ancient graphs. To address the challenge of capturing extensive historical data in ancient graphs, our cycle-aware time-encoding technique focuses on extracting distinct temporal insights from multiple time windows. Unlike existing time-encoding strategies that use an integrated approach to capture ancient history across ancient graphs, our proposed method divides ancient graphs into different time periods, encoding each period differently. Each time period is represented by a separate temporal entity with its own distinct attributes, rather than combining all ancient history into a single entity. This enables our model to capture different ancient temporal insights in different time periods. The proposed time-encoding strategy divides ancient history into different periods, extracting distinct temporal insights in each period. Next, we introduce a new loss function that incorporates an entropy regularizer to prevent overfitting when processing extensive historical data in ancient graphs. The proposed model, called Cycle-Aware Time-encoding Temporal Knowledge Graph Embedding (CAT-KGE), is evaluated on a range of experimental datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing time-encoding strategies.

Using the Random Phase Approximation, we investigated the pole distribution associated with the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O, and found that the RPA poles fall within a broad energy range of 12.0 to 20.0 MeV, consisting of 57 distinct particles-hole configurations. By classifying these configurations based on particle and hole energies, we found that their energies follow the linear relationship expected from the sum of particle and hole energies, and demonstrated that the skewness observed in the RPA pole distribution is a result of the dispersion relation of particles and holes. Additionally, we found that the skewness has a significant influence on the strength functions, and that the width of the energy distribution is determined by the dispersion of the RPA poles, which is controlled by the strength of the particle-particle and hole-hole interactions.

The Koopman operator concept has been successfully applied to a variety of complex system types, including those with linear and nonlinear dynamics, spatiotemporal dynamics, and stochastic dynamics, serving as a powerful analytical tool for complex dynamical systems. This special issue aims to showcase recent advancements made possible by the Koopman operator approach, with a focus on theoretical and computational aspects. By leveraging its computational realization, the field has seen significant progress in the discovery of invariant sets and the development of efficient data-driven reduction methods for complex systems, particularly those exhibiting stochastic behavior. Additionally, work presented here has demonstrated the ability to extract valuable dynamical information from data by applying the Koopman operator, and this research has also offered promising outcomes for the data-driven analysis of nonlinear and stochastic dynamical systems, offering prospects for further investigation.

Neural text generation has seen significant advancements in recent years, but the quality of pre-trained sentence representations still needs significant improvement. To address this issue, a novel approach called SparseGAN was developed, drawing on the principles of the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). This approach used two different GANs, specifically conditional and unconditioned variants, to create multiple sentence representations from a single context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context context

Our study suggests that open clusters, stellar streams, and the Galactic field are the most plausible regions to examine the possibility of interstellar panspermia. We developed a statistical model to assess the survival of microorganisms within these environments under intense radiation in the Earth's vicinity. Our analysis indicates that extant life forms could persist for approximately 100 million years in stream systems and the Galactic field, and around 10-20 million years in open clusters. We also found that the extinction rates vary greatly, depending on factors like the radiation exposure and microorganism resilience.

To determine the distribution of large-scale structures in the universe, scientists use a method called photometric survey analysis. This technique uses data from astronomical observations, specifically information about the brightness of distant galaxies as they appear through various lines of sight, to reconstruct the spatial distribution of these celestial bodies. A key step in this process involves using a model of these galaxies to estimate the average distance of the galaxies from the Earth, or their redshift, based on their observed spectra. A recent study has raised concerns that a common preprocessing technique used in this analysis, called foreground removal, may significantly impact the accuracy of these estimates. To investigate this issue further, the authors of this paper examined the effects of foreground removal on the accuracy of these estimates, or photometric redshifts, using data from the SDSS and LAMDA galaxies. The study found that removing foregrounds has a non-linear impact on the accuracy of these estimates, especially when certain galaxies are heavily affected. The authors also found that removing these galaxies, or outliers, can improve the accuracy of these estimates in certain cases. The findings of this research may have implications for other analyses involving these galaxies, such as studies of galaxy groups and clusters based on photometric redshifts.

We propose an alternative perspective on dark matter, which posits that dark matter fields possess a own hierarchy of energy levels mirror-ing that seen in the context of the holographic principle. This idea is explored within a framework inspired by both string theory and the concept of smooth gravity. The interplay between the various dark matter energy levels is shown to be connected to the onset of complexity and chaos in our observable universe, which in turn emerges as a result of the universe's self-organizing properties. The proposed perspective provides a theoretical framework for understanding the universe's structure and the emergence of chaos and complexity beyond our observable cosmos.

Identifying population densities is a crucial goal for animal studies that often utilize capture-recapture (CRC) methods. The expansion of CRC into a spatial framework (SCR) has increased the availability of software using Bayesian and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for analyzing data, despite the limitations of these approaches due to their slow computation times and difficulty in interpreting results. The development of a least-squares method within the spatial capture-recapture framework (LS-SCR) offers a more efficient and transparent alternative to these complex methods. This study demonstrates the application of the LS-SCR model using data from white-tailed deer studies in Pennsylvania, a region with diverse landscapes. The analysis demonstrated significant associations between population density estimates and variables such as cover type, elevation, and distance to roads. The inclusion of these environmental factors in the analysis demonstrated a clear understanding of the population's response to its surroundings, thereby providing valuable insights into animal behavior that could inform forest management practices.

The Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths problem asks to find k edge disjoint paths in a network between two points, where the total cost of the edges in the paths is minimized. This problem has significant applications in various fields such as electronics, biology, and transportation. Due to its complexity, solving it exactly is difficult, even for small instances. Therefore, research has been conducted to develop heuristic and approximation algorithms to solve this problem. This paper presents a new algorithm to solve Min-Power k Edge Disjoint st-Paths, which is an extension of the k edge disjoint st-Paths algorithm using the Lagrangean relaxation method. The algorithm finds the minimum power k edge disjoint st-Paths by solving a series of subproblems, where each subproblem is solved using the k edge disjoint st-Paths algorithm. To evaluate this algorithm, experiments were conducted on real-life telecommunications and web graph instances. Results show that it can effectively find the minimum power k edge disjoint st-Paths quickly. Furthermore, this algorithm was compared to other heuristic algorithms, and its performance was analyzed in terms of solution quality and computation time.

This paper adapts a cutting-edge algorithm called Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli (GLMB) for predicting the motion of multiple targets, particularly those within a swarm that follows similar paths. We began by modifying the standard multi-Bernoulli filter (MEMBER) to account for target interactions, and then developed a more advanced predictor to improve computation efficiency. In a simulated scenario, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by accurately predicting the positions of multiple targets, even in swarms that displayed dynamic behavior.

We've developed a universal measure that quantifies flu spread in network models.
This measure rises with increasing disease prevalence in the network's disordered phase.
It reaches a maximum at the phase transition point, after which it drops in the ordered phase.
We discovered that this measure rises in the same way as a similar quantity that was recently studied in network models - specifically, it rises in a power law that is the same for all network models we studied (with the same exponent as the power law that describes how this quantity rises as one looks at larger and larger parts of the network).
We were also able to show that this quantity is not the same as another quantity that measures how easily disease spreads in network models.
This distinction holds even when the network models are the same, but near the phase transition point only a small part of the network has become disordered.
Instead, this quantity is most closely related to the size of the largest part of the network that has become disordered, especially when the network models are highly clustered.
As a result, we were able to use this quantity to study a phenomenon that has been hard to explain in recent studies of network models - specifically, the way that the prevalence of disease spreads can rise quickly even in parts of the network that are far away from the parts that became disordered at the phase transition.

The value of expected points remains a widely used metric in American Football, but it has limitations in forecasting the additional yards gained from a single play. A novel valuation approach is introduced, which converts the potential scoring opportunities into points equivalent. This method is versatile and applicable to various phases of the game, but its optimal implementation depends on factors like down, yard line, time remaining, ref status, and ball gain potential. A notable aspect of this approach is that it provides a systematic way to evaluate the value of expected points, which can be predicted through statistical modeling of past games. By utilizing advanced forecasting techniques, teams may enhance their decision-making processes, especially in situations lacking recent data.

To accurately identify connections between pre-printed text and input text in scanned documents that contain errors, we propose a novel task called inaccurate document interaction detection. Our research introduces a new model called DDI, which utilizes a spatial temporal memory network to analyze the spatial arrangements of text within the document and extract vital contextual information from recently introduced simple layout observation, resulting in superior performance according to our experimental results. Our method achieves outstanding effectiveness by incorporating a text spotter that automatically identifies text within the document, allowing for the efficient collection of large scale annotated datasets. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of DDI over conventional object detection approaches and showcase the significance of accurate text spotting in patching document content. Additionally, our research highlights the challenges posed by recent homogenous format documents that lack structural organization.

Dynamic systems often feature subtle, constant variables that significantly affect their behavior. Recurrent state space models have learned complex interactions between these variables and observations, but their hidden components have hindered learning and inference. This is addressed by a novel approach called Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), which offers multiple state spaces for different variables, allows for their learning, and facilitates their inference. We demonstrate the capabilities of HiP-RSSMs by creating models for two challenging applications - multi-modal oscillations and electrical circuit learning - and show that its components can be easily incorporated into existing software tools, while achieving results that outperform traditional state space models.

Previous studies have demonstrated that matrices with specific properties can exhibit consistency in their spectral behavior. Specifically, it has been shown that under certain conditions, matrices whose spectra show consistency will also exhibit conditional freeness. In this paper, we investigate the reverse idea, proving that conditional freeness can be used to derive spectral consistency, including the means and distribution of spectral extremes. We also provide an analysis of the rate of convergence in these cases. Our methods build upon existing techniques for managing residual matrices, and our results demonstrate the equivalence of conditional freeness to another set of conditions that can be more easily verified. Ultimately, our findings relate the concept of conditional freeness to common practices in statistical applications, such as the use of spectral normalization to bound matrix norms.

We develop a novel method to create a genus 2 curve at a rational point in a specific isogeny class, using a genus 1 curve and a genus 3 curve, both defined over the same field. The genus 3 curve must have a non-hyperelliptic representation in a specific isogeny class, corresponding to a genus 1 curve. The genus 2 curve is constructed through a cover defined by the product of two curves, one being the genus 1 curve covering the genus 3 curve, and the other being the genus 3 curve covering the genus 2 curve. The genus 2 curve's cover is in a specific isogeny class, given as G2d2(u) in the paper's notation. A novel algorithm is presented to create a genus 2 curve with rational point, using a genus 1 curve and a genus 3 curve, both defined over the same field. The genus 2 curve's cover can be used to provide examples of non-trivial isomorphisms between genus 1 curves, previously found by Leo Goldstein.

Measuring polarization within social networks is crucial, yet the standard methods used to assess polarization, such as percentage of friends outside your group and the distance between groups, can be misleading or difficult to interpret. These measures fall short because they don't account for underlying factors that influence opinions, such as the strength of connections between individuals, the distribution of opinions within groups, and how people within groups are connected to each other. To address this limitation, a new approach called the "measuring polarization calculator" is introduced, which takes into consideration the complexity of polarization in social networks by estimating a polarization score for each individual, grouping, and network. This approach also allows for comparative analysis across networks by standardizing measurements and performing statistical tests. Through theoretical modeling and empirical analysis on Facebook data from 500 users, the measuring polarization calculator is shown to provide a more accurate assessment of polarization.

In complex systems, understanding the stability of various states is crucial, especially those exhibiting abrupt transitions. Multiscale and highly interconnected networks are particularly challenging to study due to their elaborate structure. Our research divides such large networks into smaller, independent modules and investigates the stationary states within each component using standard stability analysis. We then examine the coexistence of these states by considering how they are affected by the network's interconnections. By simplifying the problem, we are able to identify key factors that influence the stability of these states and precisely estimate their stability margins. Unlike conventional methods, our approach is transparent and free of assumptions, providing a comprehensive understanding of how states evolve in multilayer networks. Through extensive simulations and theoretical modeling, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by investigating sudden transitions in dual-layer networks composed of dynamic modules that interact with each other in various ways.

Becker's work on connecting differential operators to Gauss-Von Neumann correspondences has been expanded to incorporate flat coefficients. This expansion holds for extended differential modules, a type of differential module that incorporates modules of differential forms. For a differential module $M$ over the field $\mathbb{C}$, we define the corresponding differential operators $D(\Gamma(M))$ and show that they correspond to the automorphisms of $M$ when viewed through the lens of extended differential modules. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach aligns with Becker's framework by showing our differential operators are equivalent to the operators defined by Becker.

In our previous research, we introduced an automated algorithm for error detection in programming tasks. This algorithm is designed for a testing environment that provides a list of error messages to programmers. However, identifying errors is just the first step; the more critical task is to locate and correct these errors in the original program code. Typically, programmers rely on error messages to find the issues, but often, these messages are vague, making it difficult to determine the course of action. Additionally, finding the correct repair operation among the numerous options is a challenging task. In this research, we examine the assumption that the algorithmic errors can be isolated from other programming mistakes. Under this condition, we propose an automated repair strategy that leverages the algorithm's error detection capability. When an error is detected, the associated error message is used to determine the required repair operation to fix this specific error. Since different errors can be concurrent, fixing one error may not necessarily correct all issues; hence, the repair process is considered a concurrent error resolution task. In this research, we define a new task called concurrent error resolution and provide an automated repair strategy that achieves exactness in a limited number of repair operations, reducing the complexity of the problem. The proposed strategy is demonstrated to improve error correction efficiency by at least two times in comparison to the alternative methods. Moreover, the advantage of this research is highlighted through a real-world example, where a library function with over ten thousand lines of code is used to evaluate the algorithm.

We introduce HyperPrompt, a framework that utilizes HyperNetworks to facilitate efficient task execution on pre-trained language models. Within this framework, hyper tasks are first converted into prompt styles, and these prompts are then optimized through backward adaptation. In evaluating HyperPrompt, we found it achieved notable gains in NLP performance, with just a few hundred words of prompt resulting in exceptional performance on low-finance classification and sentiment analysis. Notably, HyperPrompt showcases the potential for prompt-based natural language processing to enhance current LMOs beyond current limits.

The concept of involution can be applied to the root systems of types A_l and D_l.
When this type of involution is combined with the one-dimensional lattice Z^l,
it results in the group algebra C[Z^l] that involves the root system.
The maximal root in these types of systems has the highest intensity and is
located at the furthest point from the origin. It is unique in the D_l type
and there are several in the A_l type. The Weyl group of the root system
is generated by a set of reflections corresponding to the roots,
with one exception in the D_l type where the reflection associated
with the maximal root is replaced by that associated with the minimal root.

Quantum-emitted light from atomic ensembles, offered through multi-phonon Raman transitions, holds promise for the coherent generation of correlated photons. However, achieving controlled emission of even or odd correlated photons proves challenging with conventional cavity QED techniques. This work introduces a novel approach, employing a cavity coupled to two atomic media, for the synchronized production of two photons of different correlations. By adjusting the photon escape rates in the two Raman transitions, we demonstrate the transition between correlated and anti-correlated photons production. Additionally, we demonstrate a trimer Raman transition system providing a combination of correlated and single photon emissions, which can be modified through varying the photon escape rate in different modes. These designs lay the groundwork for complex correlated light production utilizing varying cavity QED configurations.

We introduce a novel randomized discrete-time algorithm for estimating the size of a large general static network that consists of multiple interconnected clusters. The network and the algorithm it employs are outlined below. The network segment, where the algorithm is applied, is a part of a larger network that includes multiple interconnected subnetworks. There are $m$ nodes in total within this network segment, where each node is assigned a unique identifier. The algorithm is run on this network segment. The algorithm is described in the method section. The algorithm's performance is evaluated in the theory section. The algorithm was inspired by a similar approach outlined in the paper titled "Optimal upper bound for estimating the size of a network" by C. Wang, Y. Wang, and W. Wang.

This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of algorithms used to estimate the average queue length at an intersection based on single-point measurements, with focus on their sensitivity to arrival rates and service capacities. The accuracy of these estimates is assessed using real-world data, with comparisons made between sophisticated machine learning methods and more traditional parametric approaches. The findings show that, despite providing reasonable results in controlled environments, these algorithms are vulnerable to fluctuations in arrival rates and service capacities. In contrast, simpler nonparametric estimators consistently demonstrate greater accuracy and stability, suggesting a need to reevaluate the complexity of existing solutions.

A novel numerical approach has been developed for solving the Hamiltonian constraint in the finite-element method with non-zero boundary values. This method bypasses the regularity issues associated with conformal factors by utilizing a redefined conformal factor that satisfies specific constraints within a defined domain. A corresponding potential function is then used to establish a relationship with the original conformal factor, allowing for the determination of associated metric components. This approach, centered on the conformal factor, serves as the basis for developing a suitable variational formulation and associated boundary conditions within the defined domain, thereby enabling the solution of the Hamiltonian constraint with non-zero boundary values. Numerical implementations and simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this method for solving complex problems, such as conformal factor singularities and boundary effects in cosmological spacetimes.

We describe a search for the phenomenon $\Sigma^+ \to p \nu \bar\nu$ that is
constrained by existing experiments and set a new, more stringent upper limit
for its occurrence. This limit is derived from a total number of $2.97 \times
10^{20}$ protons-on-target in data collected with the ATLAS detector in 13
TeV $pp$ collisions at the LHC. To facilitate the interpretation of
experimental results for potential $\Sigma^+$ decay anomalies, we have updated
$\Sigma^+$ particle properties in accordance with the current most up-to-date
$\Sigma^+$ decay branching fractions.
