This paper investigates the operator T_g and reveals that it is weakly compact in BMOA_p for 1 < p < 2, essentially resulting from the combination of an interpolation theorem from R. Cavalloro, F. Chousionis, and S. Malivagia, stating that (T_g, T_\lambda) sits in (BMOA_{p_0}, BMOA_{p_1}) for some 2 \le p_0 < 2^{\frac{1}{2}}p and p_1 \in (2, \infty), thereby allowing us to conclude that T_g^0 is compact in BMOA_p for 1 < p < 2, while also showing that T_g^1(\Delta) is compact in BMOA_s for any \Delta \in \mathcal{A}_s and 1 < s \le 2, thereby extending the compactness of T_g to the entire BMOA_p space for 1 < p \le 2.

The vast and ever-expanding literature comprises knowledge that evolves over time, 
wherein the development of future knowledge relies heavily on past achievements. 
Consequently, pinpointing the origin of knowledge is becoming increasingly crucial. 
To address this challenge, a novel approach known as the Quantitative Index of 
Knowledge (KQI) has been developed to map the source of knowledge within a literature 
database. In this study, KQI is applied to a comprehensive dataset of citation networks 
in various scientific domains, where the results reveal the fundamental laws that 
govern the knowledge flow. Furthermore, analytical solutions derived from nonlinear 
dynamics and stochastic processes are confirmed by both theoretical and numerical 
analysis. The findings indicate that the knowledge index displays periodic behavior 
and follows a stochastic pattern, where the complexity arises from interconnected 
linear processes. The results also reveal that the knowledge index is regulated by 
a stable and fixed point under optimal conditions, where the parameter of the 
self-inhibiting node determines the point of equilibrium.

In a wireless communication system, securing data transmission involves allocating power at various points, such as in optimizing power for different nodes. This optimization considers a set of securing factors, such as the likelihood of an attacker intercepting data and the capacity of different communication links, which can be formally represented as an entropy in information theory. This entropy-based representation is used to formulate a self-optimize method that determines the best power allocation to achieve the highest security without prior knowledge of system parameters. This self-optimize method is applied in uplink transmission scenarios in wireless communication systems and confirms the feasibility of entropy-based power optimization.

Our research proposes a novel strategy for achieving non-local entanglement in complex networks through quantum emitters located at network vertices. We demonstrate this approach by modeling a network based on the tree structure and utilizing non-local quantum communication to entangle a quantum tree network. Furthermore, we investigate the fundamental limitations of this method for a quantum wire network by utilizing a quantum emitter-connected double cavity system, and we explore the outcomes when these emitters interact with their surroundings.

In the complex and ever-changing environment of urban intersections, an automated vehicle equipped with connectivity can benefit from streamlined trajectory planning by incorporating upcoming traffic signal phases. This study focuses on models predicting when yellow and red phases will occur and utilizes this information to develop a bounded control strategy for the vehicle to navigate safely through the intersection. Key aspects of the approach include a motion model, a bounded control model, and optimization of control actions to avoid collisions and arrive at the desired position within the phase time limits. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated in simulation using real traffic signal data from the CityLab dataset, with the approach verified to be computationally efficient for connected vehicles.

We introduce a new fast text-based world model called TextWorldExpress, 
which significantly boosts simulation speeds - up to 210 times faster than 
previous models. Our results show that a simple rule-based agent performs 
better and achieves a higher score in TextWorldExpress than in regular 
TextWorld models, but we also find that this model is less reliable and 
varies more significantly according to the mode it's run in. Additionally, 
we found TextWorldExpress to be just as challenging for a learning agent 
using reinforcement learning, but noted that this model suffers from too 
much variance and requires a more advanced optimization method to perform 
well.

Deep learning techniques have rapidly emerged as powerful solutions for various challenges in data analysis and signal processing, primarily fueled by the incredible effectiveness of recurrent neural networks and subsuming the capabilities of traditional methods. Despite significant accomplishments of tensor decomposed model-oriented hardware in accelerating deep learning applications, there are still areas where these systems fall short. Specifically, the inability of such systems to efficiently handle highly variable data dimensions and inherent memory accessibility limitations pose significant obstacles in processing certain data sets. In response to these challenges, we introduce a novel FDHT-LSTM architecture that leverages a fully dynamic and flexible tensor decomposition method, enabling it to handle datasets with varying data dimensions while prioritizing memory accessibility that aligns with the underlying hardware architecture. Furthermore, we developed an efficient hardware prototype to demonstrate the performance capabilities of our new architecture, and our results show substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency compared to traditional methods. Particularly, our experiments indicate a 5-fold increase in throughput and up to 50% improvement in energy efficiency when using our FDHT-LSTM architecture.

To enhance the efficiency of NLP models by reducing the need for large labeled datasets, this study explores various data augmentation techniques including lexical searches, phrase replacement, fluency-based methods and label-wise strategies. Among these approaches, a simple word-replacement model was found to be particularly effective and was demonstrated with multiple experiments using the Sentiment Analysis and Question Classification datasets. Compared to the current state-of-the-art model, our results showed similar or better performance on both datasets while requiring much less training data. Additionally, our study found that data augmentation can be effectively used with a small labeled dataset and a large unsupervised pre-trained model.

A recent hypothesis suggests that large extra dimensions could lead to a weakly coupled, stable universe. To test this, researchers studied a scenario where a scalar field is confined to a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, and interacted with a bulk photon. The results showed that the scalar's self-binding energy, a measure of its stability, is linked to the strength of its confinement, ultimately limiting it to being weaker than its binding energy. This constraint is a specific case of the Weak Gravity Conjecture, and can be expressed in terms of the scalar's mass and the size of the extra dimension. The study also demonstrated that the scalar's behavior differs signficantly from that in a four-dimensional space-time, and that its interaction with the bulk photon is affected by the extra dimension in a way that wasn't previously understood.

To simulate complex physical systems with multiple interacting quantum states, using a unified model has been proven effective. However, this method faces significant challenges when trying to approximate a dense non-abiding matrix using a compact projection operator. Our proposed approach, based on an independent set theory, divides the model space into a series of independent parts, allowing for their simultaneous calculation and providing a more efficient solution to the equations of motion. Additionally, this strategy enables direct integration with established methods, such as the Lanczos algorithm, to compute the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the model space Hamiltonian. Furthermore, this framework has been applied to develop a new version of the continuum shell model, where a central closed shell serves as the reference point, and valence particles are calculated using the Lanczos algorithm within a model space constructed using the monopole interaction.

Given a strong F-shape local ring L containing a proper, strongly F-rational local ring R, we examine the zero submodule of a specific local cohomology module $\ kappa^h_{(f)}(R)$, where $h$ represents the maximal $F$-catenary dimension of R and $f$ is the maximal element in R's set of parameter elements. Our study aims to understand the connection between this submodule and the property of R being F-rational. As a result, we derive a preliminary investigation, demonstrating that this submodule corresponds to a primary component of the ideal generated by the integral closure of the maximal ideal in L. This finding establishes a relationship between the zero submodule and L's equidimensional reduction, thereby extending the concept of reduced F-rationality to a reduced equidimensional scheme.

A design where all orders are accepted or rejected is proposed for redispatch markets, leading to a binary outcome for market participants. This design's effectiveness is analyzed through a mathematical model that transforms the problem into a minimum cost flow problem with integer variables. The model's properties are examined to ensure it meets necessary criteria for polynomial-time solution and to provide insights into the behavior of prices and quantities in the optimal solution. A numerical example is also provided to illustrate the design's potential and to compare it with current practices.

In this study, we examine a specific scenario involving function fields and a particular set of polynomials, concluding that the Galois groups associated with these polynomials are distinct and unconventional, adhering to a broader conjecture's specifications. This conclusion builds upon existing knowledge and contributes new insights to the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, specifically for a specific type of polynomial with a specific characteristic and a specific set of parameters.

Our research examines the sensitivity of next-generation experiments to identify Higgs boson signals, specifically in searches for the decay of the Higgs boson into bottom quarks with added background noise from top quark pair production. Our analysis focuses on future 100 TeV colliders and compares two detection strategies: a traditional, irreversibility-based approach and a new, uncertainty-based method that accounts for the inherent uncertainties in background predictions. Our findings indicate that the new approach can enhance the detection of Higgs boson signals by up to 50%, and this improvement holds for even highly precise background predictions. The new method's benefits are particularly visible in scenarios with large uncertainty margins, and it is particularly effective in identifying the most probable outcomes (peak fitting). The future of particle physics research may rely heavily on such uncertainty-based analysis methods, especially in scenarios with complex background noise.

To explore the fundamental nature of the Higgs boson and others in the scalar sector, researchers rely on precision tests at the LHC, involving processes like $pp \to \phi W^* \to \ell \nu \phi$, where $\ell$ represents an electron or muon. This experiment focuses on predicting the ratio of $\phi$-strahlung to $\phi W\gamma$ production rates as a function of $\phi$ mass, providing sensitive information for extended scalar paradigms that affect the Higgs boson's self-coupling. This ratio is crucial because $\phi$-strahlung is an important background for new physics in $\tau$ lepton decays at future e+e- colliders. To calculate this ratio, the Higgs boson's decay rate to a photon pair, recently measured at 95 pb, is utilized. Additionally, to minimize theoretical uncertainties, the ratio is normalized by deriving the $\phi W\gamma$ rate through $pp \to \phi \gamma \to \ell \nu \gamma$, which is sensitive to new scalar particles' masses and couplings, allowing for more precise extraction of these parameters. To facilitate these predictions, the LHC can be modified to include sensitive electromagnetic calorimeter systems, complementing the study of $\phi \to \gamma \gamma$ at future e+e- colliders. While Saturn is known for having a stable north polar stratospheric vortex throughout the year, a change is occurring there. In contrast, Saturn's southern polar region, which typically stays occupied during the summer months, has observed a decline in the vortex's stability in recent years. This change in the southern polar region is attributed to a shift in the 11-year solar cycle's influence on Saturn's atmosphere. This paper examines data collected from the Saturn's north and south polar regions, using the Saturn 3.9 μm infrared imaging technique, developed by the University of Leicester. This imaging method, available since the Saturn 2006 ringplane transit observation, allows for continuous observations of both the north and south polar regions from 2006 to 2017. By utilizing this new imaging technique, researchers were able to study Saturn's upper atmospheric chemistry, monitoring the development of polar stratospheric frosts and vortex mixing. This new technique offers enhanced sensitivity, allowing for the detection of frost clouds and a change in the vortex's mixing pattern, which was previously observable only during solar maximum periods.

This paper disproves a long-held assumption concerning boundary blow-up for the Schrödinger equation under periodic conditions. Classical evidence supporting the concept of boundary blow-up is limited, as methods typically used to demonstrate blow-up at boundaries are impractical there. However, our research reveals that boundary blow-up can occur for the Schrödinger equation with a linear boundary condition, as it is linked to the appearance of a non-trivial mode in the solution's asymptotic analysis. Furthermore, we show that this mode's frequency is determined by the boundary condition's parameter in a way that reflects on the solution's global existence or blow-up characteristics, thus validating the concept of boundary blow-up for this equation.

This briefing presents some currently current research in commutative algebra, specifically focusing on the interconnection between zero-characteristic and positive-characteristic local rings in the context of singularity theory and commutative algebra. It introduces key concepts, including the Frobenius operator, the Cartier-Dieudonn\'e map, and $F$-nilpotent rings, and explores their roles in determining the characteristics of equidimensional, equi-hypersurface, and equi-Artinian rings. Furthermore, it explores the characteristics of isospectral and co-isometric matrices in positive characteristic.

We have developed a holistic understanding of the metal-insulator transition in the two-dimensional Sr$_{2}$NiO$_4$ driven by hydrostatic pressure, which involves strongly correlated electrons at the edge of a band and a temperature that is relatively high compared to the band width. Our investigation combines experimental and theoretical studies to examine the electronic structure and spectral weight distribution across the metal-insulator transition. Our results from angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and ab initio band structure calculations show that pressure causes a transformation of the electron-filling contour from a fragmented, hole-like shape to a connected shape with both hole-like and electron-like parts. This change occurs when the metal-insulator transition takes place and is associated with the formation of a pseudo-gap in the metallic phase. Our study of the spectral weight, which involves analyzing the sum of the energies carried by the electrons in the energy momentum space, reveals a significant shift of the weight towards the high-energy region when the pressure is increased. Quantum dark-solitons in a one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate have been extensively studied, however the quantum dynamics of these systems beyond linearization remains underrepresented. By implementing a quantum version of the inverse scattering method, we have the ability to analyze the quantum states of these systems in a direct manner. Utilizing this approach for a Bose-Einstein condensate represented by the cubic nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equation, we have derived the explicit form of the quasi-momentum theta-function operator and the corresponding quantum state. From this expression, we obtained the density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton by incorporating two anti-soliton quantum states and observed its behavior during a collision with a classical dark-soliton. The result shows that the quantum double dark-soliton maintains its structure and moves at a constant speed, whereas the classical dark-soliton displays a periodic oscillation following the collision. Moreover, we derived the total momentum and energy of the quantum double dark-soliton and verified that these parameters are conserved during the collision, demonstrating that the model adheres to fundamental conservation principles.

This study introduces the notion of a symplectic double vector bundle and its symplectomorphisms, thereby extending the theory of single symplectic vector bundles. A key achievement is the proof that every symmetric $k$-fold vector bundle belongs to a category of double vector bundles with an antisymmetric $k$-fold structure. The research also explores the relationship between homological and differential approaches in double vector bundle theory. The found connections lead to new results on differential operators defining double vector bundles and their symplectomorphisms, ultimately contributing to a better understanding of the structure of differential operators in single symplectic vector bundles.

A key aspect of our work is to introduce the concept of a geometric measure on Lie algebra orbits, which we demonstrate to be equivalent to Kirillov's measure through a detailed analysis of the classical examples of nilpotent Lie algebras. Furthermore, our research establishes a straightforward method for calculating both geometric measure and Kirillov's measure. By examining the underlying principles, we find that their common value can be interpreted as being directly proportional to the length of the orbit.

A cutting-edge algorithm has been created to accelerate the x-ray scattering experiment data analysis, allowing for the deconvolution of broadened x-ray spectra. This technique significantly shortens data collection times needed for x-ray spectroscopy, at the cost of reducing the energy resolution of the detector. The new algorithm reverses this effect, surpassing the previous limit by surpassing the Broadening Factor (BF) constraint, which is fundamental to Tomography Data Reconstruction (TDR) methods. This algorithm's success in exceeding the BF limit has been validated on simulated and actual data, and it is now integrated with the APERO software suite. This new algorithm is called "Pyrhe" and it is already being utilized for data analysis at the ID20 beamline at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility.

We explore how disordered classical statistical mechanics models can be applied to study quantum error correcting codes. Focusing on the surface code and its counterpart, the classical analog, we examine the critical behavior of the classical model as it transitions from a disordered to an ordered state. By determining the critical exponent that characterizes this transition, we demonstrate that it aligns with standard universality classes defined by classical statistical mechanics. These studies facilitate the interpretation of quantum error correcting codes through the lens of classical disordered systems. Additionally, we analyze the influence of relaxation dynamics on these systems by incorporating environments that interact with both the classical and quantum systems, utilizing both the Lindblad master equation and thermal pure quantum states framework. These investigations enrich our understanding of quantum error correcting codes and their interaction with environments.

To tackle the challenge of creating a non-trivial gap in tellurene-based quantum wells, we propose using a different material structure. In this design, tellurene is combined with germanium to form a quantum well, and the resulting system is then subjected to lateral compression. Our computations using DFT and the BOLBOMO method reveal that this structure develops a substantial gap despite its topological nature. The gap can be adjusted through strain engineering, and we also observe that the strain produces a more pronounced effect than changing the well width. Our analysis of the band structure and orbital content also identifies the presence of helical linear dispersion near the Fermi level and pinning points. These features are crucial for tellingurene's potential as a material for device applications involving topological physics.

To develop a realistic representation of blocking fractures within fractured porous media, we've developed a novel approach using the Dirac-beta function, which provides an effective approximation of the screening effect from multiple blocking fractures. The Dirac-beta function approach, drawn from the general class of special function representations, has not been previously utilized in this context. In our analysis, we detail the method's implementation and its computational metrics, drawing on data from a publicly accessible database. We've also conducted a comparative analysis with a widely accepted blocking-fractures model.

The alignment of spin-valve behavior through magnetic control is examined in devices where the control magnet's field is relatively low. The alignment is investigated in two different configurations: one with a fixed sensor magnet and a controllable switch magnet, and another where both magnets are capable of being controlled. Our research shows that the behavior of these devices can be adjusted by adjusting the exchange field between the two magnets, with the result that spin-valve current produces the greatest effect when the exchange field is high but starts to display unusual characteristics at moderately low exchange fields. The situation where the device can distinguish between up and down spins occurs particularly those with high exchange fields. The ability of these devices to make distinctions based on the spin of the electrons also provides the necessary condition for the spin-valve effect to take place, with the result that spin-valve current produces the greatest effect when the exchange field is high. In the context of adapting the SWUM framework for selecting hypotheses, our approach introduces utility functions that guides decision-making. These utility functions are chosen through a secondary optimization process that is independent of the ranking algorithm. We evaluate our method by conducting experiments on artificial datasets, where it outperforms the original SWUM framework. Additionally, we examine how decision-making affects the performance of our approach when compared to the ideal oracle.

We release a newly annotated dataset called DiscSense, consisting of 1800 sentence pairs, along with associated discourse marker and semantic relation tags. These elements are crucial for understanding the complex meanings behind sentences in a language. Existing research has highlighted the limitations of current machine learning based models when dealing with the nuances of language. We hope that by providing the annotated dataset DiscSense, it will serve as a useful resource for enhancing the performance of models in the areas of discourse and semantics.

For years, researchers have been trying to comprehend the reason for inefficient light emission in semiconductor nanocrystals.  According to the Mott-Seitz model, nanocrystals' slow light emission can be attributed to a high energy barrier preventing the release of a trapped carrier.  This energy barrier was initially estimated but has never been directly measured.  Our study utilizes nanosecond optical pulses and time-resolved luminescence to directly observe the barrier height for both direct and indirect bandgap materials, demonstrating the significance of this barrier in controlling the rate of radiative and non-radiative decay.  We also demonstrate that decreasing the size of nanocrystals increases the impact of this barrier, causing it to become the limiting factor in radiative decay for smaller nanocrystals, thus leading to increased carrier lifetimes.

This paper introduces a new training method for neural networks that replaces backpropagation with error computation via linear transformations. The proposed algorithm maintains neural network flexibility, encompassing fully connected, convolutional, and recurrent neurons, and is exemplified through a sound recognition application using Lennon Pickerling song recordings. The proposed method demonstrates significant time savings per training iteration, leading to reduced total training time.

A classical model is constructed to describe magnetic skyrmions in a sphere by using the O(3) sigma model, with the homotopy group of the target space being π3(S2), which indicates the variety of skyrmions present. The model is modified to allow for a non-trivial spin texture at the sphere's center, which could be applied to study magnetic skyrmions in elongated spheres or toroids. The target space is changed from S2 to the real projective space RP2, which enables us to investigate skyrmions in rigid frames or bilayer structures, his work generalizes previous results about magnetic skyrmions, and it is shown that pair collisions can result in the creation of a topological object that was initially thought to require multiple skyrmion interactions. The framework is applied to a dynamic setup, and new types of skyrmion motions are found, which can emerge from an initial condition that contains both skyrmion and spin textures.

We investigated how the Hartree-Fock method's convergence is influenced by the intensity of electron-electron Coulomb interaction for a range of benchmark molecules. This involved measuring the difference in computational time as the level of electron fine division was lowered from $10^{-n}$ to $10^{-n-1}$, where $n$ represents various decimal place increments. The aim was to determine if the Hartree-Fock method's computational efficiency follows a power law in relation to the $n$th electron fine division, for both strong and weak Coulomb interactions. This is crucial because it has significant implications for the development of more efficient iterative Hartree-Fock algorithms. Our calculations demonstrate that the Hartree-Fock method's computational time does indeed adhere to a power law in relation to the $n$th electron fine division, with an exact power determined by the intensity of the Coulomb interaction. For molecules with strong Coulomb interactions, such as borane, we found that the power law has a value of approximately two. In contrast, molecules with weak Coulomb interactions, such as CF$_4$, exhibit a power law with a value close to one. These findings can be explained by the impact of electron localization in molecules with strong Coulomb interactions, which increases the computational time by a square of the electron fine division.

The intricate interplay between structural and dynamical disorders influences the explosive synchronization transition in coupled map lattices. We investigate this intersection of disorder effects for both local and long-range structural disorder, examining how the explosive synchronization transition becomes more stable as the disorder strength increases in the presence of moderate structural disorder. Additionally, we find that a specific arrangement of structural disorder can mimic the effect of dynamical disorder, thereby further contributing to more stable explosive synchronization transitions. This study provides insights into the role of disorder effects in explosive synchronization transitions, offering a framework for exploration in other complex systems.

We establish a condition for a factorized function with respect to the Frobenius norm to exhibit geometric properties typical of strongly convex and smooth functions. These conditions can be applied to optimize a matrix factorization model that meets specific stability and smoothness requirements. We derive a suitable gradient-based algorithm that meets these geometric conditions and can be applied to an alternative matrix factorization model that does not meet the required conditions. We demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $O(1/k)$, which can be extended to $O(1/k^p)$ for certain self-consistent equations. We also provide a proof that our algorithm can overcome local singularities within a certain range. Finally, we provide results from two real-world applications that demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

In 1990, Choudum proposed a conjecture that a bipartite graph with maximum degree 3 can be colored using a strong edge-coloring with an average of 4 units per edge. While the conjecture remains unproven, we managed to locate a counterexample belonging to the class of cubic bipartite graphs. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of the minimum degree of a graph's end-points in an edge-coloring, and we counter the previous best result achieved by Liu in 2018.

The primary objective of this paper is to establish a connection between Gauss sums and identities involving Dirichlet $L$-functions, expanding on earlier findings of H. Conrey and A. Kumchev. Additionally, this paper presents a series of related identities to those already established in the literature. These new identities can be viewed as extensions of a earlier investigated area by H. Conrey and A. Kumchev, relating Ramanujan's $L$-series to Dirichlet $L$-functions. The proposed identities are expressed by utilizing Gauss sums and elementary factors and can be verified through the application of character sums and Gauss sums.

Researchers examine the long-standing issue of heavy particle generation in the early universe's primordial soup. They recognize that these particles might still exist today, potentially leaving a distinctive signature on cosmic microwave background radiation. Furthermore, they propose a new background signal in gravitational wave detectors could be explained by these particles, leaving a specific imprint on the CMB in the process. Using existing data, they constrain the underlying theory at a level never before achieved. This research opens up the possibility of multivariate analyses to achieve more precise constraints.

Our research investigates the motion of helical swimmers in a viscous fluid near a flat surface, aided by force generated by impurity diffusion. We find that these swimmers exhibit an snowman-like phenomenon, where the surface has a significant impact, causing their motion to reverse and leading to the formation of a small-scale snowman-like structure. The model shows that the swimmers' speed can be influenced by the surface for a limited range, determined by their length and the strength of diffusion-based force. As this range is small, the surface has a minimal impact on longer swimmers. However, helical swimmers may be able to use the surface to increase their speed by up to ten times, which could benefit their effectiveness in tasks such as cleaning and mixing.

Our research investigates how the Hamming distance from Nash Equilibrium changes over time in co-evolutionary genetic algorithms, using both individual and social learning processes. We found that both learning methods converge to a Hamming distance of zero, but at significantly different rates. Additionally, we observed that the Hamming distance is generally smaller when using social learning. To further analyze these findings, we developed theoretical models to estimate the expected Hamming distance for individual and social learning, which yielded valuable insights into the learning processes.

The rapid dissemination of crisis information through social media during emergencies constitutes an increasing threat, causing users to rely heavily on misleading news due to the speed of its spread. Consequently, there's a pressing need to create automatic systems to identify vulnerable concepts that could be misused by malicious actors. These systems would alert administrators to potential threats, thereby enhancing overall network security. To address this challenge, we need to develop efficient methods for extracting security-relevant notions from textual content. Prior research has utilized Recurrent Neural Networks in this context but has primarily focused on simple classification tasks. In contrast, our innovative approach leverages Bidirectional LSTMs to capture the underlying relationships within massive datasets of textual data, demonstrating exceptional performance in critical applications like inference and link prediction.

To examine the dynamics of magnetic ordering within a spin glass system, we introduce a mixed opinion formation model that combines Ising spins and binary opinion holders. The model operates on a regular graph and allows for head-on interactions between Ising spins and binary opinion holders. The model also permits Ising spins to interact with other spins and opinion holders to change their opinions. The model is mathematically equivalent to the Bethe Ising model for spin glass, allowing us to derive exact equations for the magnetization and opinion distribution. By analyzing these equations, we find that the model exhibits phase transitions similar to those in the pure Ising model and explore the implications for spin glass dynamics.

We've developed an empirical model predicting the spread of COVID-19 infection 
through respiratory droplets, and we've tested it with verified case data from 
Seoul, South Korea, Shanghai, China, and Qom, Iran. The model accurately forecasts 
future infections and case peaks despite its simplicity. Analysis of the model 
reveals that the size of droplets plays a significant role in spreading the virus, 
along with weather conditions and human behavior. If left uncontrolled, the model 
indicates that COVID-19 could infect up to 4.2 million people in the United States 
and 1.7 million in Germany by the end of June. However, implementing non-pharmaceutical interventions as proposed by the World Health Organization can significantly reduce the number of predicted infections.

The convergence of neural networks in solving ill-posed problems and inverse ill-posed problems has long been observed, yet the underlying reason for this success has not been fully understood. Traditionally, experts relied on regularized methods or stochastic algorithms to train these networks. In this study, we explore the fundamental aspect of whether neural networks can solve ill-posed problems and inverse problems by means of a representation of signals in a higher-dimensional space, where the solutions are embedded within a manifold of dimension O(n^2) rather than a high-dimensional space itself. We utilized the Bergman diamond strategy to devise and evaluate multiple scenarios that test the ability of neural networks to overcome ill-posed problems and inverse problems. Our results show that these networks can indeed solve such problems without any regularization or stochastic optimization, and that traditional methods can be viewed as variants of the parameterization representation. We also provide theoretical evidence for the dimension of the manifold on which solutions to these problems are embedded.

This study examines a specific equality between the symbolic and ordinary power sets of oriented graph edge ideals, with a focus on weighted oriented graphs. The resulting equalities can be used to determine the depth and depth equality of these power sets, and may be applied to various subcategories of weighted oriented graphs. Additionally, new methods are developed for computing the depth and depth equality of weighted oriented graphs.

Using a recently introduced method for computing partition functions in a finite-N approximation, we extend our analysis to SU(N) and U(N) symmetries. By applying a similar approach, we derive the finite-N and large-N limits of the partition function for a given theory, finding that the finite-N result cannot be inferred from the large-N limit alone. Instead, we observe that the finite-N result can be modified by incorporating N-dependent corrections into the U(N) representation factor, effectively redeeming the partition function. This discovery holds significant implications for applying the SU(N) large-N limit to physically relevant U(N) theories.

This paper introduces a novel uniform sampling method for reducing data corruptions in neural networks, based on the concept of non-uniform data masking. We demonstrate that this method successfully mitigates silent data corruptions caused by hardware errors, resulting in a significant improvement in classification accuracy and the avoidance of inaccurate predictions due to data alterations. The proposed technique, achieved through the application of non-uniform masking, yields no additional computational overhead. Our results indicate that, compared to existing techniques, this method achieves greater than 3 times improvement in accuracy and a 20% reduction in misclassifications in our evaluated examples.

This paper introduces a novel parameterized complexity classification framework for graph algorithms that takes into account multiple optimization objectives. The proposed framework is demonstrated through a groundbreaking application in economic theory: finding the most efficient graph-based method for interbank settlements (netting). The parameters in this case are influenced by real-world data and serve as a basis for a concise and clear analysis of the complexity classifications. The study offers precise complexity classifications for various graph algorithms and reveals the significance of careful parameterization in graph algorithms. The research in economic theory is an original contribution that highlights the value of graph algorithms in realistic contexts.

We investigate the Jordanian twist's generalization, developing an explicit formula for it in the process. We demonstrate that this generalization's form mirrors that of the simple Jordanian twist, thereby reaffirming the 50-year-old conjecture of Bayen and Flato. Additionally, we derive the simple Jordanian twist from its generalized form, leading to a more direct understanding of the term'simple'.

We introduce a novel technique for language name identification that can also translate names into another language, multiple times, without needing a large dataset. Typically, machine translation and part-of-speech tagging rely on context from nearby words but we demonstrate that just having the word form is enough for low-resource languages. By doing this for each word individually, instead of assuming a specific order, we improve performance in low-resource language name tagging compared to previous methods. My work specifically addresses the challenge of naming entities in code-switched text. I develop a type of multi-task learning model that can perform both the word translation and naming tasks. I evaluate my approach on data sets for three code-switched languages: Hindi-English, Spanish-English, and Portuguese-English. I compare my results to a baseline model that uses context from nearby words to predict names and find that just having the word form is enough for better performance.

Our findings based on ALICE data reveal similarities in particle ratio trends across various collision systems from small to large scales. Specifically, we observed consistent trends in $K^./p$ and $p./K$ ratios as collision energy increased from 7.7 GeV to 13 TeV. These ratios exhibited energy and system dependence similar to those found for $K^+/p$ ratio. Furthermore, we discovered proportional increases in $K^./p$ and $p./K$ ratios with increasing atomic number in collisions across different energy spectra. These results can be understood through the freeze-out mechanism and the density of partonic systems, which has significant implications for interpreting data in future experiments.

The growth of available data does not directly translate to proportionate performance improvements for dialogue state tracking models, due in part to the presence of flawed labels. The issue is compounded by the limited amount of clean data, particularly in newly emerging domains. The presence of noisy labels affects not just the model's accuracy but also its reliability in real-world applications. The proposed approach, named Smart Data Augmentation, addresses these challenges by leveraging the capabilities of weakly supervised learning and the efficient use of data. The model employs a unique data processing technique that divides the cleaning process into two stages: initially removing the most noisy labels to focus training on a less noisy subset, and subsequently refining the model using the cleaned labels for an additional iteration. The experiment demonstrates that the proposed method achieves the best balance of accuracy and reliability on the Dialogstate '20 dataset, outperforming the baseline model in many evaluation metrics despite being trained with only partially clean data.

Inspired by the need to understand and improve urban development, researchers are beginning to study cities as living networks. These networks, composed of interconnecting districts, reflect the city's layout, economy, and social structure, and can provide valuable insights for planning and policy-making. In this study, we examine the spread of violent protests within a city by applying epidemiological models to different network topologies, including a real representation of Baghdad's connections from 2004 to 2007. Our findings indicate that the structure of Baghdad's connections, defined by its long-power-law distributed node degrees, contributed significantly to the rapid spread of unrest during that period. Specifically, the city's connectivity allowed protests to spread quickly, and our model showed that this level of disruption could have been mitigated by changing the distribution of node degrees to a shorter power-law curve. This effect was evident even when other network characteristics, such as the presence of clusters and centralization, were controlled for. Our research suggests that the high levels of violent unrest observed in Baghdad during the Iraq War and its impact on civic dynamics were influenced by the city's infrastructure and social structure.

Using the BASS/SPARKS sample of edge-on galaxies, we leverage the precision of star formation rate determinations through the Prospector framework by using a new observable, Br gamma luminosity, in a new, single-component model. We first test the consistency of this model with a set of control galaxies that have been thoroughly observed and studied, and then apply it to the entire BASS/SPARKS sample. Our model yields a high correlation with observed Br gamma luminosity and shows low scatter when compared to other star formation rate indicators. We also find that this model is more robust in low-metallicity environments. Additionally, we find a metallicity-scale mass profile for the gas phase and investigate the variability of the mass-to-light ratio in a way that hasn't been previously done. We use our model to calculate the mass of gas, stars, and total gravitational mass across the entire BASS/SPARKS sample, and provide these calculations along with the Br gamma luminosity and other derived star formation rate measurements in our catalog of predictions. These predictions can be validated or contradicted with observations or other modeling efforts as new data becomes available.

We provide a detailed analysis of the number of polynomials in a sum of squares decomposition over the real numbers. This involves identifying the maximum number of polynomials in such a decomposition for a given polynomial, as well as establishing connections to the rank of matrices within the Gram spectrahedron. These investigations are carried out using the tools of the real and complex Schur complements, drawing on principles from matrix near-decomposability and the study of positive semidefinite matrices. Additionally, our findings are compared to their counterparts in the context of nonnegative polynomials and unimodular polynomials.

To explore neutral long-lived particles at the LHC, the FASER experiment, located in the far-detector, considers the case of neutrino non-standard interactions which could significantly reduce the expected event counts. Conversely, such interactions might result in neutrino spectra alterations that could be detected by observing missing energy spectra in high-$p_T$ events. A an analytical approach to neutrino non-standard interactions is examined, focusing on the potential discovery in the FASER experiment, and it is found that it can surpass existing constraints on the CKM matrix's unitarity when $10^{12}$ neutrino interactions are detected, with a possible finding of neutrino non-unitarity at 95% confidence level in the context of existing neutrino data. Additionally, the most likely neutral long-lived particle in the LHC data, the one associated with R-parity violation in the context of a specific supersymmetric model, can be constrained by a factor of 10 more tightly than expected in the case where the ratio of neutrino and hadron interactions ratios is known.

Brzozowski's operator has been combined with complementation, which enables the symbolic evaluation of regular expression containment and inclusion checks. However, the Brzozowski operator's effectiveness is conditioned on the regularexpressions having distinct letter sets. To address this limitation for isomorphic letter sets, the paper introduces an modified Brzozowski operator that accommodates for congruence relations between regular expressions, including those with isomorphic letter sets. Additionally, the paper shows how this operator can be used to develop a symbolic decision procedure for containing and inclusion checks in regular expressions, specifically by combining it with the accepted regular expressions and checking the relation between the modified preimages.

Deep learning-based Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) models have successfully combined computer vision and inertial measurement unit data for accurate state estimation. Despite such advancements, a comprehensive comparison of these deep VIO models in various scenarios remains unexplored. Our comprehensive evaluation across five leading deep learning-based VIO models reveals their diverse architectures and showcases their strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, our analysis highlights significant variations in these models' performance in challenging scenarios, prompting recommendations for future improvements and state estimation best practices.

Our investigation focuses on the higher-order Weyl semimetals described by the Hamiltonian Hk, q, which incorporates multiple branches of Weyl nodes and higher-order terms. We are interested in systems where all Weyl nodes are equivalent and have the same Berry curvature, and we aim to determine if this situation allows for square-root topology in 3D materials. Our study shows that such systems can exhibit double-Weyl semimetallogy's hallmark, the nontrivial connection between paired Weyl nodes, but only locally. Therefore, this instance represents an exotic example of square-root topology. As a result, pair-Weyl nodes should act as sources and sinks for fermionic monopoles, and we propose that this relationship reflects itself in the topological invariants of a double-Weyl semmetal. Furthermore, we find that this model's square-root topology can be probed through square-root-like singularities in the spectral function, along with side bands related to the Weyl nodes and the dispersion of fermionic monopoles.

This study examines various finite element techniques for edge-based and face-based methods in the numerical solution of data completion problems, specifically recovery of functions and vector fields within a domain when certain values on the boundary are known. Our investigation compares the effectiveness of these methods in achieving the desired numerical solution. We first introduce a general framework for formulating the problem using mixed formulations that can be applied to both edge and face-based elements. Then, under certain assumptions, we establish the uniqueness of the solution for both finite element methods. Additionally, we derive conditions for the stability of these methods and provide evidence of their convergence to the desired solution. Our findings are demonstrated through explicit analysis of two and three-dimensional scenarios. Furthermore, we present theoretical bounds for the error measurement. We also present numerical examples illustrating the impact of element size on accuracy and highlighting the advantages of edge-based elements over face-based elements. Our research suggests that edge-based elements may offer better resolution, especially when facing ill-posed problems.

This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with the affine superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, for $n \geq 3$. We identify three generators - the zero mode algebra, Charish operators, and shifted vertex operators - that generate the vertex operator algebra. We establish the vertex operator algebra structure using the affine superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, drawing inspiration from similar structures seen in $osp(1|2)$. We outline the construction of the highest weight vertex operator algebra using integrable highest weight states from the affine superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$. Furthermore, we explore the extension of this construction to the affine superalgebra $osp(2|2n)$, revealing the vertex operator algebra structure for the simple irreducible modules $A_{2l}^{(1)}(k)$, $A_{2l+1}^{(1)}(k)$, and $D_{2l}^{(1)}(k)$.

This paper introduces an innovative approach that accelerates the student model's training by identifying and focusing on ambiguous areas. The proposed method involves employing the student model itself to determine the areas where the teacher and client datasets overlap the most, and prioritizing training on those sections. The new algorithm, called Salient Knowledge amalgamation, is an iterative process consisting of two phases: the first involves computing the salience and combining knowledge, and the second involves updating the student model through iterative self-correction. Theoretical and empirical analyses confirm that the proposed method achieves optimal results and significantly outperforms existing techniques.

Previous research suggested that grid cells, which form a key component of the brain's spatial coding system, generate robust, internally-generated patterns of activity in response to virtual navigation scenarios. In contrast, our findings indicate that external visual cues can significantly impact grid cell functionality, with oscillatory cellular activity shaped by local boundaries and virtually projected boundaries alike. This influence of visual cues is particularly evident when animals are subjected to changes in environmental lighting. Additionally, our data reveal that grid cells are in fact synchronized with other cellular populations within the entorhinal cortex through mechanisms of cellular communication, which are both local in nature and narrowly focused. Together, these insights contribute to a revised view of the brain's spatial coding system, with grid cells serving as an integral part of a broader network that integrates multiple cellular modules capable of simultaneous operation and interplay.

The development of stable magnetic cycles in low-rotation stars remains poorly understood. Recent research suggests that kinematic dynamos play a major role in creating cycle persistence in these stars. A computational model using the magnetic grid technique has been developed to simulate nonlinear, rotational magnetoconvection dynamos in star layers. The model was applied to a two-dimensional space and an artificially reduced rotation rate in a radiation-driven model. The simulations showed how magnetic cycles could emerge from weakly nonlinear interactions between convection bubbles in the star's outer layers. A cyclical pattern appeared when the model included spatially extended magnetic structures and turbulent transport, despite the artificial rotation being less than required for supercritical symmetry breaking. This finding suggests that stars with moderate rotations and extensive magnetic structures may easily develop cycle persistence, supporting the idea that kinematic dynamos play a significant role in creating cycle persistence in these stars.

We examine a particular type of S4 quartic field extension with four real roots,
where $\phi$ is a Galois friend of the form $x^4m^2=x^4m$ with m being a positive
integer. We investigate all possible $\phi$ extensions that have a specific form,
namely $\phi_{4,2}=\Phi_{4,2}$, where this Galois extension has a base field of
$\mathbb{Q}$ and is described by the equation $x^4-u^2=x^2$. Our research aims
to analyze the rational points on various elliptic curves, particularly those in
$\Phi_{4,2}(\sqrt{m})$, and and determine how their ranks are determined by $m$.
We provide a condition under which all $m$ will have a rank of 1 on these elliptic
curves, and further provide a vast majority of cases where $\Phi_{4,2}$ will be
enough to gain a rank of 1 for multiple elliptic curves, including those described
by curves of Néron diagrams shaped like $A_1^{(1,0)}$, $A_1^{(1,1)}$, $A_2^{(2,0)}$,
$A_3^{(3,0)}$, $S_3^{(3,1)}$, $C_4^{(4,0)}$, $C

We examine the heat and entropy production in a system that undergoes lattice inflation, Wigner rotation, and sudden changes in coupling and Hamiltonian, using both exact and approximate calculations to analyze the total system-irreversible entropy, heat, and temperature. Specifically, we investigate different entropy measures, including the linear entropy, von Neumann entropy, and total system-irreversible entropy, deriving expressions that demonstrate the relationship between these quantities and heat, entropy, and temperature during the process. We also determine the time-to-equilibrium for the linear entropy and total system-irreversible entropy, and observe that the scale-inflation process results in an infinitely long equilibration time for the total system-irreversible entropy. Furthermore, we compare our findings for the lattice-inflation process to those for the Wigner-rotation and coupling processes, and discuss the practical implications of using the linear entropy as a proxy for the total system-irreversible entropy.

We investigate the time it takes for a combined system and environment to lose distinguishability from a given state, examining both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary evolution, we find that this time correlates with the rate at which the system's state changes, as indicated by the system's trace decay or its entanglement with the environment. We also identify that this time is linked to the minimum time required for two states to become distinguishable under unitary evolution. In non-unitary dynamics, we determine that this time still limits the rate at which the system's state changes, as constrained by the Lindblad equation, and further establishes that it cannot be smaller than the inverse of the system's decay rate. Furthermore, we specify that this time becomes infinite in the limit of strong system-environment coupling, and determine that it is connected to the time it takes for the system's state to become mixed under this type of evolution.

We examine the existence of a nondegenerate regular simplex within the unit cube $Q_n$, with reference to an $n$-dimensional system defined by linear equations. The simplex will not be unique if it exists; therefore, we seek a specific simplex for our analysis. Assuming the number of interpolation nodes exceeds the smallest possible quantity of $n+2$, we can establish an upper limit for the number of nodes within any particular facet of the simplex. Furthermore, we can demonstrate that if the number of nodes exceeds $n+3$, the simplex cannot be nondegenerate.

We examined the carrier concentration in etched silicon, a critical component for
high-temperature Hall sensors, and discovered its significant impact. Two distinct
etching methods were investigated: buffer oxide etching and etching with a silicon
etchant. The results showed that the former yields a much higher carrier concentration
at 500°C, 25 times greater than the latter, with a concomitant increase in
resistivity. The increased carrier concentration in the former is attributed to the
presence of iron impurities, which are partially active at this temperature. As a
result, the sensor based on the etched silicon exhibits a significant Hall effect,
considerably increased signal-to-noise ratio, allowing for accurate measurements
at 500°C.

This study combines the principles of cdh descent and Milnor excision with the multiplicative formalism of twisted homotopy K-theory, ultimately leading to the derivation of a cdh-invariant form of Gelfand-MacPherson's twisted homotopy K-theory formula. As a result, we obtain an expression for the twisted homotopy K-theory of a scheme in terms of its cdh-sites of support, given that the scheme has a cdh cover in the form of an étale, finitely presented scheme over a finite extension of the rational numbers.

The evolution of an planet's atmosphere is intricately linked to its internal structure and the gravitational interactions between worlds. For temperate, long-lasting systems like the Earth, a plausible internal-atmospheric feedback loop likely drove evolutionary pathways. This feedback loop, fueled by the release of heat and volatiles from within the planet as it cooled, may have triggered periodic explosions of atmospheric gases, pulsing out volatiles and gases that cycled between the interior and exterior. This paper explores the possibility of such an internal-atmospheric feedback loop existing within exoplanetary systems, particularly those similar to the Earth-Uranus system, and examines its implications for the formation and evolution of planetary atmospheres.

A computational study employs a range of methods to thoroughly examine
1,2-diphosphatidylglycerol (1,2-PDO) and 1,3-diphosphatidylglycerol (1,3-PDO)
molecules within a soybean phospholipase C (SpcC1) enzyme environment.
Previously, an investigation of these molecules used a simple method but was
defective in treating certain aspects of electron interactions; the current study
redresses this shortcoming for 1,2-PDO but faces a complication in treating
the entire 1,3-PDO system due to technical limitations.
In contrast, an improved approach is used for 1,2-PDO but the results raise
more questions about the enzyme's reaction mechanism.

Our work investigates the concept of translating tensor network algorithms into the language of parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs). By doing so, we aim to combine the precise control offered by tensor networks with the easy scalability of PQCs. Specifically, we show that major tensor network algorithms, including multi-scale entropy-based ansatz and the decomposition of Hamiltonians using tensor networks, can be efficiently converted into corresponding PQCs. Furthermore, we outline strategies for transforming tensor network algorithms into those utilizing quantum circuit learning, an even more versatile category of algorithms. Using a case study with a Hamiltonian simulation, we demonstrate the practical applicability of our approach, showcasing significant improvements in task performance when our method is employed.

Cancer research utilizes Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to distinguish between tumor and normal tissue representations through learning robust features from anatomical MRI and CT images. Creating accurate training data is crucial for this method. Unfortunately, collecting extensive, high-quality annotation data is costly due to imaging guidance required for precise tumor segmentation. This paper proposes a novel approach that reduces the need for extensive annotation data. It combines self-segmentation techniques with a class imbalance correction method, allowing for training and evaluation of GNN models using only tumor annotations. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance on multiple public datasets, outperforming current standards and achieving impressive results with limited annotations. Notably, it surpasses state-of-the-art performance on the CAMEL dataset despite being trained with only tumor annotations, a significant class imbalance.

This paper explores a new type of linear Hawkes process that extends the standard linear model, enabling the capture of interactions via external sources, a phenomenon observed in various multivariate point processes, including network-based events and financial transaction times. A novel, efficient Monte Carlo method is developed for recovering the parameters of this complex Hawkes model, although the algorithm's consistency is previously established. A new result is proven to add to the algorithm's effectiveness: under specific conditions, the Monte Carlo estimate of the parameter vector converges to the same distribution as the conventional maximum likelihood estimator. This research is accompanied by realistic simulations addressing publication bias in Hawkes parameter estimates and an empirical analysis of actual transaction times.

We have developed a comprehensive linearized Bessel and spherical harmonic
approximation to the fast multipole method, enabling its application to
high-performance computational simulations of gravitational interactions in
astrophysical systems. By leveraging this implementation, we have conducted a
key evaluation of the algorithm's performance and sensitivity to various
parameters, particularly relevant to the computation of gravitational effects in
systems of oscillating, self-gravitating spheres consisting of multiple
non-osculating objects. Our findings demonstrate the significance of accurately
precalculating trigonometric functions and polynomial evaluations, as well as
the optimal selection of FMM parameters, which significantly influence the
efficiency of the computation. Ultimately, our study reveals that the most
time-efficient solution is achieved when the radius of the multipole radius is
approximately equal to the square root of two times the number of local
interactions, and that this optimal value can be viewed as a universal
benchmark for similar applications. By addressing the limitations of existing FMM
algorithms and offering a more efficient alternative, we hope to provide a
valuable reference for researchers and scientists working on complex computational
astrophysical simulations in the future.

Cross-domain adaptation is a key issue in medical image segmentation, where there is a significant anatomical difference between source and target domains. This challenge is compounded by the limited availability of labeled target domain images. This paper introduces a new method for semi-supervised cross-anatomy domain adaptation, called Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross-Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA). To achieve adaptation across different anatomies, CS-CADA incorporates a cross-domain projection module that uses contrastive learning to reduce the gap between source and target domains. This method enhances robustness and helps overcome the limited target domain data constraint. In the target domain, CS-CADA employs a semi-supervised learning approach that leverages both labeled target images and the cross-domain adapted source images to improve segmentation accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that CS-CADA yields a highly effective approach for semi-supervised cross-anatomy domain adaptation and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on two complex medical segmentation tasks, specifically renal cortex segmentation and liver/lesion segmentation from abdominal computed tomography scans.

To comprehend 4D supersymmetric gravity, we suggest transforming it into a non-gravitational model via a change of variables, which would seemingly compromise the implementation of BRS symmetry. In this research, we demonstrate that by employing an appropriate modification of the Legendre transformation, BRS symmetry can be maintained and therefore we re-establish the connection between the original and transformed models, thus upholding the concept of BRS cohomology. The proposed approach facilitates a proper understanding of 4D supersymmetric gravity and allows for the interpretation of the non-gravitational model as the original gravity model. This is made feasible by our previous proof that the BRS operator contains the gravitational field when acting on the non-gravitational model.

In a stellarator, a plasma waveplate can be generated by applying a non-uniform magnetic field to a specific area of the device, potentially allowing for the conversion of circularly polarized heating waves to linearly polarized ones. Determining the optimal thickness of the waveplate is crucial, as it depends on the specific properties of the plasma, particularly its electron density and the strength of the magnetic field, in accordance with the specific behavior of plasma waves. A part of this research involves developing a method for automatically determining the waveplate thickness through the solution of a Laplace equation. Additionally, this study demonstrates the effective implementation of the proposed method in a specific stellarator configuration. The results show that even in a scenario where the rotation frequency of the plasma waveplate does not match the frequency of the heating waves, the waveplate can still effectively convert the waves, as demonstrated in a simulation.

We investigate how the Standard Model can be expanded through a two-Higgs doublet model with a specific variation, known as the type-II scenario, to address the discrepancy in the muon anomalous magnetic moment and to explore the potential for a significant electric dipole moment in the tau lepton. Our analysis indicates that, in order to attain a tau electric dipole moment of the order of $10^{-26}$ $e\,\mathrm{cm}$, which is on the order of the sensitivity that is on the horizon for current and future experiments, it is necessary to incorporate an extra dimensionless parameter in the type-II two-Higgs doublet model that is of the order of $0.1$. This parameter has the potential to contribute to $\Delta \epsilon$ which is responsible for the discrepancy in the muon anomalous magnetic moment, of the order of $16 \times 10^{-10)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in this model it is possible to avoid too significant of an electric dipole moment for the neutron and proton, and that it is also in line with the constraints of $B$ physics.

Rank metric codes have garnered significant interest due to their versatile properties and versatile applications. Often, these codes exhibit significant error correction capabilities, but if the error rate approaches half, they can become unreliable. A recent study revealed that certain rank metric codes can maintain a high level of accuracy even in high error rates. This paper builds on that research, presenting a novel decoding algorithm that expands the code's usable range for rates above half. The author demonstrates that with this new method, a specific type of Reed-Solomon code can accurately decode messages even in error rates of up to 0.9. Furthermore, the author shows that this new algorithm enhances the code's performance in comparison to conventional decoding methods.

The structure of conformal block operators in two-dimensional conformal field theory can be examined through a change of variable that relates them to operators in AdS space. Specifically, this ad hoc method can be used to explore the operator product expansion (OPE) blocks generated by conserved currents in CFT$_2$, and to compare their representations to those obtained using AdS$_3$ and AdS$_2$ geodesic operators. It has been found that the AdS$_3$ geodesic operator representations match the standard CFT OPE block forms, whereas the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representations yield novel, semi-classical limit applicable to certain four-point functions involving the stress-tensor, for which the standard CFT OPE decomposition holds, showing the precise relationship between the two. Furthermore, this method allows for the derivation of mass and diameter parameters, previously defined through semi-classical AdS$_2$ boundary value problems, and demonstrates the conservation of these parameters in the OPE, and also reveals an AdS$_2$ geodesic operator contribution in the OPE of general massless conserved current OPE blocks in CFT$_2$.

Using the HALO collaboration's data, we compare various methods for reconstructing galaxy mappings, including traditional and neural network approaches. Our analysis indicates that neural networks demonstrate superior results and that a specific method, which we introduce as the Analytic Neural Network, yields the most accurate performances. The ANN employs an analytic estimator and incorporates massive neural networks with multi-layer perceptron layers, achieving a high accuracy of 2.17 $\mu$K at a spatial frequency of 0.5 $h^{-1}$ Mpc. The ANN's performance surpasses traditional methods, such as the Harvenge estimator, by a factor of approximately two-and-a-half.

This paper discusses recent works of Gelfand and MacPherson, who have been exploring combinatorial differential manifolds through a combination of their earlier findings. In particular, Gelfand and MacPherson have shown that every combinatorial differential manifold is essentially a geometric object derived from a simple combinatorial object called a flag complex, which can be constructed by applying a differentiable projection to a higher-dimensional space. They have also established that the properties of this flag complex can be used to derive information about the original combinatorial differential manifold. Furthermore, they have demonstrated that several fundamental geometric properties, including dimension, connectivity, and topological characteristics, are preserved in this construction. However, they found that other properties, such as whether a manifold is fillable or not, are not necessarily preserved. Interestingly, they observed that combinatorial differential manifolds share similarities with another type of geometric object called a polyhedral manifold.

We performed high-resolution spectroscopy of the young stellar system N159F2,
within 20,000 years from which the stellar content has derived the elemental
abundances of multiple elements including nickel, iron, silicon, and oxygen.
Specifically, we analyzed pre-explosion spectra from 2013 and post-explosion
spectra from 2020, and obtained data from the VLT/UVES, VLT/XShID, and the
ESO/FLI at the La Silla and the APO/Garcia at the National Solar Observatory
in New Mexico. Our analysis of SN~2020jfo showed a high ratio of nickel to iron
about five times the solar ratio, indicating a supernova explosion with a
significant neutron-star component. This is consistent with the absence of
hydrogen and helium lines in the spectra and with spectral similarities to V838
Monore and AT2019tore. Further analysis suggested that the explosion occurred
within a compact area about 0.1 parsecs in diameter, and that the new star
was at a distance of about 5,500 parsecs from the galactic plane, based on its
line width and metal content.

A lobster-eye optics system can be divided into four equal parts, each responsible for detecting polarization properties in a specific direction. Here, we present a novel idea where a cross-like image is used, and by rotating it, we can determine the direction of detection. Specifically, we show that rotating the cross by 45 degrees allows us to identify which part of the optics system is detecting polarization properties. Additionally, we propose using two types of cross-like images, one rotated 45 degrees and another rotated 135 degrees, to determine the detection direction. Here, we derive the mathematical relationship between the rotation angle of the cross and the detection direction. Finally, we examine two methods of retrieving original image information from a distorted cross-like image, namely Wiener deconvolution and Bayesian estimation, and apply these to our specific case.

We employ level set methods in conjunction with technique adaptations from first order equations to analyze second order fully nonlinear partial differential equations. Our approach enables us to investigate solutions with smooth boundaries and certain discontinuous solutions for equations involving maximum and uniform continuity operators.

Using highly resolved $N$-body simulations within a massive box of $10^4$ times the critical density, we evaluate the impact of using density-only models on halo mass prediction accuracy.  Focusing on the $z=1$ era and identifying 300,000 halos with $M\ge10^{10}M_{\earth}$ within our simulations, we power-law fit the mass function and find it to be $dN/dM \propto M^{\alpha} dM$, where $\alpha$ equals $-0.93\pm0.02$ regardless of the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations.  However, we discover a significant discrepancy in the accuracy of halo mass predictions, particularly at the smaller end, where structure has begun to form.  Using an exact solution to describe the evolution of a given mass spectrum under expanding scales, we determine the mass scale at which matter starts to fragment into distinct structures, and from this we can estimate the mass of the first generated halos.  We find that in our simulations, structure begins to form around the mass scale $M_{struct}\approx 10^{7.5}M_{\earth}$, and that this mass scale is directly proportional to the inverse power of the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations.  Therefore, we find that in our simulations where $n_s=0.96$ (or $\Psi\approx 0.80$) and $A\approx

This study introduces a semi-supervised Convolutional Neural Matrix Factorization (CNMF) method for piano transcription. Unlike standard CNMF and its deep learning equivalents, our method is designed to incorporate limited labeled data. We utilize a sparse correlation model, combining its efficiency and effectiveness, and apply non-negative matrix factorization to analyze acoustic features of piano recordings. A neighborhood model with a low-rank factorization is developed to represent local piano sounds and their co-articulations. We minimize the gap between observed factors and their representations through a CNMF objective function, which is optimized using Alternating Least Squares. To leverage labeled data, a distance-based loss is defined and incorporated into the CNMF objective function. Our semi-supervised CNMF (ssCNMF) is evaluated on the MaEst dataset, demonstrating superior results compared to state-of-the-art low-rank factorization techniques and supervised deep learning methods for piano transcription. The code is available online for replication purposes.

This research introduces a novel approach to assigning properties like mass, angular momentum, and flux to individual fluid elements within stars that rotate. Unlike conventional methods, this approach bypasses the utilization of corotational coordinates. Instead, an average value is used for the mass and angular momentum of each element, based on its contribution to the overall stellar mass and angular momentum. The method incorporates an average specific angular momentum and a mean specific mass for each element, making it suitable for rotating stars. The research demonstrates that utilizing these average values results in established conservation principles for angular momentum, mass, and energy within the star. The proposed method extends the applicability of traditional one-dimensional hydrodynamic techniques to rotating stars.

Using a limited amount of selectively labeled data efficiently is crucial for the effective deployment of machine learning models. Another important consideration is making the modeling process transparent and interpretable. A proposed new method, called Selective Labeling with Latent Differential Privacy, efficiently utilizes high-quality labeled data and leverages the simplicity of linear models by addressing the challenge of selective labeling. The method ensures the consistency of the learning algorithm under various noise conditions and maintains the privacy of the labeling process. Additionally, a proposed new metric measures the difference between the accuracy of a machine learning model and its average performance across different labeling probabilities. The method is further evaluated in a simulated environment and with real-world data, incorporating a well-known image recognition dataset.

The concurrent observation of gravitational, electromagnetic, and high-energy radiation in neutron star mergers significantly boosts the confidence in their association. The exceptional detection potential of NSMs in the Galactic population lies within their electromagnetic and high-energy radiation, making it crucial to differentiate them from other transient events. The global network of gamma-ray telescopes and the rising number of electromagnetic survey telescopes soon to be operational enhances the chances of detecting SGRBs and their mergers. Nonetheless, the difficulty remains in identifying gravitational waves from low-luminosity events or those occurring too far from Earth to be visible to the network of gamma-ray telescopes. Nonetheless, the potential for multi-messenger discoveries in the coming era of third-generation gravitational wave detectors and the impending initiation of electromagnetic survey mode in LIGO makes it imperative to have automated methods for identifying potential NSM sources within gravitational wave candidate data sets. This study presents an enhanced iterative method for identifying candidate neutron star mergers within gravitational wave data by leveraging the characteristics of corresponding electromagnetic and high-energy radiation transients. This new method surpasses previous approaches by incorporating the characteristics of electromagnetic transients associated with low-luminosity GRBs and incorporating probability calculations based on the availability and field-of-view of observational telescopes.

The understanding of social determinants of health can be elevated by
extracting information from clinical notes. These notes, typically written by
physicians, contain valuable data on patients' social circumstances, which can
be used to tailor disease prevention and treatment. For instance, knowing that
a patient lives in a homeless shelter can help prevent the spread of infectious
